The steady ensuing wave of studies since then have resulted in the elevation of this tribe and its sister into families, the descriptions of 16 new genera, and ~70 new species (within just the Carphodactylidae and the insular radiations of the Diplodactylidae) with many more awaiting description. The good Dr. Bauer has played a major role in most of these changes, and we will discuss the history and trajectory of these taxonomic shifts. I will also highlight some unique biological traits of these taxa that have served as careerlong curiosities for Dr. Bauer (and myself), particularly the evolution of exceptional tail morphologies—from adhesive surfaces to defensive glands, demonstrating that these taxa remain fertile ground for future research. Emme Nix
1055: The late Cretaceous fossil Konkasaurus mahalana is the oldest known Madagascan lizard, the oldest known Gondwanan scincoid, and possibly the earliest crown-group cordyliform. Represented by a series of cranial and postcranial bones and osteoderms, it was tentatively assigned to the girdled lizards (Cordylidae), although its evolutionary affinities have never been tested in a phylogenetic framework. The dearth of crown-group scincoid fossils means that Konkasaurus has been widely used as a calibration point in squamate evolutionary studies, despite this phylogenetic uncertainty. This study re-examines the holotype and new material using micro-CT, allowing new skeletal elements to be digitally reconstructed and scored for phylogenetic and quantitative analyses. We incorporated Konkasaurus into a large morphological-molecular dataset and compared its osteoderm and mandibular shape with a broad sample of living scincoids using morphometrics. Our phylogenetic and morphometric results consistently support Konkasaurus as a member of the Plated Lizards (Gerrhosauridae) and specifically place it within the Madagascan subfamily Zonosaurinae. Reclassifying Konkasaurus as a crown-group gerrhosaurid has major biogeographic and phylogenetic implications. It extends the minimum age of gerrhosaurid radiation back to the Late Cretaceous and implies that the family colonized Madagascar once, before 66 Ma. This is significantly later than the breakup of Gondwana and supports a hypothesis of over-water dispersal, making Konkasaurus the earliest known terrestrial vertebrate colonizers of Madagascar from Africa. Riley Stanton
1056: Adaptive radiation is often characterized by rapid species and/or phenotypic diversification into distinct ecological niches. One such radiation is the species rich group of Anolis lizards found across the Greater Antillean Islands. These lizards have independently evolved into various morphological specialist, deemed “ecomorphs”, which exploit distinct microhabitat structural supports, such as twigs and tree trunks. However, little is known about the patterns of covariation among morphological traits and the rates of trait evolution through the lens of trait modularity and integration. A key prediction of the modular evolvability hypothesis is that traits in more modular clades will demonstrate greater variation attributable to their independence. Determining the level of trait modularity, amongst morphological traits, and the rate of evolution of those modules can allow us to glean insights relating to how trait diversification proceeded during the adaptive radiation of Anolis lizards. Lindsay K. Bomgardner Lindsay Bomgardner; Paul Grammer; Michael Andres; Anna Millender; Jeremy Higgs; Jennifer Green; Christopher
1057: The Dunes Sagebrush Lizard (Sceloporus arenicolus) is federally listed as Endangered under the ESA and is a habitat specialist endemic to the shinnery oak-sand dune ecosystem of southeastern New Mexico and Texas. Their populations are threatened by continued habitat fragmentation and destruction associated with oil and gas mining. Previous studies have delineated ten genetically distinctive conservation units that correspond with geographic breaks in suitable habitat. Effective management in the face of habitat loss and fragmentation requires further assessment of these units as well as a better understanding of the evolutionary uniqueness of each including historical demographics and patterns of local adaptation. We use a recently constructed reference genome for the Dunes Sagebrush Lizard to analyze whole-genome resequencing of 100 individuals throughout the range. We reevaluate genetic groups, reconstruct recent evolutionary history, and estimate historical demographic parameters. In addition to underscoring the value of genomic data in conservation, these results add to our understanding of this species and the evolution of habitat specialists more broadly. Houston Chandler
1058: Like most North American whiptails (genus Aspidoscelis), the parthenogenetic Dixon’s whiptail lizard (A. dixoni) has a confusing taxonomic history, and it is considered a distinct form of the more widelydistributed A. tesselatus rather than its own species. Using haplotype-resolved reference genomes from both A. dixoni and A. tesselatus, we analyzed population-scale ddRADseq data to understand the evolutionary history of parthenogenesis in this complex and to address whether tesselatus and dixoni should be distinct species. We found that there is effectively a single origin of parthenogenesis in tesselatus/dixoni that originated in the late Pleistocene, with dixoni as its own unit within tesselatus that arose approximately 25,000 years ago as a result of post-formation mutation. These findings highlight the confusing nature of naming parthenogenetic species - is Aspidoscelis dixoni a species, or not? Matthew Fujita
1059: Islands have long been viewed as evolutionary laboratories by ecologists and evolutionary biologists. Species that colonized islands therefore tend to be welcomed by an environment which lacks interspecific competitors and predators they encountered on mainland, but over time, faced with increasing intraspecific competitions. With these processes acting on the islands, together with the prolonged isolation, species that inhabit them tend to show marked differences with their mainland relatives. On a longer evolutionary time scale, these differences could show up as elevated rate of diversification and morphological traits for island taxa. Here, we will use one of the most complete, in terms of number of species included, gecko phylogeny to date to test whether colonizing islands will confer species with a higher rate of diversification and morphological traits. Among its 2450 or so species, almost 40% of gecko species have its range confined exclusively to, or have its range extended to islands, making it an ideal system to study island evolution. We will perform GeoHiSSE model in RevBayes to compare diversification rate between island and mainland clades. We will also estimate tip rates using MiSSE model and identify rate shifts using R package RRphylo, and check if these rate shifts correspond to island colonization. Finally, we will test the rate of morphological evolution on islands using morphometric data, using R package OUwie and others. Preliminary results show that the diversification rate does not differ between island and mainland taxa. Baian Lin
1060: Lizard scales vary in size, both within and across species, and the variation they exhibit often appears related to the environment in which they are found, suggesting an important functional role. The heat sink hypothesis proposes that scales help to dissipate excess heat and predicts that lizards in warmer environments should evolve larger scales to increase skin surface area and aid in thermoregulatory cooling. The interstitial skin hypothesis posits that moisture is lost via the thin skin between individual scales. Accordingly, large scales should mitigate such loss by reducing exposed interstitial skin, leading to selection for larger scales in arid environments. Although these hypotheses have been tested several times, there is no consensus on which best predicts observed patterns of lizard scale evolution. We reexamine these hypotheses by investigating the evolution of scale size across broad climatic gradients within 3 widespread Anolis lizard species. Surprisingly, two of these species – those with the broadest climatic ranges – evolved large scales at both warm and cool temperature extremes, a pattern not anticipated by existing models. We thus propose a generalized “heat exchange hypothesis” in which large scales may facilitate both heat loss in warm settings, and heat gain in cool ones, via behavioral thermoregulation. Our results suggest scale size indeed evolves as a function of temperature in lizards, but non-linearly, particularly in species inhabiting a wide range of temperatures. Alicia Mathis
1061: Limb reduction has evolved independently at least 25 times across squamate lineages. Squamate species that convergently evolved varying degrees of limblessness also commonly share additional morphological features that are interpreted as adaptations for a burrowing lifestyle such as reduced eyes, smooth scales, reduced or absent ear openings, and reduced jaws. These latter adaptations are presumed to be associated with reduced visual and auditory abilities. However, as these animals engage in hunting and mate-seeking, they must have a way to obtain long-distance sensory information. This study hypothesized olfactory capabilities would be enhanced in species for which other senses were reduced, i.e. burrowing species. This study utilized computed tomography scans to obtain 3-D models of brain endocasts from squamate species with varying degrees of fossoriality to investigate whether a correlation exists between burrowing activity and olfactory bulb size. Using olfactory bulb size as a proxy for olfactory acuity, we measured the ratio of olfactory bulb size relative to whole brain length. Squamate species with more fossorial behavior were found to have relatively large olfactory bulbs and none had small olfactory bulbs. Assuming that a larger olfactory bulb relative to whole brain size is indicative of enhanced olfaction, we can then infer that fossorial species of limbless lizards do indeed have enhanced olfactory capabilities. It was also found that extinct fossorial lizards had smaller olfactory bulbs than their extant relatives, suggesting an increase in olfactory acuity over the course of evolution. These results indicate that in addition to dramatic morphological changes, fossorial species exhibit changes to their sensory systems. Tyler Muller
1062: Biological invasions offer an opportunity to observe evolution across contemporary timescales as populations confront novel selective pressures. The Italian wall lizard (Podarcis siculus), introduced to Long Island in the 1960s, has established populations across Long Island and New York City. To examine how genomic variation has changed during this invasion, we analyzed whole-genome resequencing data from 91 individuals sampled from four populations at two time points spanning 20 years, including 44 individuals collected in 2005 and 47 collected in 2025. Genomic change through time was not uniform among populations. Genetic diversity declined, but the magnitude of loss varied by population. We also found increases through time in the proportion of the genome contained within runs of homozygosity (ROH), along with population-specific shifts in ROH length distributions, indicating continued demographic change after establishment. Analyses of structure and differentiation demonstrated that, even approximately 40 years after establishment, populations were not at equilibrium and became more differentiated over time. Genome scans identified loci associated with both spatial and temporal axes of environmental variation, with overlap between candidate sets across time and space. These results suggest that shared selective pressures in the invasive range have produced rapid parallel genomic responses, even as populations continue to diverge through local processes. These findings show that substantial adaptive change can occur over fewer than 20 generations despite declining diversity and ongoing demographic instability, highlighting the dynamic interplay of selection and drift during contemporary microevolution in novel environments Grace Solevilla-Moreno
1063: Urban environments impose novel selective pressures that can shape morphology and behavior in species that occupy human-modified habitats. In this study, we examine two urban-adapted gecko species, Tarentola mauritanica and Hemidactylus turcicus, to investigate how urbanization influences phenotypic variation across both native and introduced ranges. We measure morphological traits and behavioral responses, including flight initiation distance and post-capture behavior, across populations spanning an urbanization gradient. Fieldwork was conducted in each species’ native range as well as in urban introduced populations, allowing us to compare patterns across anthropogenic contexts, introduction history, and species. We find significant differences in morphology associated with urbanization and between native and introduced populations. These results suggest that urban environments may drive phenotypic divergence, with responses varying by species and introduction history. Jacqueline Wilson
1064: <span lang="EN-US" style="font-size: 12.0pt; line-height: 115%; font-family: 'Aptos',sans-serif; mso-ascii-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: Aptos; mso-fareast-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-hansitheme-font: minor-latin; mso-bidi-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-bidi; mso-ansilanguage: EN-US; mso-fareast-language: EN-US; mso-bidi-language: AR-SA;">Extreme thermal events (ETEs) have changed notably within South Carolina (SC) estuarine systems, with marine heatwaves (MHWs) increasing and marine cold spells (MCSs) decreasing from 1983-2024. These events exhibit substantial seasonal and spatial variability, exposing fish to extreme temperatures capable of lethal and sublethal impacts throughout the year. Despite these concerns, localized studies linking ETE characteristics to biological responses remain limited because they require long-term, fine-scale environmental and fisheries datasets. To address this gap, we integrated long-term water temperature records with fishery-independent surveys to evaluate associations between ETE metrics and estuarine finfish abundance across coastal SC. SC estuaries support several economically and ecologically important species – including red drum, southern flounder, and spotted seatrout – which face both heavy recreational fishing pressure and exposure to environmental stressors that may compound population-level effects. Of the three focal species, only spotted seatrout exhibited a clear relationship with ETEs, as catch per unit effort (CPUE) declined with increasing accumulated exposure to cold extremes. Associations for red drum and southern flounder were weak or inconclusive. These findings suggest MCS exposure may be an important driver of spotted seatrout dynamics and demonstrate how integrating climate extremes into fisheries assessments can inform adaptive, temperature-based management strategies as ETE characteristics continue to change under future climate conditions. Brooke Bodensteiner
1065: The Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata) is a small, freshwater turtle listed as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need in all 21 State Wildlife Action Plans in which it occurs. Reports suggest populations are declining range-wide due to habitat loss, illegal collection, and other anthropogenic stressors. The 2022 Eastern Spotted Turtle Status Assessment and Conservation plan identified the southeastern U.S. as a data deficient region. In response, the Southeastern Spotted Turtle Working Group was formed and in 2023 received funding from a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Competitive State Wildlife Grant to enhance knowledge and conservation capacity for Spotted Turtles from West Virginia to Florida. Our goals included surveying suitable habitats without recent Spotted Turtle records, conducting population viability analyses, improving survey methods, providing technical assistance to stakeholders, restoring habitat, and engaging law enforcement to reduce illegal collection of turtles. From 2024– 2025, we surveyed 130 sites, performing 7,253 trap nights and 651 visual encounter surveys. Our efforts resulted in 12 new populations discovered, 823 unique captures, and 488 recapture events. Catch per unit effort was 0.16 for trapping and 0.24 per visual survey across all states. During 2026, we will continue to expand our survey efforts, create population viability models, and assess the efficacy of eDNA sampling for Spotted Turtle in the southeast. This work will culminate in a region-specific conservation plan for Spotted Turtles. Caden Comsa (They/He)
1066: The fishesoftexas.org website and its underlying data has been evolving for more than two decades with varied institutional support, but recent application of Artificial Intelligence allowed quick implementation of major improvements, as well as expansion of the website and data across a broader geography that extends well beyond Texas into adjacent northern Mexico. We will briefly review the history and evolution of the project and provide an overview of how it can be used to explore historic records of fish occurrences and related content about fishes of the region in ways that are relevant for diverse research and conservation applications. Jessica Henry Jessica Henry; Janelle Deneau; Parker Gibbons; Micheal Skibsted; Barney Hall; Tom Pop; Zachary Siders; Andrew
1067: Antipredator behavior of darters in streams polluted with heavy metals: Heavy metal pollution resulting from mining wastes can contaminate streams decades after mining activities have ceased. Although many species are unable to persist in metal-contaminated areas, some species can tolerate at least some degree of exposure. Even so, sub-lethal effects might still have negative impacts that ultimately influence populations. We conducted two studies examining antipredator behavior of Orangethroat Darters (Etheostoma spectabile) that occur in metal-contaminated streams in the Tri-State Mining district, where metal levels continue to be elevated despite remediation efforts. Previous research demonstrated that darters from uncontaminated streams produce chemical alarm cues that warn nearby conspecifics of predation-related threats. In our laboratory trials, darters from a heavily polluted site were less active overall than darters from a more moderately polluted site, but darters from both sites produced and responded to alarm cues with appropriate fright behavior. In field trials, we observed darters in contaminated and reference streams while snorkeling and recorded how individuals responded to the threat of an approaching predator. Darters from heavily and moderately polluted streams showed a reduced tendency to flee relative to darters from the uncontaminated reference stream. Studies of free-living individuals are relatively rare in toxicological studies. Although data from these correlational studies could be due to either direct or indirect factors, the results indicate that nonlethal effects of mining activities can be present even for fishes that are able to persist in contaminated habitats. Hope Matteson
1068: Swamp eels native to SE Asia were introduced to Florida, USA and established in the Greater Miami and Greater Tampa areas by 1997. We conducted extensive field sampling in the Greater Orlando area, where swamp eels had previously not been collected, with emphasis on the middle and lower St. Johns River and the Upper Kissimmee River watersheds. From March 2023 through July 2025, four-hundred-and-three Monopterus, mostlikely Sunda Swamp Eel, Monopterus javanensis Lacepède 1800, were collected from ten waterbodies. Fifty specimens of Cuchia, Ophichthys cuchia (Hamilton 1822), collected from six waterbodies, constitute the first records of Cuchia from Florida's open waters. Florida follows Louisiana and Texas as the third US state between 2019 and 2023 found to harbor established populations of Cuchia. Three multi-agency bio-blitz events referred to as “Fish Slams,” consisting of dozens of biologists intensively sampling a focal area for nonnative fish species, were instrumental in discovering low-detectability swamp eels. Reduced effort targeted sampling capitalized on the results of the Fish Slams. Live swamp eels, including both Sunda Swamp Eel and Cuchia have for decades been sold at food markets throughout the United States, including Louisiana, Texas, and Florida. Ongoing trade in live swamp eels is likely leading to their introduction and establishment in the United States with potential deleterious effects for aquatic ecosystems and human health. Samuel Robinson
1069: Habitat loss is a primary threat to seahorses, pipefishes and their relatives (family Syngnathidae) globally. Syngnathids are often ecologically specialized and closely associated with threatened habitat-forming species including seagrasses, corals, sponges, and mangroves. Previous research has documented syngnathid population declines following the loss of habitat-forming species. This research presents the results of habitatstratified surveys of 79 sites in Biscayne National Park (BNP), a Marine Protected Area (MPA) in southeastern Florida. Nine syngnathid species were recorded in BNP. Hippocampus zosterae, Syngnathus scovelli, and Syngnathus floridae were the most frequently recorded species, while other species occurred infrequently. While seagrass coverage was an important predictor of syngnathid presence, logistic regression analysis of presence/absence data against a suite of environmental variables indicated that local sediment characteristics were the strongest predictors of syngnathid occurrence across the BNP landscape. The strong association between fine sediment—a variable that indicates locally low current velocities—and syngnathid presence suggests that syngnathid occurrence is mediated by velocity thresholds within seagrass beds. Further analysis of the variation in habitat use among the three most abundant syngnathids in BNP revealed niche partitioning based on salinity, local hydrodynamic regime, and seagrass coverage. This study points to the importance of incorporating spatial data frameworks that capture sediment properties into existing habitat-based mapping and modeling initiatives. Furthermore, our findings highlight that conservation efforts should consider sheltered, low-velocity seagrass habitats when prioritizing the protection of seagrass habitats and seagrass-associated species. Eric Suarez Melissa Miller; Derek Yorks; Benjamin Stookey; Maria Ojeda-Rojas; Alexander Romer; Eric Suarez; Jenna Cole;
1070: Remote sensing using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) allows for the rapid monitoring of aquatic habitats at fine and coarse habitat scales, which can benefit conservation and management efforts. Traditional fieldbased approaches provide measurements of habitat, but their limited coverage may not capture continuous patterns across channel and riparian zones. We used UAV imagery, alongside traditional surveys, was used to quantify continuous habitat features and characterize areas associated with the presence of imperiled fish species. Five (1km) reaches along the Neches, Angelina, and Sabine rivers in Texas were surveyed. Field measurements were recorded at 10 equidistant transects, and fishes were sampled using seines and gillnets. High-resolution RGB orthophotos were captured at each 1-km site using an Anzu Raptor T drone with >50 m buffer on both sides. Photos were taken at 2-s intervals at 90°, 250 ft altitude, and >80% overlap. Orthomosaics were generated in WebODM photogrammetry software and polygons were drawn around identifiable habitat features (e.g., active channel, inactive channel). Sabine Shiner was present at sites with low (<5% active channel) woody debris and greater sand bar areas (>40% inactive channel). One site supporting multiple imperiled species such as Sabine Shiner, Shoal Chub, Gumbo Darter, and River Darter had minimal woody debris and no sand bars. Our traditional field sampling confirmed this site had shallower waters with faster flows. UAV imagery provides continuous, reachscale habitat data that complements traditional surveys and fully characterizes physical features. Future research will refine these techniques and across seasons to assess temporal changes in habitat. Anastasia Umstott
1071: Predation and feeding events are primary mechanisms by which species interact, but these rare events are often difficult to capture. In order to fully understand the feeding ecology of an organism, diet studies require expertise in both the predator and prey species. Consequently, this research can provide new opportunities for crossdiscipline collaborations, such as those between herpetologists and ichthyologists. Sea snakes are the most diverse group of living marine reptiles (>65 species) and they operate as mesopredators within a wide array of marine ecosystems. Studying the feeding ecology of sea snakes gives us a unique opportunity to also learn about diverse fish communities that are usually inaccessible. By harnessing the power of museum specimens, survey data, and natural history observations for both sea snakes and fishes, we investigated broad patterns of sea snake foraging ecology across species and habitats. In addition to using published diet records, we also radiographed and micro-CT scanned over 200 preserved sea snake specimens to identify new diet items and address gaps in the current diet literature. Preliminary results suggest that sea snake species fall into one of two broad foraging categories; estuarine/near-shore foragers that feed primarily on shallow water fish families, or divers who consume prey spanning a wide range of depths within the open-ocean water column. This study provides new insights into sea snake foraging ecology and also demonstrates the power of cross-taxa collaboration and how bioimaging can maximize the value of natural history research while minimizing the impacts of destructive sampling techniques. Jenny Crum
1072: Eastern diamondback rattlesnakes (Crotalus adamanteus; EDBs) are a long-lived species, but little is known about their maturation and growth rates. We used a modified Von Bertalanffy growth interval equation to analyze EDB growth interval data collected between 2008 and 2024 at a sea island in South Carolina, USA. We assessed growth intervals (mean = 3.7 years, range = 0.1 – 15.4 years) collected from 299 EDBs (females = 162, males = 137). Male age at maturation averaged 5.7 years and female age at maturation averaged 5.2 years. The smallest reproductively mature males and females were 97 and 99 cm snout-vent length, respectively. Age at maturation corresponded to the average age in which individuals bred (i.e., copulated), thus suggesting that the earliest females give birth is in their sixth year of life. Knowledge of maturation and growth is necessary for future efforts to characterize population viability and for understanding life history variation and plasticity in an imperiled reptile. Emily R. Gray Emily Gray; Carissa Adams; Sarah Ebert; Casey Hitchens; Stacey Leonatti Wilkinson; Mary Cate Miller; Will
1073: We review literature on the movements of North American pitvipers to identify geographic and taxonomic biases in research; conduct meta-analyses using commonly reported spatial metrics; characterize best practices; compare general patterns of movement and behavior across species; and suggest future directions for research. We found large disparities across species and locations, with four rattlesnake species (Crotalus horridus, Sistrurus catenatus, C. oreganus, and C. viridis) accounting for more than half the total studies and very limited spatial ecology research outside of the USA and Canada. Several different metrics for movement distance and space use are reported, but perhaps the most useful for general comparisons are average distance moved per day, minimum convex polygons, and kernel density estimators. Our meta-analysis revealed a modest relationship between body size and both movement distance and space use, with larger bodied species moving further and occupying larger home ranges. Nonetheless, a substantial amount of variation in these parameters is not explained by body size. Among the most reported spatial patterns across species were increased movement of adult males compared with females and decreased movement of pregnant females compared with nonpregnant females; however, we discuss some apparent exceptions to these near-ubiquitous patterns. Spatial ecology studies also frequently reported aggregation behaviors for overwintering and gestation and commented on high degrees of site fidelity, underscoring the overarching impact of seasonal environmental conditions on pitvipers in temperate climates. Future research might focus on neglected Mexican species, social behavior, and use of new technology to continuously monitor individuals. Maresa MacKenzie-del Toro Maresa MacKenzie-del Toro; Peter Wainwright
1074: The common garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis) is the most northern ranging reptile in North America, placing the animal in arguably one of the most challenging environments faced by any reptile on the planet. Recently, however, naturally-limiting factors such as short, cool summers and hibernacula scarcity have been superseded by large-scale wildfire. The object of our research was to examine the impacts of extremely large and intense wildfire on the northernmost populations of this snake, in the Northwest Territories and northern Alberta, Canada. Population size and characteristics were determined using a mark-recapture survey. Body condition was estimated from snake lengths and weights using a scaled mass index. The population estimates and body condition data were compared against those from previous studies in the area and, while population size appeared unchanged, female snakes had decreased body condition relative to males following wildfire. These results indicate that individual responses, such as changes in body condition, may act as early warning signs of reduced fitness even in the absence of immediate population decline. Maya Stokes
1075: Individual-level monitoring programs are critical for understanding ecological and evolutionary processes that affect wildlife populations. We used radio telemetry data collected under a long-term monitoring framework to evaluate the effects of time and reproductive state on the spatial ecology of a long-lived pit viper (eastern diamondback rattlesnake, Crotalus adamanteus; EDB). Between 2009 and 2023, we recorded 16,039 radio locations from telemetry-equipped EDBs in South Carolina and used these data to calculate full and core annual activity ranges, daily movement, and annual range overlap. We evaluated interactive and additive effects of sex, time (years), and reproductive state (based on individual capture histories) on movement parameters. We detected a significant effect of sex and reproductive state on activity-range area and daily movement but failed to detect significant similar effects on range overlap. Rather, annual range overlap was negatively associated with time. Overlap of core and full annual activity ranges averaged 44% (± 29) and 62% (± 28), respectively, and the annual ranges were separated, on average, by 2.2 years (± 2.2; range: 1-12 years; n = 190). Our results indicate that EDB’s exhibit high site fidelity, with range overlap shifting slowly over time. Jordan Waldron
1076: The invasive Burmese python (Python bivittatus) is established across South Florida and is implicated in negative impacts to native wildlife. For over a decade, scientists and natural resource managers have investigated python ecology to develop targeted removal and control tools. Several successful python removal programs and tracking efforts have been implemented across South Florida. With few exceptions, these programs are focused in high ground habitats containing a mix of hardwood hammock, pinelands, prairie, cypress swamps, and estuaries that constitute only a portion of South Florida wildlands. As such, there is an information gap regarding python ecology and removal efficacy in the central Everglades region, where landscapes primarily consist of sawgrass marsh interspersed with sloughs and tree islands. To address this need, we initiated a collaborative multi-year study to integrate radio-telemetry field techniques and advanced modelling approaches to provide critical information on movements, behaviors, and habitat use to inform python removal efforts within the central Everglades. To analyze our telemetry dataset, we used a dynamic Brownian bridge movement model analysis to assess python spatial use, autocorrelated kernel density estimates to quantify python home range, and integrated step selection functions to identify any associations with habitat types. Our results show male pythons exhibited larger occurrence distributions and home ranges than female pythons, average home ranges and occurrence distributions were larger in the central Everglades than in their native range in Thailand, and pythons in the central Everglades showed a positive association to anthropogenic habitat types. Florence Wen
1077: Overfishing during the 1980s and 1990s caused significant declines in sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus) along the U.S. Atlantic coast, leading to their designation as a prohibited species. Recent evidence suggests recovery, with increasing occurrences in previously depleted regions such as Nantucket Sound, Massachusetts. To inform management of this species, we used acoustic telemetry and catch data to evaluate occurrence, site fidelity, and movements in Nantucket Sound. From June through September 2019–2025, 276 sandbar sharks (113–190 cm FL; mean ± SD = 146.3 ± 17.3 cm) were captured. More juveniles (n = 179) were caught than mature individuals (n = 97), and more adult females (n = 89) than males (n = 8). From 2022 to 2025, 83 of 84 acoustically tagged individuals were detected on the receiver array from June through October for 1 to 93 days (mean ± SD = 28.3 ± 24.9 days). Water temperature was a significant positive predictor of shark presence. Spatial network analyses and annual returns indicated high site fidelity to Nantucket Island, with 83.5% of individuals tagged prior to 2025 returning for ≥ 1 years, and both juvenile and mature sharks aggregated at the island’s northeastern end. Our findings provide the first documentation of an annual sandbar shark aggregation north of Delaware, and support consideration of the area as an essential fish habitat for this species. Guarino R. Colli
1078: Reproduction in placental viviparous sharks has been described for most coastal carcharhinid sharks, with annual, biennial, and triennial reproductive cycles occurring. More recently, plasticity in reproductive cycles has been found with cycles switching between annual and biennial, and possibly biennial and triennial cycles. This plasticity has been observed in species found in the Gulf of Mexico, as well as the U.S. Atlantic. The prevalence of this phenomenon is poorly understood, but has significant implications as a stock’s potential productivity can vary dramatically based on the reproductive cycle. Here we report on our current understanding of reproductive plasticity focusing on case studies of blacknose sharks (Carcharhinus acronotus), finetooth sharks (Carcharhinus isodon), and sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus). Ryan Freedman Ryan Logan; Kady Lyons; Eschelle Burns; Vanessa Van Duesen; Patrick Rex; Zachariah Merson; Emily Spurgeon;
1079: A brief reflection of Jeff's impact on shark science from his work in the Florida Keys to the origins of the Sharks and Their Relatives Book Series. Teke Helms
1080: This study compared the swimming kinematics of three co-occurring shark species that differ in morphology and migratory behavior. We analyzed aerial drone footage of blacktip (Carcharhinus limbatus), lemon (Negaprion brevirostris), and nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum), free swimming in their natural habitat, to quantify tailbeat frequency (Hertz), tailbeat amplitude (body length), stride length (body length per tailbeat), and velocity (body lengths per second). The blacktip exhibited the greatest tailbeat frequency (1.04 Hz), the nurse had the lowest (0.62 Hz) and the lemon was intermediate (0.74) and did not differ from the other species. Tailbeat amplitude also differed among the three shark species. The nurse had the greatest tailbeat amplitude (0.34 BL), whereas the blacktip (0.24 BL) and lemon (0.24 BL) did not differ. Blacktip sharks exhibited the greatest velocity (0.92 BL/sec), the nurse had the lowest (0.42 BL/sec) and the lemon was intermediate (0.48 BL/sec), and did not differ from the other species. For all three species, there was no significant relationship between increasing tailbeat amplitude and frequency. The high aspect ratio (AR) caudal fin of the blacktip (AR=4.2) is 2.5x greater than the nurse shark (AR=1.7) and provides reduced drag, greater thrust and a greater velocity, all of which are important for a highly migratory species. These results may provide a mechanism to correlate swimming kinematics with migratory patterns that can be used to predict the extent of migration exhibited by a given species, including species for which studying long distance migration is particularly difficult. Danny Kalke
1081: Elasmobranchs have seen an increase in the severity and the number of threats they face in the Anthropocene. The Atlantic nurse shark (Ginglymostoma cirratum) is an abundant mesopredator widely distributed through the coastal tropical and subtropical Atlantic. This species is relatively understudied, apart from at a seasonal aggregation site in the Dry Tortugas National Park (DTNP) in the Florida Keys, that has been the subject of a 30year study on mating behavior. In 2023, a marine heatwave hit the Keys and caused high mortality in corals, but the effects on large predators such as nurse sharks are unknown. We assessed genetic diversity, a measure of population health and viability, in the nurse shark population in the DTNP before and after the heatwave. If the population experienced a bottleneck, fewer nurse sharks would return to the DTNP to mate compared with previous years, lowering overall diversity. We genotyped 10 microsatellite loci, a type of DNA fingerprinting, in 80 nurse sharks in the DTNP and surrounding areas, and measured nucleotide diversity and allelic richness prior to and after 2023. Shifts in allele frequencies associated with weather extremes like marine heatwaves can occur rapidly, and the resulting diversity loss could have a catastrophic effect on the ability of species to recover. This is especially important for Elasmobranchs, which are already experiencing high rates of extinction. These data will contribute to the understanding of how extreme climate events can influence shark populations, and to improve future mitigation of vulnerable species under environmental stress. Daniel Knapp
1082: Elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) are large-bodied fishes whose slow growth and low fecundity make them vulnerable to extinction. Because so many elasmobranch species are depleted and in decline, it is increasingly important to understand reproductive behavior and movement patterns in order to create effective management. Nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) are large, benthic sharks and common to the Atlantic, where they function as keystone predators in vulnerable coastal ecosystems like coral reefs. Nurse sharks are relatively understudied apart from reproductive behavior, which has been documented at a mating aggregation site in the Dry Tortugas National Park (DNTP), in the Florida Keys, for over 30 years. These studies have provided insight on the specific mating practices of mating sharks like time of mating, body positioning and social interactions during copulation, but little is known about the conservation status of this population. To that end, we examined relatedness, kinship, philopatry, and multiple mating among nurse sharks from the DNTP nurse sharks using highly polymorphic microsatellite loci. Taken together, the results of this study will help describe the nurse shark genetic mating system and dispersal patterns, and shed light on the population dynamics that shape genetic diversity, a known buffer against extinction. Results will allow for a better understanding of how reproductive strategies shape diversity and viability in this species, adding much-needed information to improve climate-based conservation strategies. Christopher A. Searcy
1083: The Convention on Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) define migratory species as those where a significant proportion cyclically and predictably cross international jurisdictional boundaries. Currently 39 species of shark and ray are listed in at least one of the CMS Appendices. Lists of transboundary and migratory species of sharks, rays and chimaeras have previously been developed, but have not used a consistent methodology. This work aimed to develop an approach for determining the likelihood that a species meets the CMS definition of migratory, and then applied it to 425 species that had the potential to be added to the CMS Appendices. Since the data available to determine whether a species meets the criteria for migratory varies greatly a hierarchical approach was developed. Where sufficient movement data was available it was used to directly assess the criteria. But for species that lack sufficient a new scoring approach using body form, size, indirect indicators of migration (e.g. natal philopatry), evidence of cyclical occurrence, and habitat specificity, were used to determine the likelihood of meeting criteria. 132 species were included in a new list of migratory sharks, ray and chimaeras. This included 22 species where there was direct evidence that they crossed international boundaries, 88 species determined to have a medium or high likelihood of being migratory using the scoring method, and 22 species that were special cases based on international boundary configuration (e.g. riverine species). The list included 60 rays, 72 sharks and no chimaeras. Madelynn Sinclair
1084: Historical data show that the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), on the east coast of Florida, was once a nursery for the endangered smalltooth sawfish and supported large numbers of individuals from multiple life stages. In recent years, adults have been known to frequent nearshore ocean waters off the southern IRL, but until recently there have not been any tagging studies to answer questions about their movement patterns, residency, and association with the estuary. To date, 50 large juveniles and adults (2.3–4.8 m stretch total length) have been acoustically tagged in the lower St. Lucie River and St. Lucie Inlet. The goal of this talk is to present preliminary data on movements of these size classes in the region and relate patterns to previous work. In addition, this presentation will highlight our collaboration with the late Dr. Jeffrey C. Carrier and his contributions to this ongoing study. Dan Wright
1085: Understanding the drivers for brain diversity is dependent upon an understanding of an organism’s evolutionary history. Indeed, broad variability has been documented within and across cartilaginous fishes regarding the size and complexity of the brain and its major regions (olfactory bulbs, telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, cerebellum and medulla). This variability is often associated with primary habitat, life history traits, or specific behavior patterns, even in phylogenetically unrelated species that share certain lifestyle characteristics, potentially allowing for predictions of sensory specialization and cognitive capacity. Equally important in the ‘evolution’ of a scientific career are the shoulders we each stand on, be it through discoveries that came before, technical training we receive, or a word of encouragement when it’s needed the most. This talk will review much of what we know about patterns of brain organization in cartilaginous fishes, through the lens of both brain evolution and career evolution. We will explore neural adaptation across three major axes: (a) how brain organization varies interspecifically across cartilaginous fishes, including ways we’re incorporating high resolution bioimaging to explore the brain in situ; (b) how brain organization varies intraspecifically, both in terms of how the brain changes normally throughout the life of a single species and between the sexes; and (c) how a scientist’s evolution is equally plastic, with a particular emphasis on the key mentorship and support of Jeffrey C. Carrier. It is rare that one singular thing drives evolution; that is true of the brain and true of the scientist. Harrison York
1086: The Highly Migratory Species Management Division of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NOAA Fisheries) is responsible for the management of the U.S. federal shark fishery in the U.S. Atlantic. Federal management of the Atlantic shark fishery began in 1993, following years of expanding shark harvest. In the mid1990s, many of the commercially harvested shark species were declared overfished. As such, consistent with U.S. fisheries laws, the management focus has been on ensuring commercial and recreational shark fishermen maintained fishing opportunities to harvest sharks while also ensuring shark stocks were rebuilding. Early on, most of the comments and concerns received by NOAA Fisheries were from fishermen who wanted to fish for sharks or conservationists who wanted sharks to be rebuilt faster. Overall, everyone wanted more sharks. Subsequently, due in part to the regulations, fishing effort has declined and shark stocks are becoming rebuilt. Additionally, over time, public concerns have shifted and now the comments are generally split into two groups: either the commenter wants NOAA Fisheries to increase shark harvest in an attempt to reduce the number of sharks to prevent depredation, or the commenter wants NOAA Fisheries to decrease shark harvest to increase shark populations and ensure sharks do not go extinct. Neither perspective fully reflects an understanding of the reality of the current state of U.S. Atlantic shark fisheries. This presentation will discuss these shifting concerns and the changing state of the fisheries over the past 30 years using the sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus) as an example. Meven Le Brishoual
1087: La Jolla is a known aggregation site for several iconic elasmobranch species, including Leopard sharks (Triakis semifasciata), round stingrays (Urobatis halleri), white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias), and tope sharks (Galeorhinus galeus). Leopard sharks and round rays are charismatic, shallow water species that frequently interact with beachgoers. Tope sharks and white sharks are highly threatened and elusive species, which makes observations of their movements and abundance vital to conservation efforts. Several studies have investigated the aggregations, movements, and reproductive cycles of these species in this location over shorter time periods. However, there is limited information on the abundance and seasonality of these species in La Jolla over longer, multi-year periods. Environmental DNA is a promising tool to observe elusive species without making physical or visual contact with organisms, reducing costs and invasiveness. This project aims to use an existing white shark assay and develop novel eDNA assays for the other three species to estimate their long term and seasonal abundance trends from a 13 year biweekly eDNA dataset collected from the SIO pier. In particular, we will develop speciesspecific droplet digital PCR assays, which offer reliable measures of DNA abundance and semi-quantitative estimates of organismal abundance through eDNA sampling alone. These eDNA trends will be paired with other data streams, including acoustic tagging or visual citizen science observations, as well as environmental metadata such as SST and photoperiod. Overall, this study aims to provide a long-term picture of nearshore elasmobranch abundance in La Jolla and continue developing eDNA techniques for monitoring elasmobranchs. Robert Cooper
1088: The Highly Migratory Species Management Division of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NOAA Fisheries) is responsible for the management of Atlantic commercial and recreational shark fisheries in federal waters. Federal management of Atlantic sharks began in 1993, and the management measures established at that time are the basis for those in place today, including permitting and reporting requirements, management complexes, commercial quotas and retention limits, and recreational bag limits. The majority of those management measures are based on new science and information available through shark stock assessment results. Some stock assessment results have recommended that some revisions of domestic shark management are needed. Consistent with efforts to rebuild overfished stocks and prevent overfishing, NOAA Fisheries plans to utilize these stock assessment results to optimize the ability for commercial and recreational shark fishers to fully harvest the available, science-based shark quotas. Any potential management revisions will continue to need strong scientific research and support. Matt Duggan
1089: Rising temperatures and increased coastal pollution in Florida coastal waters are leading to increasingly frequent harmful algal blooms. These red tide events produce mass blooms of Karenia brevis, a dinoflagellate known to produce a potent neurotoxin called brevetoxin and lead to large-scale coastal mortality events. While brevetoxin exposure has been measured in coastal species, the bioaccumulation and biomagnification of these toxins has not been fully characterized, particularly when studying predatory elasmobranch species already adapting to environmental disturbances. To bridge this research gap, we will carry out a captive elasmobranch study to examine the role they play in the trophic transfer of brevetoxin across functional groups in two parts. The first part, 72-hour prey exposures to K. brevis, addresses how consistent exposure affects baseline brevetoxin levels in local shrimp (Penaeus sp.) as the chosen food source for coastal bonnethead sharks (Sphyrna tiburo). The purpose of the second part, a six-week predator captive study, is to test the mechanism and rate of transfer of brevetoxin across trophic levels through ingestion of prey with a large toxin load. We will also investigate whether brevetoxins accumulate in four vital elasmobranch tissues and if so, at what concentrations through performing enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. In doing so, we’ll analyze if non-lethal sampling methods can be used as a proxy for toxin load. This data will inform future exposure studies on wild elasmobranch populations and will be shared with Florida coastal communities to advocate for natural resource management, red tide policy solutions, and public health initiatives. Austin Garner
1090: As shark management has started to yield conservation gains in some jurisdictions, fishers are reporting increased incidence of shark depredation (i.e., removal or damage of catch). In some places there is growing pressure for shark population control by removing or culling the more common depredating shark species, reversing the successes from decades of management efforts. The use of deterrents could be a viable alternative and non-lethal solution to reduce shark depredation. An Electronic Pulse Device (EPD) developed by Fishtek Marine produces a low electrical pulse designed to overstimulate the sharks ampullae and make them turn away from the EPD at close range. We tested this EPD as a depredation mitigation tool for anglers by conducting controlled trials on bonnetheads (Sphyrna tiburo; all adults) and sandbars (Carcharhinus plumbeus; adults and juveniles) in a captive setting. EPDs were affixed to angling gear ~ 25 cm from bait and active (functional) or inactive (non-functional) EPDs were exposed to the sharks. A total of 354 trials were conducted showed the EPD can be an effective tool for depredation mitigation. Bonnethead trials showed the bait was consumed significantly less often (51% of the trials) using the active EPD compared to the inactive EPD (93%). When bait was consumed, feeding was significantly delayed using the active EPD (~ 3X longer). Sandbar trials showed the active EPD doubled the time to consume the bait because the sharks exhibited significantly more rapid withdrawals from the bait (1 to 43) with an active EPD compared to the inactive EPD (0). Kat Mowle
1091: Sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus) are a large, coastal shark with a wide-ranging distribution, occupying waters throughout the Western North Atlantic Ocean, including the Gulf of America. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, sandbar sharks were the primary target of the U.S. shark bottom longline fishery and were declared overfished and experiencing overfishing in 2006. Since 2008, they have been a prohibited species under the Atlantic Fishery Management Plan for Highly Migratory Species. More than 25 years later, fishermen routinely claim that sandbar shark populations have exploded, giving rise to increased depredation rates. Here, we generated a standardized index of relative abundance for sandbar shark in support of the current stock assessment (SEDAR 101). Data were collected from a fishery-independent bottom longline survey in the coastal waters of Alabama from 20102025. A total of 875 sandbar sharks were captured across 763 sampling sets. A two-step delta-lognormal model was used to standardize the index by removing the effects of temperature, depth, salinity, and dissolved oxygen. Nominal and standardized indices aligned closely and varied throughout the survey period, with maximum values observed in 2014 and minimum values observed in 2016. The majority of individuals captured were mature (mean = 193 cm Total Length). These data will provide updated information regarding the current status of this prohibited species, while highlighting the complexities involved with managing human-shark interactions. Caleb Z. Mullins Caleb Mullins; Christopher Schalk; Daniel Saenz; Matthew McBroom; Reuber Antoniazzi; Gabriel Andrade-Ponce;
1092: Since the early 1990’s the United States shark fishery has been closely regulated and monitored for sustainability. The Gulf of Mexico lands and exports a majority (60%) of US harvested carcharhinid sharks including blacktip (Carcharhinus limbatus) and bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas). The shark fishery in Louisiana is historically an important offseason stopgap for shrimp fishermen that switch fisheries during shrimp fishery closures. In 2023, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) listed all carcharhinid sharks under Appendix II, which implements additional permitting for the import and export of the largest share of sharks landed in the Gulf. Since the listing of carcharhinid sharks, shark fishery landings in the Gulf of Mexico have declined by 65 – 70%, in addition and the remaining allowable blacktip harvest was at its highest level 15 years (76% of the Annual Catch Limit remaining) at the end of 2024. While the circumstances of the reduction in shark harvest are complex, the suspected cause of the reduction in harvest is a function of increased and conflicting regulation. The role of CITES according to USFWS is to “ensure international trade in wild plants and animals is legal, traceable, and biologically sustainable”, which are also hallmarks of modern fisheries management in the United States outlined in the Magnuson-Stevens Act. The decline of harvest in shark fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico reflect the consequences of well-intentioned but redundant conservation measures – which potentially result in harm to proven sustainable shark fisheries. Ashlie Poland
1093: Due to targeted and bycatch fisheries triggered by demand for shark, ray, and chimaera (sharks) products, one-third of all species are threatened with extinction. Global dynamics and extent of the shark fin trade are relatively well-understood, but the extent of the shark meat trade remains significantly under-investigated, preventing the assessment of its impact on populations and the accountability of nations trading CITES-listed species. Within the Global Shark Meat Project, this study examines the scale, scope, and market dynamics of the shark meat trade in Mexico, the world´s fourth-largest shark producer. Surveys and interviews with fishers and supply chain actors were conducted at key ports, landing sites, and markets to investigate catches, local consumption patterns, and the shark meat value chain. Internal consumption of shark meat accounts for most of the sharks caught in Mexico, with a small part exported, mostly to the USA and Taiwan. National production is insufficient to meet national demand, as ~2,000 t of meat are imported annually, mostly from Costa Rica. While sometimes mislabeled, the majority is sold as shark meat. Demand for shark meat exists year-round, peaking during Lent and the Christmas season. Most consumed meat comes from threatened species, juveniles, and small sharks. These findings highlight the complexity of Mexico's shark trade, driven by high consumer demand and localized distribution networks rather than solely international trade. Understanding domestic market forces is fundamental to developing effective fishery management strategies, improving species-specific conservation efforts, and strengthening the implementation of CITES regulations in this important shark-fishing nation. Julia Saltzman
1094: Florida’s multimillion-dollar shellfish aquaculture industry faces persistent challenges in the survival of grow-out stage hard clams (Mercenaria mercenaria) due to predation. However, predator monitoring by the industry is anecdotal, and is generally biased towards benthic invertebrates. More mobile species such as rays, sea turtles, and bony fishes, are difficult to detect due to their dynamic nature. This lack of knowledge limits our understanding of how these species interact with these operations, and whether those interactions are positive, negative, or neutral. To address this gap, we conducted seasonal surveys of mobile fauna at an active clam lease in the central Indian River Lagoon, FL where we passively monitored predator presence and behavior using underwater time-lapse cameras. Here, we describe our observations using this system, which recorded 12,117 observations from 43 unique taxa (including 7 species of elasmobranchs – 4 batoids and 3 sharks). Stingrays (Hypanus spp.) were present year-round and the percentage of foraging observations (5.1%) varied seasonally. The only other elasmobranch species observed foraging was the whitespotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari), which although only encountered 4 times, was observed foraging twice (50%). The three shark species observed included the bull (Carcharhinus leucas), bonnethead (Sphyrna tiburo), and lemon (Negaprion brevirostris), but only exhibited swimming behaviors. Preliminary models of environmental conditions associated with batoid presence on the clam lease suggested temperature was the main driver of these interactions. These insights into predator visitation patterns can inform more effective mitigation strategies for shellfish aquaculture while contributing to ongoing shellfish restoration efforts using analogous methods. Natasha Stepanova Natasha Stepanova; Anne Kort; Daniel Rabosky; Alison Davis Rabosky
1095: Freshwater ecosystems provide plenty of opportunity for species to genetically diverge without morphologically diverging. On the West Coast of North America, Cottus, a freshwater genus of sculpin, has become the face of problematic species due to the vast genetic variation and constrained morphological variation. Development of genetic trees to define relationships within this genus has only brought chaos to the understanding of Cottus. Cottopsis, a subgenus of Cottus in the Pacific Northwest, contains two particularly perplexing species (C. gulosus and C. perplexus) that dichotomous keys fail to clearly distinguish. Recent genetic models found specimens identified as C. gulosus and C. perplexus formed multiple clades within the Pacific Northwest. This allowed us to test whether the voucher specimens used in these genetic phylogenies can be morphologically differentiated. We performed morphometric and meristic analysis to build a model of the diagnostic characters that define the 8 clades found in Western Washington. We developed a new dichotomous key and tested its efficacy by assigning clade identifications to newly selected specimens that include all identified Cottus species in Western Washington. These specimens were then included in the genetic analysis to produce a new phylogeny and confirm whether our dichotomous key was effective at predicting clade placement. The ultimate goal will be to accurately describe the true diversity of Cottus in Western Washington which may require new species descriptions. Viviana Astudillo-Clavijo
1096: The ghost knifefishes (Apteronotidae) are the most diverse family among the Neotropical electric knifefishes (Gymnotiformes) with about 100 species. Within Apteronotidae, the genus Sternarchella is comprised of nine species, which are primarily restricted to the main channels of large river systems. Sternarchella species are characterized by reduced eyes and pigmentation, robust dentition, and a high frequency electric organ discharge. We explore the evolutionary history of Sternarchella using mitochondrial and nuclear legacy markers as well as genomic ultraconserved elements (UCEs), sampling seven of the valid species from the upper, middle, and lower Amazon. Both datasets reveal complex phylogenetic relationships that fail to resolve clades corresponding to well-established morphospecies. We evaluate several hypotheses that may explain this discordance and explore the temporal and hydrogeographic context of diversification within this clade. Arianna Berrios
1097: NOAA’s Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument (PMNM) conducted plankton-net surveys throughout the 1980s-1990s, where ichthyoplankton specimens were collected and preserved, but not all were identified. As this historical collection has been transferred to the Bishop Museum, efforts have been made to sort through mixed lots and identify the larval fishes. During this process, there have been two significant findings from this transfer. Two larval specimens of Tosanoides obama, an endemic species first described in 2016, were identified, making it the first known larval record of this species in any U.S. collection. There was also a leptochephalus belonging to Faciolella, a genus of deepwater eels, discovered from this transfer. Despite being the only specimen, based on its morphology and geographic location, this leptocephalus could be an undescribed species. These findings indicate the importance of historical collections and how valuable recurations can be to generate new scientific data. Eric Coburn
1098: Accelerated Late Miocene to Pliocene tectonic uplift of the Andes Mountains is a well-documented driver of evolutionary diversification in various plant, amphibian, and bird lineages. Less studied is the impact of Andean uplift on the diversification of fishes specialized for life in the flashy, turbid, high-gradient habitats of Andean rivers. Chaetostomatini is a tribe of six suckermouth armored catfish genera (family Loricariidae) and 66 currently valid and several undescribed species that predominantly occupy Andean rivers from Panama to southern Peru, where they resist currents and graze algae using large oral disks and parallel rows of numerous small teeth. Precise taxonomic resolution of Chaetostomatini has long been complicated by evolutionarily conserved body shapes, intraspecifically variable color patterns, and scarcities of fresh specimens and tissues. Over the past two decades, I have documented Chaetostomatini diversity via field collections of specimens, tissues, and live photos at type and non-type localities in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, and molecular phylogenetic and computed tomographic analyses. Here I present a fossil-calibrated phylogeny showing widespread species and population-level cladogenesis correlated with Andean uplift, especially in the genus Chaetostoma. Other Chaetostomatini genera show deeper divergence and widespread paraphyly, including primary types of Dolichancistrus atratoensis. Especially exciting is the recent discovery of three highly flow-specialized undescribed species of ‘Cordylancistrus’ in upper reaches of the Marañon River in northern Peru. With small body sizes, restricted vagility, and ranges limited to wetted channels, the tribe Chaetostomatini provides an excellent model for understanding how geologic uplift can influence diversification in aquatic species. Nathan Lujan Tiago Faria; Donald Taphorn; Flávio Lima; Gabriel Deprá; Claudio Oliveira; Hernán López-Fernández; Nathan
1099: Tulane University’s Biodiversity Research Institute (TUBRI) houses The Royal D. Suttkus Fish Collection – the world’s largest collection of post larval fishes. In the summer of 2017 and in partnership with others, we devised a plan to rescue millions of specimens from the University of Louisiana Monroe’s Neil H. Douglas collection, which had abruptly become orphaned and was in jeopardy of loss. Our ongoing curation and incorporation of the remaining ULM collection expands TUBRI’s Suttkus Fish Collection’s holdings from 8 million to just under10 million individual specimens. This unprecedented growth came with unique and universal challenges. We will discuss these challenges and lessons learned, including how (and how not) to transport millions of specimens 260 miles, fill the information gaps of an incomplete database, and store so many additional specimens in a vast space already near capacity. The curators of the Suttkus Fish Collection are proud and excited to be the custodian of the Neil H. Douglas collection, highlight the opportunity collections like it provides, and communicate the impact such collections can have on future research. Madeline Mann
1100: It has finally come time to underscore that the ridiculous volumes of literature written over many decades on the topics of species and their conceptualizations (not definitions!) are simply absurd, to put it mildly! The time spent discussing, arguing, and writing about these topics is likely better served by finding, discovering, describing, conserving, and protecting natural diversity – that is, lineages, in the Darwinian and Hennigian senses. The workings of concepts of species in the global discipline of “Biodiversity Science” is not that difficult to understand and put into practice, if and only if, the person’s (not always a trained systematist) idea of “species” includes the critical prerequisites: 1) things must be evaluated with reference to time and space, 2) lineages exist, 3) individual organisms and/or their homologous, heritable attribute(s) may or may not change in time and space, 4) lineages do ecist as independent aub masquarade nas intergrades/hybrids because of ancestral polymorphisms, 5) what indeed qualifies as a heritable, homologous attribute in a lineage, and 6) the basics of the Philosophy of Science. The type of character does not matter as long as it is heritable and discoverable by the observer (in this case, H. sapiens; but other lineages are capable of accurately recognizing lineages – why can’t H. sapiens), but must be interpreted in a phylogenetic framework. Homology is critical. Only by fully understanding all six (and more) of these key areas can anyone hope to understand the diversity of, in the simplest cases, sexually reproducing organisms. Elizabeth McAlpine-Bellis
1101: While the limits of the dragonfishes (Stomiiformes) have been largely stable for nearly fifty years, the limits and relationships of the included families have remained contentious. Several recent phylogenomic studies have proposed new hypotheses of relationships among the major stomiiform clades. Here, we compare those studies and present results that highlight broad congruence between morphological and molecular data, moving toward an integrated phylogenetic hypothesis and congruent taxonomy that includes three families (Gonostomatidae, Sternoptychidae, and Stomiidae). Lora L. Smith
1102: The genera Eviota and Sueviota are a speciose group of cryptobenthic fishes distributed across IndoPacific coral reefs. Known as dwarfgobies because of their diminutive size (< 30 mm), species of these genera have a very short life span (<100 days). Integrative taxonomy in conjunction with underwater photography employed in the last thirty years has led to an explosion in descriptions of species, with Eviota currently containing 133 species and Sueviota, nine. Two clades are currently recognized within dwarfgobies, one group having completely unbranched pectoral‐fin rays, and a second group that possesses some branched pectoral‐fin rays. Sueviota pyrios Greenfield and Randall, 2010, is a rare species from the Red Sea known only by its holotype and described as possessing unbranched pectoral fin rays. With recent studies suggesting the non-monophyly of Sueviota, the position of S. pyrios remained uncertain. Examination of specimens from Mauritius in the NHM (London) discovered new occurrences of Sueviota pyrios. Despite the lack of fresh material and tissue samples, these specimens allowed a deeper investigation of their skeleton, offering insights in its phylogenetic position. The shape of opercular and ethmoid bones, in addition to vertebral counts, place Sueviota pyrios within the brachedclade of Eviota, similar to other species of Sueviota. Examination under high magnification of pectoral fin rays of S. pyrios (including the holotype) found a specific condition of some fin rays with partial branching, a distinct condition from the observed in species of the unbranched clade, as well distinct from the closely related Sueviota lachneri. Zack Vegso
1103: Pachydactylus is the most speciose genus of gecko endemic to sub-Saharan Africa with 56 described species. Within the genus, the serval/weberi species group includes 20 species from southwestern Africa, many of which occur in the Orange River Valley or the adjacent \Ai\Ais-Richtersveld Transfrontier Park. We present the most complete phylogenetic study of the species group, to date, using a molecular dataset that contains samples from all members of the serval/weberi species group. We compare phylogenetic results from Sanger and genomic data for the genus to identify introgression among species in the Orange River valley and assess the taxonomic status of P. montanus onscepensis, a putative endemic to a small stretch of the Orange River. Previous mitochondrial phylogenetic work has established P. m. onscepensis as sister to all other P. montanus, however, nuclear data are needed to better understand relationships. Our results suggest that P. m. onscepensis does represent a unique evolutionary lineage, and that historic hybridization events have occurred between P. m. onseepensis and other sympatric Pachydactylus along the Orange River. María Antonia Izurieta Burbano De Lara Maria Antonia Izurieta Burbano de Lara; Andrea Vera; Diana Pazmiño; Gabriela Gavilanes; Luisa Tituaña; Alex
1104: The stapedial foramen is a distinct feature of the stapes in the Reptiliomorpha or Pan-Amniota, known in Permian forms like Diadectes and Araeoscelis, widespread among synapsids including mammals. This trait is also found in some squamates, where is correlated with the path of the stapedial (internal carotid) artery. This artery has three possible paths in squamates: 1) anterior to the stapes, 2) through the stapedial foramen, 3) posterior to an imperforate stapes. Squamates with the stapedial foramen include dibamids, numerous gekkotans, and also amphisbaenians. This trait is generally considered primitive feature for squamates, in part due to the general idea that this trait is also primitive for vertebrates. Underwood and Greer considered the presence of the stapedial foramen as an indication of primitiveness among lepidosaurs, and an indication of close relationship of geckos and dibamids. Here we study the distribution of this trait among Reptiliomorpha and determine that most likely the stapedial foramen evolved de novo in Squamates. Depending on the phylogenetic hypothesis, it originated independently in Dibamids and Gekkotans, or it originated in the base of Squamata, and is most likely it is a shared plesiomorphy. In both topologies, it has multiple losses among Gekkotans. This plesiomorphic character documents an early stage of the ear in squamates, and multiple losses in Pygopodomorpha, several groups among Gekkonidae and Phyllodactylidae and Bifurcata. The distribution of the stapedial foramen among squamates is congruent with higher order relationships implied by molecular data.
1105: The Scincoidea are a clade of lizards that vary greatly in body size, morphology, and ecology, and together comprise about 20% of all squamates. Within the four families (Scincidae, Gerrhosauridae, Cordylidae, and Xantusiidae) the evolution of an extremely small body size has occurred multiple times. We hypothesized that these extreme reductions in body size are due to the repeated evolution of a miniaturized body form within this clade. To investigate this, we created a micro-CT scan dataset to digitally dissect and reconstruct representatives from the four scincoid families. We performed a review of the primary literature to look for morphological traits associated with miniaturization in other squamate lineages and employed 3D geometric morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods to investigate the relationship between size, shape, and phylogeny. Preliminary results indicate morphological and statistical evidence to support the repeated evolution of a miniaturized body plan within scincoidea. Allyson Fenwick Allyson Fenwick; Travis Hagey; Krista Ruppert; Scott Rush; Malorie Hayes; Worth Pugh; Eli Maynard; Christopher
1106: The composition of gecko families was in a state of flux until the early-to-mid twentieth century. Much of this confusion resulted from the use of digital characters to assign gecko species into genera. Digital morphology, however, is highly convergent, resulting in difficulties estimating relationships within and among genera. Broadening the scope of morphological characters used, research by Camp, Underwood, and McDowell and Bogert significantly revised our understanding about which taxa are geckos and how they are related to other squamates. Further work by Underwood, Russell, Dixon, and Kluge provided some additional resolution to relationships among gecko genera, however the paucity of characters and frequent homoplasy made such efforts challenging. As herpetological systematics entered the molecular age, the use of DNA sequence data promised to solve many of the longstanding problems facing higher-order gecko taxonomy. But, in practice the task was daunting due to practical issues of sampling the large number of gecko taxa coupled with their global distribution. Combining decades of field work with strong international collaborations, Bauer and colleagues produced phylogenies generated from multiple genetic loci with broad taxonomic sampling that has transformed our understanding of higher-order gecko taxonomy. These molecular phylogenetic hypotheses provided a framework for both taxonomic revision and comparative evolutionary research. I will discuss the history of higher-order gekkotan taxonomy through the lens of current phylogenetic hypotheses and emphasize the work of Bauer and colleagues in the early part of this century. Maritza Gamez
1107: Evolutionary transitions to diurnality are often associated with specialized ocular morphology, such as pits (foveae) in the retina. Foveae are required for high visual acuity and are found primarily in diurnal vertebrate taxa, including lizards. Although turnover in diel activity is generally considered rare among tetrapods, geckos have undergone repeated evolutionary transitions between nocturnality and diurnality. Aristelliger is a nocturnal lineage embedded within a largely diurnal clade and represents a putative reversal to nocturnality. We investigated eye development and morphology of Aristelliger geckos. Despite sharing a most recent common ancestor with its diurnal sister lineage over 60 million years ago, Aristelliger exhibit a fovea. Fovea development is coordinated by dynamic elongation and retraction in eye shape during embryonic development. In Aristelliger embryos, these elongation and retraction phases occur in the same region where the fovea forms, closely resembling the pattern seen in Anolis, a diurnal lizard with two foveae. Given the retention of a fovea in Aristelliger, we hypothesize that the transition to nocturnality is relatively recent. Incorporating these results into comparative phylogenetic methods results in a hypothesized diurnal ancestral temporal niche for sphaerodactylid geckos. Brandon A. Gross
1108: Speciation often results from the accumulation of reproductive isolation associated with lineage divergence, but secondary contact between diverged lineages can reshape the trajectory of speciation and reveal its underlying processes. The Indonesian island of Sulawesi is a tectonically complex island formed by the fusion of many paleo-islands, resulting in replicated cases of secondary contact among once-isolated lineages. Unlike secondary contact on continents where hybridization often results from unpredictable range shifts, Sulawesi’s fauna presents a replicated set of geologically constrained natural experiments to test how the magnitude of evolutionary divergence predicts outcomes of secondary contact and hybridization. Using thousands of genome-wide loci from Eutropis sun skinks spanning Wallace’s Line on Sulawesi and Borneo, we reconstructed a reticulate evolutionary history shaped by overwater dispersal, isolation, island fusion, hybridization, and character displacement. We delimited five distinct species (three undescribed) and uncovered multiple ancient hybridization events following island fusion leading to distinct outcomes. These outcomes — speciation reversal, parapatry, and sympatry putatively through reproductive character displacement — were associated with increasing levels of prior divergence consistent with evolutionary theory. Sympatry, specifically, was preceded by substantial introgressive hybridization and body size divergence that likely confers reproductive incompatibility. Together, these results provide empirical support for divergence-dependent tipping points along the speciation continuum. The sun skink radiation also includes a rare instance of reverse colonization of Borneo across Wallace’s Line that established a narrowly divergent species with a uniquely intermediate body size absent from Sulawesi. Lucas Kebow
