1254: Coastal shark populations are increasingly at risk as marine habitats degrade globally due to climate change, fishing pressure, and other human impacts. Effective conservation requires a spatially explicit understanding of species’ ecology and habitat use. Fiordland, a remote and complex fiord ecosystem in southern New Zealand, supports several threatened coastal shark species, including the globally Critically Endangered school shark/tope (Galeorhinus galeus), and the Vulnerable broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus). The fiords encompass a wide range of diverse habitats, some of which are protected within marine reserves. However, the ecological value of the fiord ecosystem for these shark species remains poorly understood. Here, we used acoustic telemetry to quantify residency and movement patterns of both shark species and assess their spatial use of the fiords. Preliminary results suggest broader spatial distribution and use of fiord habitats by male broadnose sevengill sharks than females, with females showing greater residency within the fiords. Possible aggregation areas were identified in shallow protected bays that also serve as high use anchorages. The influence of food availability and habitat structure were assessed using baited underwater video and suggest the potential that spatial use by both species may be driven by abundance of prey. Research is ongoing, but this project aims to evaluate how effectively Fiordland’s marine reserves protect coastal shark populations and to inform evidence-based management.

1256: Coastal systems are a vital resource to marine biodiversity, facilitating many essential ecological functions. However, proximity to human populations exposes aquatic animals in these systems to substantial levels of anthropogenic pressures. An understanding of the environmental factors influencing how species use coastal resources can help managers reduce the impact of human stressors on these coastal species. Southern eagle rays (Myliobatis tenuicaudatus) are distributed broadly across southern Australia and are highly resident to Gulf St Vincent, Adelaide, South Australia. We used standardised, repeated drone surveys at two locations on the Adelaide coastline (Christies Beach n = 70; Seacliff Beach n = 71) to assess the influence of environmental factors and backyard feeding (i.e., non-regulated provisioning of food) on the abundance, habitat selectivity, behaviour, and distribution of southern eagle rays. Southern eagle rays were observed times and were more frequent off Seacliff Beach where backyard feeding occurs. Ray abundance was driven by water temperature at both sites, by time of day at Christies Beach, and by tidal phase at Seacliff Beach. Southern eagle rays at Christies Beach selected for macroalgal reef over sand, while the opposite was observed at Seacliff Beach. Behaviour at Christies Beach was influenced by environmental variables, but by human presence at Seacliff Beach. This study provided insight into southern eagle rays on a localised scale which can be used to inform managers and reduce the possible influence of backyard feeding on ray abundance, habitat use, and behaviour.

We map reproductive seasonality, assess semen quality, and characterise hormone profiles for males and females. The outcomes will define breeding windows, clarify male function across wild and managed contexts, and provide practical guidance for assisted reproductive technologies. By delivering protocols that are ready for use in conservation breeding, this work supports ongoing rewilding of leopard sharks and offers a transferable framework for other threatened elasmobranchs.

1258: Reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) in southern Africa have experienced significant population declines reflecting increasing pressures on regional populations. Long-term sightings records have revealed a shift in reef manta behaviour and habitat use at aggregation sites such as Závora in southern Mozambique. Over the past years, there has been a transition from historically consistent year-round sightings to pronounced seasonal aggregations, coinciding with increased reproductive activity. Through the integration of ultrasonography and in-water observations, we have identified a higher frequency of pregnancies among females during these seasonal peaks, suggesting that Závora may serve as a key reproductive area for the region’s remaining manta rays. Acoustic and satellite telemetry (n = and n= 24, respectively) have highlighted the transboundary nature of this population, with individuals exhibiting site fidelity to Závora during the reproductive season as well as high residency within South Africa’s iSimangaliso Wetland Park. These patterns highlight the complementary roles of Závora as a reproductive hotspot and iSimangaliso’s sanctuary zone as a critical refuge for this vulnerable population. Together, these findings reveal a complex picture of decline, adaptation, and resilience, emphasizing the need for coordinated, cross-border conservation strategies in a region where management remains fragmented and underdeveloped. Moreover, we demonstrate the importance of informing marine policy through lessons learned from terrestrial transboundary initiatives in the region. Strengthening regional collaboration, equitable governance, coordinated monitoring and shared data will be essential to ensure effective protection of manta rays and other threatened elasmobranchs throughout southern Africa.

1259: Elasmobranchs detect electrical fields generated by other organisms through a network of Ampullae of Lorenzini, which they use to detect prey, identify conspecifics, avoid predators and navigate using geomagnetic fields. The distribution and internal anatomy of the Ampullae of Lorenzini has been linked to feeding strategy, and investigating electrosensory systems can therefore provide insight into the ecology, behaviour and trophic interactions of elasmobranchs. This is a useful avenue of research for deep-sea elasmobranchs where traditional monitoring methods are unfeasible. Apristurus is an under-researched genus of deep-sea shark which is thought to have an important ecological role in deep-sea ecosystems due to its abundance and relatively large size. This research investigates ampullary and mechanosensory distribution, grouping and internal anatomy of six species of Apristurus (A. laurussonii, A. melanoasper, A. manis, A. microps, A. indicus, A. aphyodes). Pore mapping found interspecific variation and enabled patterns to be identified between the subgroups spongiceps and brunneus. Dissection of an A. laurussonii specimen confirmed the presence of unusual mechanosensory pore regions so far only found in the family Pentanchidae, as well as the position of the Superficial Ophthalmic and Buccal clusters and the absence of the Mandibular clusters. The results demonstrate that pore mapping can provide additional taxonomic diagnostic features, and that Apristurus’ sensory anatomy is divergent from that of other Carcharhiniformes due to the lack of the Mandibular cluster and unusual concentrated regions of mechanosensory pores. This research adds novel biological insight to a highly understudied genus of elasmobranchs.

1260: Cabo Verde hosts one of the most diverse elasmobranch assemblages in the Eastern Atlantic but faces intense fishing pressure and a historical scarcity of local data that highlights the need for effective conservation actions. Since 2019, the Shark and Ray Programme of Biosfera I has conducted continuous monitoring using multiple methods, resulting in more than tagged individuals and underwater observations across the northern islands of the archipelago. These data revealed high species richness (13 species recorded) and critical aggregation and nursery zones for threatened species such as the Blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) and the Atlantic weasel shark (Paragaleus pectoralis), particularly within Cabo Verde’s largest Marine Protected Area, the island of Santa Luzia. In 2025, Cabo Verde reached an important milestone with the official designation of Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs), including Santa Luzia and adjacent islands, many of which overlap with existing Marine Protected Areas (MPAs). The emerging integration of these spatial tools highlights the potential for a reciprocal relationship: MPAs and ISRAs can strengthen the conservation of sharks and rays, while these species can serve as indicators of ecological integrity and management effectiveness. The results illustrate how locally generated scientific data can contribute to adaptive management, support the assessment of MPA effectiveness, and inform progress toward global conservation goals such as the 30×30 target. Cabo Verde is emerging as a promising example of how science, community engagement, and international frameworks can converge to protect threatened elasmobranchs and their habitats.

1262: Oceanic whitetip sharks (Carcharhinus longimanus) have undergone marked population declines due to overexploitation. Abundance trends typically rely on fisheries-dependent data that can be biased, particularly for protected species where underreporting is likely. Fishery-independent methods offer complementary insights but traditional surveys (e.g., longlines) can be costly and difficult to implement. Here, we evaluated pelagic Baited Remote Underwater Video Stations (pBRUVS) to establish relative abundance indices for oceanic whitetips using both free-drifting and boat-tethered configurations. Across two sampling periods (April–May 2023 and 2024), we deployed pBRUVS and detected oceanic whitetips on 51.52% of deployments. We used individual fin markings to estimate the minimum number of individuals per deployment (IND) and compared this to the common index MaxN (maximum individuals in a single frame). IND was positively correlated with, but typically higher than, MaxN—especially when MaxN exceeded one—and was up to three times greater where MaxN ≥ 2. In total, individual oceanic whitetips were identified; were resighted across deployments and were resighted between years. pBRUVS also recorded other pelagic and semi-pelagic taxa (four additional shark species, twelve boney fishes, one cephalopod, and one sea turtle). Our findings demonstrate that pBRUVS support individual-level identification and robust relative abundance indices, providing a scalable, non-extractive approach to track oceanic whitetip population recovery.

1263: Regional cuisines often reflect the intimate relationship between local biodiversity, cultural traditions, and food practices. Along Mexico’s southern Atlantic coast, sharks and rays hold a notable place in traditional dishes—particularly cazón, a culinary term referring to any shark under 1.5 m in total length. This term encompasses both juvenile and adult individuals from multiple species and lacks taxonomic precision, which can obscure key conservation concerns. This study combines genetic analysis of cooked and fresh tissue with interviews of local fishers, vendors, and cooks to identify the diversity of elasmobranch species present in local gastronomy across two Mexican states: Campeche and Quintana Roo. The research also explores the economic and cultural dynamics surrounding these species in the region. To date, seven shark species sold as cazón have been identified through genetic and visual records, along with two predominant ray species found in local markets. A clear difference in species composition was observed between the two states, and the identified species exhibit varying levels of conservation status. Our findings highlight the strong cultural and economic relevance of elasmobranchs in regional cuisine, emphasizing the urgent need for sustainable fisheries management that integrates both scientific data and traditional ecological knowledge. Furthermore, documenting locally captured cazón specimens provides valuable insight into potential nursery grounds, contributing to more effective conservation strategies for these ecologically important species.

1264: The broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus) is a large macropredator found in temperate coastal marine ecosystems. Despite their abundance in New Zealand’s coastal waters and their role as apex predators, the understanding of their ecology remains limited. This study aims to assess the broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus) population in Dusky Sound, Fiordland, using mark-recapture methods supported by semi-automated photoidentification. The use of non-invasive baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVs), combined with stereo-photogrammetry, allows for accurate size-distribution measurements without disturbing the natural behaviour of sharks. In addition, by utilising the unique dorsal spot patterns, individual sharks can be identified, facilitating estimates of population parameters, including abundance, sex ratio, and site fidelity. This approach will expand knowledge of sevengill shark populations in New Zealand and support management efforts. Broader distribution insights could also reveal connectivity or movement patterns among populations. Overall, this research will highlight the importance of sharks in maintaining the stability of marine ecosystems and encourage further study in New Zealand. Preliminary results indicate successful individual identification using the interactive individual identification system (I3S) and accurate size measurements using stereo-photogrammetry, along with initial insights into the areas of the fiord where sharks are most frequently encountered.
1265: Shark-diving is a growing and well-established industry emphasising the economic value of sharks as a non-extractive resource, promoting elasmobranch conservation and education. However, there remains little consensus on how to manage marine ecotourism sustainably, despite potential negative implications for shark behaviour, ecology, and long-term health. The Mexican Caribbean, home to an estimated elasmobranch species, hosts an established shark and ray ecotourism industry, with sites generating over half the annual revenue of national shark fisheries. Yet, many activities lack adequate management, and limited research has quantified their effect on the local populations' behaviour. This study examines the impact of tourist actions on the behaviour of three species: Bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas), Whitespotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari), and Nurse shark (Ginglymostoma cirratum) in the Mexican Caribbean. From March to July 2025, scuba dives were observed to quantify responses to different human behaviours. Results indicate shark behaviour was significantly influenced by tourist actions (p<0.005), while Eagle rays were not significantly affected (p=0.006). Across all species, neutral/tolerant responses occurred more frequently when tourists adhered to guidelines, whereas invasive actions elicited avoidance behaviours. Evidence of conditioning was also observed, particularly for Bull sharks during feeding dives, where anticipatory responses occurred before provisioning. These results underscore the need for science-based management and long-term regulation of shark-diving tourism to ensure sustainable conservation outcomes. Further research into the ecological, physiological, and socioeconomic impacts of shark and ray ecotourism is essential to guide the development of practices that align with conservation priorities.

1267: Local leadership and community involvement can make biodiversity protection more impactful and sustainable. Women are central to community but remain underrepresented in ocean governance, particularly in tropical regions where elasmobranch conservation challenges are greatest. Globally, women comprise just 37% of ocean science personnel. Socio-cultural and structural barriers restrict their access to ocean spaces: 68% of women worldwide cannot swim compared to 43% of men. This reduces their participation in marine activities that inspire ocean stewardship and environmental leadership. The Ocean Women project aims to increase women’s and girls’ access to ocean recreation and conservation in tropical coastal communities. Building on the Manta Trust’s Maldives-based marine education initiatives, the project applies interdisciplinary social science, education, and conservation approaches. Interview and survey research with Maldivian people found that 36% of females could not swim (versus 7% males), and only 50% of teenage girls could swim, identifying key barriers, enabling factors and recommendations for improvement. Participation in marine activities was shown to improve personal transformation and blue health, ocean literacy and marine citizenship, access to livelihoods, and social attitudes. Resultantly, we co-created a programme training Maldivian women as swimming and snorkelling instructors, who consequently developed a successful community swimming and environmental education club. By addressing gendered inequalities in ocean access, the project provides a model for strengthening community-based conservation. Insights are shared through an Ocean Connection Toolkit and mentoring network, enabling organisations to design ocean access programmes that build equitable pathways into marine science and leadership.

1268: The Mediterranean Sea is recognized as a global biodiversity hotspot, yet its cartilaginous fish fauna remains insufficiently documented and poorly understood. This study compiles and synthesizes existing scientific literature to provide the most comprehensive assessment to date of cartilaginous fish species richness across the Mediterranean Sea. Data were extracted from peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, and biodiversity assessments, focusing on sharks, rays, and chimaeras. Each record was georeferenced and standardized using the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) statistical grid system, enabling spatially consistent mapping and comparison. Species richness was calculated for each grid cell and categorized by taxonomic group (sharks, rays, chimaeras) and temporal period (pre2000 and post-2000 literature). The results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity in species richness, suggesting a distribution that diverges from earlier assumptions, with notable diversity emerging in regions beyond the traditionally recognized western and central Mediterranean basins. Temporal comparisons suggest improved reporting in recent decades but highlight persistent data gaps in certain subregions. This synthesis underscores the value of literature-based assessments as tools for identifying biodiversity patterns, research deficiencies, and conservation priorities for vulnerable cartilaginous fishes in the Mediterranean Sea.

1269: Shark conservation is vital for marine biodiversity, especially in South Asia where shark populations face increasing exploitation. In Sri Lanka, misconceptions and limited ecological awareness impede effective conservation. This study evaluated youth knowledge and attitudes to identify gaps and opportunities for awareness. An online questionnaire across Sri Lanka among youth yielded valid responses, revealing that 92.4% had consumed shark meat within the past five years. Among them, 43.2% consumed both fresh and dried shark meat, 36% only dried, and 8.99% only fresh meat. Awareness results showed that respondents disagreed that humans are frequently attacked by sharks (31.76%), with neutral responses at 45.6% (Mean = 2.85), and that killing sharks improves swimmer safety (76.5%, Mean = 1.98). Respondents were generally neutral about whether fewer sharks would enhance fish catch 36.2% (Mean = 2.52) or if too many sharks cause fish decline 39.6% (Mean = 2.45). However, 55.9% agreed that sharks help maintain healthy ocean ecosystems (Mean = 3.75), and 61.0% agreed that overfishing sharks affects other marine life and biodiversity balance (Mean = 3.60). Regarding endangered shark consumption, 63.7% were unaware, while 35.1% did not support eating it. Although 52.5% were unwilling to change consumption habits, 40.6% were open to alternatives, and 6.9% were unsure, suggesting awareness could influence choices. Mean values were calculated using a five-point Likert scale (1–5), and percentages represent response frequencies. Overall, findings indicate moderate ecological awareness but poor understanding of endangered species. Strengthening education and outreach could enhance conservation attitudes and reduce shark consumption.

1271: Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) are iconic filter-feeding megafauna whose behaviour remains poorly understood, particularly in remote oceanic regions. Understanding their foraging ecology in marginal habitats is critical for predicting responses to climate change and informing conservation strategies. To investigate fine-scale movement and feeding behaviour at the northern edge of their distribution, we deployed short-term archival tags and video cameras on whale sharks in the Azores (2019–2023). The resulting dataset comprises over hours of high-resolution depth, temperature, and tri-axial movement data, supplemented by hours of ancillary video footage. Video analysis revealed two distinct feeding strategies – active lunge feeding and passive stationary feeding – targeting small forage fish aggregations in association with tuna schools. Whale sharks exhibited strong surface-oriented behaviour (>75% of time spent within the upper m), although occasional bathypelagic dives exceeded 1500 m. These findings provide the first quantitative characterisation of active foraging behaviour by whale sharks in Azorean waters, reinforcing previous evidence of the region's importance as a seasonal habitat in the North Atlantic, and offering an empirical foundation for training and validating behavioural inference models based on non-invasive, high-resolution biologging data.

1272: Advancing shark research and conservation in remote ocean territories requires innovative partnerships that extend beyond traditional academic frameworks. French Polynesia hosts the world’s largest shark sanctuary, covering 5.5 million km². Its sheer scale and remoteness make sharks difficult to monitor using conventional research approaches alone. This presentation shows how scientists, local institutions, artisanal & pelagic fishers, naturalists, technical & recreational divers, local stakeholders, and private maritime actors can co-produce meaningful shark science in oceanic island environments. Collaborative fieldwork across lagoon, reef, and offshore habitats enabled access to diverse environmental contexts, supporting improved documentation of species diversity (including confirmations of species not previously recorded locally), horizontal and vertical distribution, seasonal patterns, and variation in relative abundance. Citizen-science initiatives played a key role in expanding ecological observations across habitats and depths, demonstrating the value of local engagement for long-term Chondrichthyan monitoring. Meanwhile, partnerships with conservation-aligned maritime operators opened access to isolated atolls and advanced tools such as ROVs and submersibles, supporting deep-reef biodiversity surveys and movement-ecology research across island corridors. Across these initiatives, collaborative frameworks expanded spatial coverage, accelerated telemetry deployments, improved detection of rare and deep-reef taxa, strengthened social legitimacy for shark protection, and fostered local ownership of conservation efforts. These results illustrate that inclusive, adaptive, and context-rooted alliances, from citizen science networks to local authorities and maritime operators, offer a powerful model to scale elasmobranch science in large ocean nations. Empowering those who live, work, and navigate alongside sharks is fundamental to securing their future.

1274: There is growing recognition that conservation is ultimately about understanding and changing human behaviour. In the context of shark conservation, there is a need to change fisher behaviour to reduce overfishing of sharks and rays. Yet many shark conservation programs fail to achieve meaningful impact due to insufficient consideration of the socio-psychological and structural factors that influence fisher behaviour. Based on my research and practical experiences, I outline a general process, set of research instruments, and customisable ‘bundle of options’ for co-designing locally-appropriate behaviourally-mediated shark conservation programs, which draw on social-psychology, behavioural economics and existing adaptive management and conservation decision-making frameworks. I provide some background and theory for each step in the process and the associated method and illustrate their application with real-world examples from shark conservation programs in action in Indonesia. I emphasise the importance of interdisciplinary and participatory research and a culture of continuous learning. By offering a general, customisable pathway from evidence to action, I hope to guide conservation scientists and practitioners in designing, piloting, and scaling programs that are technically and socially feasible, and able to deliver measurable positive outcomes for sharks and coastal communities.

1275: Whale sharks Rhincodon typus are globally Endangered. The worldwide population is estimated to have declined by around half since the 1980s, primarily due to commercial fisheries. Successful conservation efforts – and, unfortunately, rapid population depletion – have led to a large reduction in targeted catches, but the species remains under pressure from net fisheries and cryptic mortality sources such as ship strike and plastic pollution. This talk provides an overview of whale shark conservation priorities and open research questions across the species' circumtropical range, organised into five spatial units: Atlantic, Western Indian Ocean, Arabian Sea, Asia–Pacific, and the Eastern Pacific. The Atlantic and Eastern Pacific are characterised by uncertainty in abundance trends and threat profiles. Whale sharks in the Western Indian Ocean have exhibited steep, largely unexplained declines in local abundance since the early 2000s. Arabian Sea whale sharks face pressure from gillnets and shipping. The Asia–Pacific has ongoing fisheries impacts and emerging concerns about plastic ingestion. Across its range, we need to improve our understanding of population-level abundance, trends, and the influence of broad-scale environmental factors on local fluctuations in whale shark numbers. Three "elephants in the room" are (1) the bias towards juvenile male sharks at most monitored sites, (2) the lack of knowledge on adult whale sharks, which largely reside in the open ocean, and (3) the difficulty of attributing mortality to cryptic threats such as ship strike. Encouragingly, a coordinated global research network now provides a strong foundation for the next phase of whale shark conservation and recovery.

1276: Significant gaps in knowledge remain for human-shark interaction risk in nearshore environments, with climate change adding complexity to this risk. This project aims to track bull sharks with acoustic tags to correlate movements with environmental data to elucidate fluctuations in abundance off southeast Queensland, Australia. Fieldwork commenced in 2023, and catch rates in highly urbanised systems appear extremely low. Concurrently, less developed Sunshine Coast rivers appear to have healthy bull shark populations, with newborns detected by late October each year. Eighty-seven C. leucas across four neighbouring river systems have been internally acoustically tagged. Preliminary detection data indicates a significant overlap of juvenile and sub-adult habitat use. Smaller sharks (<1m TL) initially tagged upriver were prevalent in the lower reaches after rainfall, when turbidity was higher – areas usually maintained by sub-adults (1.5-2m TL). Sub-adults that have left their home estuaries are highly site attached to nearshore coastal waters, visiting neighbouring embayments and rivers, but also returning to the lower reaches of their home rivers repeatedly. Understanding this coastal connectivity is important to facilitate improved shark education and technological mitigation initiatives, as well as to advance conservation outcomes for apex predators in the UNESCO Biosphere Reserves of southeast Queensland.

1278: Cartilaginous fish are a crucial part of marine ecosystems, often playing the role of either mesopredators or apex predators. Long maturing periods and slow population recovery render many species vulnerable to anthropogenic factors such as overfishing or bycatch. Chondrites aren’t often associated with low salinity habitats such as the Baltic Sea. However, its connection to the North Sea through the Kattegat and Skagerrak creates a unique transition area. There are multiple species of cartilaginous fish that end up as bycatch during commercial fishing within FAO area 27.3. This study examined the TLW and FAO area of different species of Chondritheys from 2006 to 2023. This data was provided by ICES based on the information aquired from national offices in cooperation with Eurostat and FAO. The data gathered reveals the continuing presence of several critically endangered species such as Dipturus batis and Galeorhinus galeus, and many other vulnerable species including Chimaera monstrosa and Squalus acanthias. Additionally, we can observe multiple nonnative species occasionally being caught. The high numbers of non-commercially used cartilaginous fish being recorded within the dataset suggest a persisting issue of bycatch that may lead to reduction of individuals in local communities as well as effectively hinder the recovery of Squalus acanthias populations. Further research could identify the causes for the appearance of nonnative species and implement new conservation measures aiming to preserve the populations of the Baltic Sea and the Transition belt. 1279: Threatened chondrichthyan species play an important role in sustaining livelihoods and nutrition. In India, a top shark fishing nation, chondrichthyans are often an important secondary catch, with their retention driven by local meat consumption. In this talk, we compile multiauthor research from restaurants, households, and landing centres across India to identify localised patterns and determinants of chondrichthyan meat consumption. Using a variety of traditional and novel methods, including data from restaurant menus, semi-structured interviews, and discrete choice models, we find spatially and culturally distinct patterns of consumption across the country. While restaurants contribute a smaller proportion to consumption, this demand is reportedly growing highlighting an urgent need for conservation action. Household consumption constitutes the majority, is determined by socio-cultural status/identity and lower prices of chondrichthyes meat compared to other seafood. Chondrichthyan meat is an important protein source for lower economic and marginalised communities making planning conservation action more complex. We identify specific groups, such as tourists in Goa, or cultural practices, involving consumption of mobula rays in North Kerala, or sting rays in West Bengal that require context-specific conservation interventions. Household consumption patterns also reflect a strong local ecological knowledge and traditional dietary practices that influence consumer behaviour. We also identify broader determinants of demand that influence choice behaviour and decision making regarding consumption pattern, which is further shaped by access to marine resources, settlement type, and market availability. Results from these studies will work together to inform context-specific shark and ray policy interventions, aligned with fisher community interests.

1280: In terrestrial environments, nest site selection by birds and mammals is often related to the physical attributes of surrounding vegetation. Similarly, some elasmobranchs use different habitats, including kelps, as oviposition sites. However, habitat features that drive oviposition sites remain poorly understood. We examined the relationship between kelp morphology (holdfast diameter, number of stripes, and total length) and kelp forest configuration (density, size structure, predator density) with egg presence to identify the factors influencing oviposition site choice in the redspotted catshark (Schroederycthys chilensis). Surveys were conducted over a latitudinal gradient (19°S-40°S), identifying eight sites with nesting ground, encompassing much of the overlap between the kelp, Lessonia trabeculata and S. chilensis in Chile. At the individual scale, S. chilensis selected larger kelps within a patch, independent of the general population size structure. The number of eggs and clutches was positively associated with stipe length and holdfast diameter. Across all sites, egg-bearing kelps were consistently clustered at a similar depth in the kelp forest rather than being randomly distributed. At the site-scale, egg number had a negative correlation with their main predator, Taliepus dentatus, and juvenile kelp density. These results suggest that S. chilensis prioritizes vertical separation from the substrate when selecting oviposition sites, likely mediated by competition in areas where eggs are already present. Because patch size structure is strongly influenced by harvesting pressure, with intensive harvesting causing high densities of shorter individuals, overexploitation may reduce the availability of suitable substrates and ultimately constrain the reproductive success of S. chilensis

1281: Bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) are apex predators with ecological and economic relevance in coastal ecosystems of the Caribbean. In the Mexican Caribbean, increasing human interactions, particularly through ecotourism and fisheries, have raised concerns about the population status and conservation needs. In this project, we applied a multidisciplinary research approach aimed at elucidating the conservation status of bull sharks in the region. Using surveys of fishers and divers in this region and monitoring diving activities, fisheries, and coastal ecosystems, we aim to create baseline information that allows us to understand the conservation status of this specie in the Mexican Caribbean. We integrate data from behavioral studies in diving contexts, population genetics analyses, and habitat use assessments, with a focus on the identification of nursery areas. Bull shark is an important specie for fisheries and tourism in the Mexican Caribbean. Behavioral observations reveal patterns of site fidelity and tolerance to human presence, which may influence management strategies in ecotourism zones. Genetic analyses suggest moderate population connectivity with other regions and signs of localized structuring, suggesting the presence of a third population in the West Atlantic, highlighting the importance of regional conservation planning. We identified the existence of at least one nursery area in the southern part of the Mexican Caribbean, underscoring the need for spatial protection measures. These findings provide a scientific foundation for evidence-based conservation and management of bull sharks in the Mexican Caribbean, contributing to broader efforts in marine biodiversity conservation.

1282: In 2010, we started a research project to study the populations of sharks caught by artisanal fishing in Golfo Dulce, South Pacific of Costa Rica. We determined that sharks represented 40% of the total individuals caught, with the scalloped hammerhead shark (Sphyrna lewini) being the most frequently caught species of sharks. Since then, we have continued monitoring the S. lewini population in Golfo Dulce. Through years of scientific research, we identified the first nursery ground for the scalloped hammerhead shark in the entire Eastern Tropical Pacific. With the engagement of local communities, in 2018, the Costa Rican government declared the Scalloped Hammerhead Shark Sanctuary in Golfo Dulce, a new model of governance for Costa Rica. Our organization has developed an integrated approach where local leadership drives community awareness, education, and active participation in shark conservation. This approach also provides socio-economic opportunities for the most vulnerable groups, based on nature protection and restoration. Thanks to this approach, we have reported a significant increase in the relative abundances of the scalloped hammerhead shark (H = 19,81 p=0,0004); a community association composed mainly of fishers have restored hectares of mangroves related to the shark nursery; and more than people have been trained in livelihood alternatives. The scalloped hammerhead shark has become a symbol of pride within Golfo Dulce communities. The municipality has even changed its logo for a hammerhead shark. This is a case of study of how inclusive models in shark conservation could benefit people and nature.

1283: There is a debate amongst investigators regarding whether sharks feel conscious pain or not. The physiology of pain in sharks or fish, in general, has not yet been established due to the limited studies on the nociceptor pathways. The processing of painful stimuli depends on specific structures within the central nervous system, the most important being the cortex in mammals and its counterpart, the dorsal pallium in elasmobranchs. This project aims to determine whether there is a direct or indirect connection between the trigeminal nerve and the dorsal pallium, in order to identify a relationship between structures capable of processing painful stimuli in sharks. Using retrograde neural tracing, the intracerebral pathway of the trigeminal nerve was mapped in the carpet shark. The tracer was active from the starting point of the trigeminal nerve, through the four nuclei of the trigeminal nerve, the cerebellum, the trigeminothalamic tract, the thalamus, the thalamotelencephalic tract, and to the medial pallium. Although no connection was found with the dorsal pallium, all identified connected structures are related to long-term memory, spatial learning, and structures capable of processing and transmitting painful stimuli, such as the trigeminothalamic tract and the descending nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. These brain connections may help determine whether sharks perceive a painful stimulus, or with a degree of awareness that can be defined as pain, nociception, or an intermediate sensation.

1285: Across the southeastern Pacific, several benthic elasmobranch species remain poorly studied, hindering effective conservation and fisheries management at national scale. Among them, angel sharks (Squatiniformes) are of particular concern due to increasing human pressures and their negative impacts on population abundances. In Peru, two angel shark species are historically reported, the Chilean angel shark Squatina armata (Philippi, 1887) and the Pacific angel shark S. californica Ayres, 1859. Both are reported to be caught by artisanal fisheries and are listed on the IUCN Red List as Critically Endangered and Vulnerable, respectively. However, both species remain largely understudied, with scarce biological and ecological information. This study summarizes a 14-month project conducted in northern Peru (2022-2023), representing the first local-scale effort to collect species-specific data on the biology, ecology, and fishery of S. armata, conducted in collaboration with local fishers and students. Our monitoring revealed that angel sharks remain a target species in some communities (e.g., San José, Lambayeque), while in others (e.g., Cancas, Piura) they are mainly caught as bycatch, reflecting local perceptions of declining abundance. Fishers expressed growing concern about the species’ scarcity, though multispecies fisheries pose challenges to change fishing effort. Reproductive biological analyses indicate the presence of subadult and adult individuals, but few juveniles or pregnant females. Preliminary trophic ecology results suggest one of the most dominant groups in the diet were ray-finned fish (families Engraulidae and Sciaenidae). These findings provide essential baseline information to support future conservation and management initiatives for angel sharks in Peruvian waters.

1287: Fishing activities are the primary threat to deepwater chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras). These species are highly susceptible to overexploitation but are frequently captured as bycatch in deepwater fisheries. While international interest in understanding and reducing fishing mortality on chondrichthyans is growing, limited research has been conducted on deepwater species. Leafscale Gulper Shark (Centrophorus squamosus) are being tagged with Wildlife Computer survivorship tags (sPATs) as part of a study to understand their post-release survival in offshore fisheries in New Zealand and the wider Pacific region. To date, individuals have been tagged in bottom longline fisheries and five in bottom trawl fisheries. Survival estimates vary considerably by fishing trip, with to 60% survival in longline gear, and 40% in trawl gear. Three tags have been recovered, and tag data showed sharks engaged in regular diel movement patterns with preferred temperature and depth ranges. Survival in the longline fisheries is comparable with a study in the Northeast Atlantic, but to the author’s knowledge, this is the first attempt to tag trawl-caught sharks. While these preliminary survivorship estimates are promising, depth profiles suggest the species spends most of its vertical distribution within the reach of current fishing effort, with limited refuge at depth.

1289: Port Phillip Bay (PPB) is a large but shallow bay in Victoria, Australia. It hosts Australia’s busiest commercial port, large numbers of recreational fishers, shellfish farming, yacht clubs, and many tourist activities. PPB is subject to intense impacts from anthropogenic activities and climate change and is also home to over species of sharks and rays, many of which are endemic to Southern Australian and resident within the bay. Aside from a few key commercial and/or charismatic species, the ecology of many resident sharks is not well known. The Movement Ecology and Management of Elasmobranchs Lab (MEME Lab) has begun a largescale study on the ecological roles of the PPB residents. This work is being completed in collaboration with the Wadawurrung Traditional Owner Sea Rangers. We have a network of over acoustic receivers deployed throughout the bay and have internally tagged over individuals from seven species to-date. Tissue samples are being taken to complete stable isotope and fatty acid analyses, in addition to a fin clip for genetic studies. Preliminary results on movement of tagged species will be presented, including Melbourne Skate, Sevengill Shark, Port Jackson Shark, and Southern Fiddler Ray. Finally, future plans for the project will be described along with opportunities for collaboration. Understanding the current niche occupation of the resident species in PPB will enable monitoring of changes as other species are moving further south with warming ocean and changing current conditions.

1290: The oceanic manta ray (Mobula birostris) is a wide-ranging pelagic species threatened due to its low reproductive output and high susceptibility to anthropogenic pressures, particularly fisheries. Satellite telemetry data from individuals tracked between 2017 and 2024 in Revillagigedo National Park, a no-take marine protected area (MPA) in Mexico, were used to investigate space use, seasonal movements, and overlap with industrial fishing. This study provides the first satellite telemetry assessment of oceanic manta rays in the Mexican Pacific. Machine learning models combining state-space tracks with environmental data were applied to predict spatial occurrence. Predicted occurrence was highest within the protected area but extended well beyond its boundaries, with seasonal expansion toward the Gulf of California during summer and autumn. Over one-third of estimated positions occurred outside the park, where high occurrence probability overlapped with intense tuna purse-seine effort along MPA boundaries. Individuals varied substantially in space use, with the longest recorded movement exceeding 1,300 km. These findings underscore both the conservation value of Revillagigedo National Park and the limitations of static protected areas, underscoring the need for a mosaic of larger, and connected protected areas in the Eastern Tropical Pacific and bycatch mitigation efforts.

1291: Rays and sharks are among the most threatened marine vertebrates globally. Around one-third of all elasmobranch species are now facing a risk of extinction, with overfishing driven by human consumption threatening more than 95% of these species. Yet, despite growing conservation concerns, elasmobranchs continue to be caught and consumed, particularly in coastal regions. Understanding the socio-economic drivers behind this demand is critical for designing effective conservation strategies. This study explores the factors shaping consumer preferences for ray and shark products in West Bengal, India. Using a Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) approach, structured household surveys were conducted across inland and coastal settlements to assess perceptions related to taste, availability, price, health benefits, texture, curiosity, and convenience. Taste and texture emerged as the strongest factors influencing consumption decisions. The findings show that ray meat consumption is notably higher in coastal regions and among lower- to middle-income households, even though ray meat was often reported to be more expensive than other fish. Respondents also associated ray meat with significant health benefits, reflecting strong traditional dietary beliefs that influence consumer behaviour. Access to marine resources, settlement type, and market availability further shaped consumption patterns. Our results highlight that ray consumption is deeply embedded in Bengal’s culinary culture, and challenge the widespread assumption that economic necessity alone drives elasmobranch consumption and instead point to a complex interplay of cultural, ecological, and economic factors. Successful efforts must recognize the cultural importance and actively engage local communities through context-specific approaches that respect their values, knowledge, and livelihoods.

1292: Global shark populations are rapidly declining due to excessive fishing, weak governance, and poorly regulated trade, threatening marine biodiversity and ocean ecosystem stability. As the world’s largest shark-catching nation, Indonesia plays a crucial role in ensuring sustainable shark management. This study analyzes the biological and utilization characteristics of sharks landed in Jakarta to detect signs of biological overexploitation. Fieldwork conducted from February to December 2023 at the Nizam Zachman Ocean Fishing Port (Muara Baru) and Muara Angke combined biological measurements with interviews of fishers and traders. Analyses covered length–weight relationships, sex ratios, maturity stages, and trade patterns. Twenty shark species were identified, of which showed negative allometric growth, indicating environmental or nutritional stress. Females accounted for 62% of specimens, while 46% of males were immature (TKK I). The dominance of juveniles—particularly in Carcharhinus leucas, C. limbatus, Sphyrna lewini, and Galeocerdo cuvier—suggests recruitment overfishing. Several species listed under CITES Appendix II, such as Sphyrna lewini and Carcharhinus falciformis, were frequently landed, revealing deficiencies in trade control and enforcement. Jakarta’s shark fisheries are thus characterized by unsustainable exploitation, dominated by immature and reproductively active individuals. Strengthening monitoring, enforcing size limits, and promoting community-based alternative livelihoods are urgently needed. At broader scales, Indonesia bears a vital responsibility to curb shark population declines through proactive, science-based governance aligned with FAO and CITES frameworks.

1293: Changing ecological factors pose a challenge to many organisms. Global changes and the associated environmental changes have major impacts on marine organisms and threaten the biodiversity of marine ecosystems. It has been shown in previous experimental studies that ocean acidification caused by anthropogenic CO release into the atmosphere and subsequent dissolution in seawater will have a significant impact on various marine organisms. Here, we investigated the corrosive effects from acidification on the morphology of isolated shark teeth in an eight-week incubation at a pH of 7.3, the expected seawater pH in the year 2300. The typical littoral blacktip reef shark (Carcharhinus melanopterus), which is often kept in display aquaria under controlled conditions, has been used for this purpose, greatly facilitating minimally invasive sampling for in-situ investigation. The teeth of this typical Requiem Shark species are orthodont teeth, which show strong serration in the teeth of the upper jaw. Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) we could observe the corrosive effects of acidification on the different tooth structures, such as the root, primary and secondary serrations and the crown of the blacktip reef sharks teeth. Our results show that ocean acidification will have significant effects on the morphological properties of teeth, including visible corrosion on the crown, degradation of root structures, and loss of fine serration details under low pH conditions which could lead to changes in foraging efficiency, energy uptake, and ultimately elasmobranch fitness in future oceans.

1295: Quantifying the total catches of deepwater sharks in the areas beyond national jurisdiction (ABNJ) is challenging because of uncertainty in both the total amount and taxonomic resolution of catch reporting. The FAO Deep-sea Fisheries under the Ecosystem Approach Project aims to shine a light on catch reporting of sharks in the dark, an essential step for the assessment of the impact of deep-sea fisheries on deepwater sharks. The seven regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) responsible for the management of deep-sea fisheries in ABNJ are partners of the project and have already adopted management measures that require the reporting of sharks as part of fisheries reporting obligations. Finding ways to strengthen the implementation of these measures and improve the quality of catch data reporting were the main topics of a FAO global workshop held in July 2025. The workshop selected a group of widely distributed deepwater shark species with realistic identification potential, and data availability as a focus for ongoing activities under the project. These activities include: 1) a coordinated review of deepwater shark data in FAO Statistics; 2) the provision of guidance to RFMOs on the use of the most appropriate ASFIS 3-alpha codes, including a set of identification materials; 3) the development of a global ecological risk assessment for deepwater sharks; 4) the enhancement of industry engagement. Providing guidance on targeted, tractable improvements in the catch reporting of deep-water sharks can substantially enhance our understanding of the impacts on deepwater sharks of deep-sea fisheries in ABNJ.

1297: Globally, unsustainable exploitation of sharks and rays is driven by strong demand for component products however the role of lower-value products in driving exploitation such as shark and ray meat remains poorly understood. Addressing this knowledge gap, as to why consumers buy shark and ray meat, and which attributes and wider contextual factors play a key role, is key for advancing shark and ray conservation and policy. Such data can be used to design policies that act across value chains, to shape consumer demand, rather than focusing solely on resource user behaviours. These are likely to be more sustainable long-term, by removing drivers for exploitation that arise from consumer demand. We will present our work conducted across Sri Lanka and India that has used choice modelling, value chain mapping and semi-structured interviews to profile consumer preference and consumption patterns in both countries, elucidate socio-cultural drivers of consumption and then results from modelling of consumer choices. We hope this talk will represent a timely opportunity to discuss how a holistic understanding of demand for shark and ray meat can be utilised to better design conservation and management action across value chains.

1299: Small-scale fisheries sustain millions of livelihoods globally but can threaten vulnerable marine megafauna such as sharks. Understanding what drives fishers’ behaviour, and how they might respond to different conservation strategies, is crucial for designing effective and equitable interventions. We examined behavioural motivations and conservation preferences of seasonal, small-scale shark fishers in Goa, India, through qualitative and participatory scenario interviews. Six hypothetical interventions, ranging from social incentives and alternative livelihoods to regulatory bans, were explored with shark fishers to assess perceived impacts and willingness to change behaviour. We found that shark fishing was primarily driven by instrumental and economic motivations, enabled by access to capital and labour. Contrary to expectations, fishers expressed the greatest willingness to comply with a state-imposed shark fishing ban, viewing it as fair and enforceable because it applied equally to all. Interventions that relied on voluntary cooperation, trust, or collective action, such as the social incentives, received lower support, reflecting potentially weak local institutions. While regulatory bans may appear to be the most acceptable option, they must be co-designed with fishing communities to avoid unintended livelihood impacts and ensure legitimacy. By integrating behavioural insights with participatory scenario analysis, our study provides an empirically grounded approach for understanding fisher decision-making and conservation trade-offs in data-poor contexts. Our work informs conservation of sharks in India, and underscores the importance of combining state regulations with community participation to promote socially just and sustainable shark conservation.

1300: Fuvahmulah, Maldives, hosts the world’s largest documented aggregation of tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier), yet key aspects of their population structure, residency, and reproduction remain unexamined. Over an eight-year period, individual tiger sharks were identified using photo identification and laser photogrammetry, with a female-biased sex ratio (84.5%). Residency analyses indicate that adult females exhibit strong site fidelity, spending an average of 60.7 ± 7.5 days in the area. Underwater ultrasonography of adult females revealed that 93% were pregnant, with two distinct embryonic size groups suggesting a biennial or asynchronous reproductive cycle. The high proportion of pregnant females and extended residency suggest Fuvahmulah functions as an important gestation site within the central Indian Ocean. These findings provide novel insights into the ecology and reproductive biology of tiger sharks and highlight the significance of long-term monitoring at aggregation sites. Fuvahmulah seems to provide good conditions for gestation, given the year-round provisioning of food and warm waters.

1301: The Bay of Biscay is increasingly recognized as a biodiversity hotspot for pelagic and elasmobranch species, playing a vital role in the life cycles of several threatened sharks and rays. Recent observations confirm the presence of emblematic species such as shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus), blue shark (Prionace glauca), thresher sharks (Alopias spp.), porbeagle (Lamna nasus), basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus), and hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna spp.). This study mainly focuses on blue sharks, which exhibit unexpected year-round residency in the region. Both young-of-the-year (YOY) and large adults of both sexes have been observed, many bearing mating scars. A recent visual recording of a courtship interaction between two blue sharks provides compelling evidence of reproductive activity. Additionally, we captured rare footage of a mating attempt in pelagic stingrays (Pteroplatytrygon violacea), offering novel insights into the behavior of this elusive species. Sightings of neonate blue sharks and juvenile shortfin mako and porbeagle sharks further support the hypothesis that the Bay may serve as a nursery ground. Spatial patterns show juveniles favor coastal areas, while adults are more associated with the continental slope and submarine canyons. Behavioral and tagging data reveal a preference for upper water layers and long-distance migratory links to regions such as the Azores and Cape Verde. These findings highlight the Bay of Biscay as a multifunctional habitat essential for reproduction, development, and connectivity of vulnerable elasmobranchs, underscoring the need for targeted conservation and further research.

1303: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are often used to protect at risk species, however, their effectiveness in protecting wide-ranging species is uncertain. In the Eastern Tropical Pacific, silky sharks (Carcharhinus falciformis) have experienced large declines and may benefit from the recently expanded network of MPAs in the region. We tracked silky sharks from the Galapagos Marine Reserve (GMR) with SPOT tags for up to d to examine how much time they spent in MPAs and their overlap with fisheries. The amount of time sharks spent within MPAs varied little between the wet (Dec-May) and dry seasons (Jun-Nov), with sharks spending extended periods of time in the GMR during both seasons. Overall, females and males spent 33% and ~45% of their time within the GMR, respectively. Silky sharks, however, spent comparatively little time in other MPAs as total time within all MPAs was 44% and 55% for females and males, respectively. Although there was considerable overlap in the areas sharks and fisheries used, sharks experienced the highest risk from fishing during the dry season within Ecuadorian waters north of the Hermandad Marine Reserve. Sharks did not encounter concentrated areas of fishing risk during the wet season; however, available fishing data severely underestimate fishing effort in the region. Overall, silky sharks spent a high proportion of time within the protected waters of the GMR, but their wide-ranging movements extended far beyond the GMR and other marine reserves, putting them at risk from commercial fisheries operating in the region.

1307: This study aims to analyze the trade dynamics and product distribution of the giant shovelnose ray (Glaucostegus typus) within the management area of the Loka Pengelolaan Sumber Daya Pesisir dan Laut (LPSPL) Serang, based on quantitative analysis of verified trade data from 2021 to 2025. The analyzed product categories include meat, skin, bone, fins, and live specimens. Data were compiled from verified trade documents, export–import records, and field observations conducted across the management area. A quantitative descriptive approach was applied to evaluate annual volume trends, product composition, and the spatial distribution of trade flows. The results reveal a substantial increase in the total trade volume of G. typus, with the highest growth recorded for fin products (±1283%), followed by bone (±1220%) and dried skin (±1100%). Meat products exhibited the slowest growth (±550%) during the same period. Domestic trade activities were concentrated in Jakarta, Banten, and Surabaya as major export gateways, while China and Hong Kong were identified as the principal international destinations. These findings provide a scientific basis for strengthening management and monitoring policies concerning the trade of CITES Appendix II–listed species at both national and regional levels.

1310: There is growing global demand for deep-sea resources as a result of declining coastal fisheries and increased interest in extractive activities. Deep-sea sharks are targeted for their meat and liver, in addition to being caught as bycatch in fisheries leading to increasing conservation concern. However, information on the ecological role of deep-sea sharks is incredibly limited and there is little understanding of the ecological consequences of commercial fishing on deep-sea sharks. Deep-sea community structures may shift in the wake of increasing anthropogenic pressures and there is urgent need to determine how species will respond. Our aim is to understand the ecological role of deep-sea sharks by determining how fishing pressure is altering the trophic structure of deep-sea ecosystems over an extensively fished region - Chatham Rise, New Zealand. A time series of diet composition using stomach content and stable isotope data from historical and contemporary sample collections from the research trawl surveys will be created, to determine if and how fishing pressure has changed the trophic ecology of deep-sea sharks in recent decades. Focal species will include the commercially important School Shark (Galeorhinus galeus) and Spiny Dogfish (Squalus acanthias) and frequent bycatch and threatened species such as Leafscale Gulper (Centrophorus squamosus). Understanding the ecological role of deep-sea sharks will help inform our knowledge of which species are most resilient, and most susceptible, to changes in deep-sea ecosystems, which can guide conservation and management plans to ensure species’ persistence, recovery, and overall ecosystem stability.

1313: Elasmobranchs face constant threats from various anthropogenic stressors, one of the most pressing being microplastic pollution. Along the west coast of India, artisanal and commercial fisheries operate, frequently capturing sharks and rays as bycatch. The scaly whip ray (Brevitrygon walga) is a commonly landed species in this region and constitutes a part of the local diet. In light of this growing concern, this study aimed to quantify microplastics (MPs) in the Brevitrygon walga from Malvan, a major fishing harbour and tourism hotspot. As a demersal species, B. walga is highly susceptible to MP accumulation but there is no documented data on MP ingestion by these rays in the Arabian Sea. We collected muscle tissue, and gut tissue and content, from scaly whiprays at the landing centre in Malvan, Maharashtra and subsequently processed them. The findings confirm the presence of microplastics in B. walga, dominated by transparent fibres likely from discarded fishing gear like nets and ropes. There was no correlation between disc width and the quantity of microplastics ingested. Muscle tissue had the highest occurrence of MPs followed by gut tissue and content; their lower abundance in gut content suggests possible expulsion, while higher levels in muscle indicate accumulation in edible tissues over time. Raman spectroscopy identified pigments like PB and PR 270, commonly used in plastic. This raises concerns regarding human exposure to microplastics through seafood consumption and underscores the urgent need to monitor and manage plastic debris to safeguard elasmobranch and human health.

1314: The sawfishes (family Pristidae) are among the most imperilled elasmobranchs globally. In northern Australia, extensive wet-season flooding allows Largetooth Sawfish (Pristis pristis) pups to access vast floodplain habitat. As waters recede, sawfish retreat to isolated waterholes where they remain throughout the dry season; if rains arrive too late, these habitats dry and the sawfish perish. A long-term collaboration between Indigenous rangers and researchers was established to locate and rescue stranded individuals. This study presents ecological and molecular insights from years (2012–2024) of these ‘sawfish rescues’, examining: (a) the history of the rescues; (b) environmental drivers of sawfish occurrence and abundance in floodplain habitats; and (c) genetic relatedness among stranded juveniles using a multi-marker approach. A total of young-of-the-year sawfish were rescued. Models revealed a significant positive association between wet-season discharge; length of floodplain inundation; and sawfish presence, abundance, and size, suggesting that large wet seasons are essential for juvenile access to floodplain resources. Genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data from genotyped sawfish revealed kin pairs, comprising full-sibling and halfsibling pairs. Only half-siblings occurred between cohorts, with 85% sharing a mitochondrial haplotype (indicative of female philopatry). The effective number of breeders per cohort was estimated at 85.7–286.2 adults. These findings underscore the ecological importance of lateral connectivity between river channels and floodplains for juvenile P. pristis in the face of mounting anthropogenic pressures in the Daly River and northern Australia more broadly.

1317: Gliding has evolved as a mechanism of reducing the energetic costs of locomotion and is generally considered an important trait for species occupying fluid environments. Mobulids, such as the reef manta ray, have a dorso-ventrally flattened body that differs from that of other pelagic species occupying similar niches. Given the benthic ancestral past of this species, this body form poses the question of how well-suited reef mantas are to their now-pelagic lifestyle. We equipped species of pelagic and benthic species of bony fish, sharks and rays with biologging tags to examine their gliding performance in the form of their lift-drag ratios, defined as the horizontal distance travelled over the potential energy lost in the form of depth during steady state gliding (DHorizontal/Dvertical) where greater ratios indicate greater performance. We found the lift-drag ratio of reef mantas (13.5) to be larger than those of the other species (3.4 – 8.5). The optimal glide angles at which lift-drag ratios were maximised predicted the glide angles utilised by individuals (rho = 0.606), suggesting that maximising liftdrag ratios is important in the gliding behaviour of fishes. Surprisingly, we found no evidence that ecological importance of the behaviour leads to the evolution of higher gliding ratios. We suggest that the high gliding performance of reef mantas is a result of an evolutionary predisposition to a pelagic lifestyle, giving rise to greater performance than their fusiform relatives occupying similar ecological niches.
Manta Matters: Shaping Fisheries Policy with Mobulid Science

1320: Aerial drones provide an unprecedented opportunity to monitor fine-scale movement and habitat utilization of elasmobranchs in shallow ecosystems. Here, we use drones to investigate habitat partitioning among stingrays in a coastal lagoon in the Red Sea. We conducted aerial transect surveys (~16ha each) and actively tracked rays (total tracking time 23h). Imagery from the tracking surveys was used to train a deep learning model for automated ray detection, achieving a mean Average Precision (mAP-50) of 85%. Using a double-observer protocol (manual + model), 1,467 rays were sighted in the transect imagery, with the model detecting 97% of these observations compared to 76% detected by human analysts. Bluespotted ribbontail rays (Taeniura lymma) dominated the detections (n=1,221), followed by larger-bodied whiprays (predominantly Himantura uarnak and Pateobatis fai; n=187). Additionally, eagle rays (Aetobatus ocellatus), mangrove whiprays (Urogymnus granulatus), cowtail rays (Pastinachus sephen), unidentified rays, sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus and Negaprion acutidens), and unidentified guitarfish were observed. We identified pronounced habitat partitioning between T. lymma and the whiprays. T. lymma favored the shallowest parts (~0.2m) of the lagoon along the mangrove edge, where it was frequently observed to be digging, highlighting this area as a key feeding ground and a bioturbation hotspot. In contrast, the whiprays predominantly occupied macroalgal habitats on the adjacent reef flat. Our findings demonstrate how drone-based monitoring combined with deep learning can reveal the finescale spatial ecology of elasmobranchs in nearshore ecosystems.

1321: Conservation of sharks has gained importance due to their critical ecological role as higher order predators and alarming population declines in some species. Some shark species are potentially dangerous to humans and programs have been implemented to minimise interactions with water users. The present study evaluated the effectiveness of SMART drumlines, a relatively new shark management tool designed to minimise wildlife mortality, compared to traditional fishing gear such as bottom set longlines and gillnets. Capture data of bycatch and target shark species in the shark management programs of La Réunion (France) and New South Wales (Australia) were analysed. The capture selectivity and at-vessel mortality of target shark and bycatch species was assessed, and the efficiency and mortality of each fishing gear was compared. Traditional gillnets resulted in increased mortality rates and showed lower CPUE of target sharks than SMART drumlines and bottom set longlines. Bottom set longlines provided a balanced approach, demonstrating moderate capture efficiency with lower associated mortality than gillnets but not SMART drumlines. This research highlights that SMART drumlines can improve shark management associated with water-user protection programs by enhancing the capture efficiency of target species and reducing bycatch mortality, contributing to both public safety and conservation efforts for sharks and other marine fauna.

1323: Chondrichthyans have been the focus of numerous dietary studies, yet few have explored the processes that enable coexistence among sympatric mesopredators. Understanding resource use requires quantifying trophic niche width and overlap, from which feeding strategies and potential competition can be inferred. This study used stable isotope and multivariate fatty acid analyses to assess habitat and prey preferences, estimate niche width, and predict overlap among sympatric chondrichthyan mesopredators from southern Australia an ecosystem increasingly affected by tropicalisation, flooding, marine heatwaves, and subsequent harmful algal blooms (HABs). The current HAB affecting South Australia is disrupting food webs by altering prey availability and degrading habitat quality, further underscoring the importance of understanding how predators partition resources. Stable isotope data grouped species into pelagic and sandy/seagrass-associated assemblages, while fatty acid profiles revealed two clusters with greater interspecific overlap, suggesting complex resource partitioning through nutritional segregation or habitat differentiation. Mobile species such as southern eagle rays (Myliobatis tenuicaudatus) and bronze whalers (Carcharhinus brachyurus) exhibited the broadest niches, indicating generalist feeding strategies. In contrast, less mobile species such as southern sawsharks (Pristiophorus nudipinnis) and elephant fish (Callorhinchus milii) displayed specialist traits, feeding on high trophic-level prey. Overlap occurred across taxa and between generalists and specialists, highlighting the need for diverse and connected habitats to support prey populations and minimise competition. Given mounting pressures such as tropicalisation, trawling, and harmful algal blooms, understanding trophic interactions and resource partitioning among mesopredatory chondrichthyans is critical for effective ecosystem management.

1326: Studying individual differences in behaviour and plasticity across changing environmental gradients remains challenging in wild sharks. Utilizing a touristic shark-feeding site in Fiji, we quantified the fine-scale behaviour of free-ranging bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) over three years. We assessed two behavioural responses, both likely linked to risk-taking and riskavoidance, using video-coded observations. Mixed-effects models revealed substantial, temporally stable individual differences, not only in mean behaviour but also in seasonal plasticity. Cluster analysis of the model outputs resolved distinct behavioural profiles along potential high-risk/low-risk and high-plasticity/low-plasticity axes. Collectively, these results provide rare field evidence that sharks differ consistently in their individual behaviour and in how strongly they adjust to changing environments. They further highlight the need to recognise individuality as an important component of human-shark interactions, aiding mitigation and shaping public risk perception.

1328: Sharks remain among the most misunderstood animals in the ocean, and persistent fear-based narratives continue to hinder conservation and meaningful public engagement. This presentation explores how intentional storytelling, empathetic imagery and careful use of language can shift these perceptions and foster a more accurate understanding of sharks. Drawing from my work as an award-winning shark photographer, educator and my training under Swiss shark behaviour researcher Dr. Erich Ritter, I will illustrate how behavioural insight paired with visual storytelling can effectively challenge widespread misconceptions. Photographs that portray sharks in calm, natural or behaviourally typical contexts help audiences connect with them emotionally, which is essential for building support for their protection. Equally important is the language used when discussing shark encounters. Words such as “attack” and "aggressive" carry strong emotional weight and reinforce fear, even when incidents are minor. By choosing terms like “accident” or "curious", communicators can present a more accurate and balanced narrative. This shift in language, combined with approachable imagery, directly influences public attitudes and, ultimately, conservation outcomes. The session will also highlight the psychological link between empathy and willingness to protect a species: when people cannot relate to an animal, they are less inclined to value or defend it. By combining behavioural knowledge, storytelling, photography and reframing strategies, this presentation offers practical tools for scientists, educators, conservationists and communicators seeking to modernise how sharks are represented and inspire a more informed, empathetic public.

1329: Due to the high trophic positions sharks occupy as apex predators, they are known to biomagnify toxic metals. This is problematic because shark meat consumption is increasing throughout the world, seen as a cheap and accessible source of dietary protein. This increased consumption can expose humans to concentrations of toxic metals above those deemed safe by regulatory authorities. Shark meat is frequently dried or sold as fillets making it difficult to identify the species. We therefore used DNA barcoding to determine the species of shark used in meat products. Shark meat was collected from retail establishments in Singapore, and 1,743 samples successfully barcoded, resulting in unique shark species. Of our samples, 27% and 89% fall under CITES Appendix II as per the updates before and after COP19, respectively. of these samples were further analysed using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry to determine the concentrations of mercury, arsenic, cadmium, and lead in each. In all samples, across all species we found multiple instances where mandated safe concentrations for each metal were exceeded. Grouping samples by habitat type revealed significant differences in the concentrations of toxic metals between species from predominantly coastal and oceanic habitats. The results show that consumption of shark meat can expose consumers to high concentrations of toxic metals, with these concentrations varying significantly by species and habitat. Given these differences, accurate and detailed product labelling that indicates the species of origin and habitat would allow consumers to avoid species that pose the highest risk to health.

1333: Large pelagic sharks play pivotal roles in maintaining ocean ecosystem structure and stability, yet their populations are increasingly threatened by overfishing and climate-driven changes. Understanding their trophic ecology is essential for assessing ecological resilience and informing effective management. This research examines the trophic and competitive dynamics of two highly migratory and threatened shark species—the blue shark (Prionace glauca) and shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus)—in relation to co-occurring predators such as swordfish (Xiphias gladius). Using spatial distribution data, isotopic niche metrics, and diet reconstructions, we investigate inter- and intraspecific competition among these predators across the western Mediterranean and adjacent Atlantic waters. We integrate these findings within the context of global change, emphasizing how environmental (pelagic productivity), biological (competitor abundance), and anthropogenic (fishing pressure) stressors reshape predator interactions. On average, the potential for intraspecific competition was lowest for shortfin makos, the least frequent species. Makos had high isotopic niche overlap with blue sharks, feeding on similar prey. In the Mediterranean, the isotopic niche of blue sharks was broader than that of swordfish, which highly overlapped with the blue shark, although diet estimates suggest that swordfish rely on fish while blue sharks rely on squid. Our results suggest that pelagic productivity and competitor abundance are key drivers of intra- and interspecific trophic niche segregation between large pelagic predators, respectively. They support the hypothesis that niche partitioning is reduced under a scenario of high resource availability.
