1336: Passive electroreception is the ability to detect weak bioelectric fields produced by other organisms or as components of the Earth’s electromagnetic field. In chondrichthyans, this nonvisual sensory modality underpins essential behaviours including prey and predator detection, social interactions, and navigation. The electrosensory organs are called ampullae of Lorenzini. Each consists of an externally visible ampullary pore that opens into a canal connecting to a bulb, where electroreceptor cells are found. Ampullary pores are primarily located on the head in selachians, whereas they extend onto the pectoral fins in batoids. This study investigated whether ampullary pore distribution in elasmobranchs is influenced by phylogenetic and/or ecological factors. Data on total pore count and dorsal-to-ventral pore ratio were compiled from previous literature for species across ten orders, and categorised by phylogeny, habitat (including depth range), trophic level, and lifestyle. Phylogeny was found to be a significant factor, but interspecific differences showed no consistent evolutionary trend. Conversely, habitat and trophic level significantly influenced pore distribution, supporting previous findings suggesting that feeding ecology would best explain morphological distributions. A clear, positive correlation between trophic level and dorsal-to-ventral pore ratio indicated that benthic species possess more ventral pores. No significant differences were observed among depth zones. Overall, our results highlight the importance of ecological factors in shaping electrosensory morphology in elasmobranchs, reinforcing the relation between feeding ecology and sensory adaptations predicted in previous individual studies. Such large-scale comparative studies are important to decipher key drivers of the early evolution of sensory systems in vertebrates.

1337: The Arabian/Persian Gulf region has ~30 endemic species, and some of the most threatened Elasmobranchii populations in the world. There has been limited political will to address the situation and what will there is, is disabled by national and regional conflicts of interest, apathies and incapacities to assess, manage, conserve or rebuild stocks. There is a great data deficit pertaining to Elasmobranchii in Bahraini waters. Observations of sharks for sale at supermarket fish counters in Bahrain prompted concern and led to this independent, citizen scientist project. This presentation describes the process by which vital legal protection is now being introduced for vulnerable shark species in the territorial waters of Bahrain. To achieve this, new data was collected to justify the necessity of shark protection. At the time of data collection, no one had undertaken any shark-focused surveys in Bahrain for nearly a decade. Individual specimens of species listed as Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List were recorded as being landed, and in alarming quantities. These individuals were mostly female juveniles in number, followed by male juveniles and then pregnant females. This evidence proved the concerns that had initially prompted this project. The critical data was presented to the Bahrain Supreme Council for the Environment and a shark protection law was suggested and then written for the Kingdom and submitted for legal review. The shark protection law has been absorbed into a new raft of environment protection laws due to be ratified in 2026.

1340: The social, cultural and relational values of elasmobranchs are relatively poorly understood, despite their importance in tailoring context-appropriate conservation solutions. We conducted a systematic literature review using Boolean logic and a backwards citation search to assess how elasmobranchs are valued, what tools and techniques have been used to do so, and whether spatial and species bias existed. We analysed peer-reviewed articles using thematic coding and identified that elasmobranchs are valued for the ways they contribute to livelihoods, folklore, and community cohesion. In particular, we identified that the symbolic role of elasmobranchs is hugely varied, with elasmobranchs representing concepts ranging from natural power, the supernatural, and differing levels of social status. We found that different species are valued differently, with tiger sharks and whale sharks being valued for their ecotourism appeal, rays for their subsistence value, and white sharks for their cultural significance in storytelling and metaphor. In addition, we found that the techniques used to study elasmobranch value lean heavily towards the social sciences, that the USA and Australia dominate global research, and that there is a heavy focus on large and more charismatic species. This study highlights clear gaps in elasmobranch research especially regarding positionality, cultural context of research practices and conservation policies, and elasmobranchs’ sociocultural role which urgently needs addressing to conduct fairer and more holistic conservation.

1341: Baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS) provide a repeatable, non-extractive approach to monitoring elasmobranchs in marine protected areas (MPAs), offering valuable insights for long-term management. This study compares elasmobranch assemblages in the Admiral Cockburn Land and Sea National Park, South Caicos, Turks and Caicos Islands, across two survey periods: 2015–2016 and 2024–2025. Relative abundance, expressed as observations per unit effort (OPUE), alongside species richness and diversity, were assessed to evaluate ecological trends over time. Despite ongoing coastal development and natural disasters such as hurricanes over the interval, overall shark encounter rates remained stabl, suggesting resilience within the protected area. Ray observations increased, though not significantly. At the species level, Caribbean reef sharks (Carcharhinus perezi) remained the most abundant species within the MPA, recording a slight increase, while the nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) declined modestly, neither change was statistically significant. However, shark species richness declined from five to three, with lemon (Negaprion brevirostris) and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) absent in the recent survey—both previously rare. These findings suggest that while overall abundance remains steady, subtle shifts in species composition may reflect habitat changes and anthropogenic pressures. The slight decline in nurse sharks, though minor, warrants attention. Continued monitoring is essential to detect emerging trends and support adaptive management strategies that safeguard elasmobranch diversity in a changing coastal landscape.

1342: Nursery habitats are important to many fish populations, as they provide optimal conditions for the survival and growth of juveniles. Protection of these habitats can be critical to the conservation of endangered fish species. We investigate prospective essential habitats and movement patterns for early life stages of smooth hammerhead Sphyrna zygaena and tope Galeorhinus galeus, two highly migratory and endangered shark species. The study focusses on an oceanic island in the Azores archipelago, North Atlantic. Baited remote underwater video systems and scientific longline fishing were used to sample across a depth range of 30–135 m on the island shelf. Movement patterns were inferred from acoustic telemetry data collected over a period of years. Young-of-the-year sharks were identified based on body size measurements. Spatial and movement patterns suggest that smooth hammerhead individuals of different sizes were segregated spatially, showing an ontogenetic shift in habitat use. By contrast, tope were not confined to the nursery area but seemed to use the entire island shelf as an essential habitat. Acoustic telemetry data showed seasonal patterns in site-attached and wide-ranging movements. This study provides a first description of habitat use of natal smooth hammerhead and juvenile tope around an oceanic island in the mid-Atlantic. The results highlight that this Island is an essential habitat for critical life history stages of both species, suggesting that the Azores Archipelago might have a more important role for the North Atlantic populations of these sharks than previously thought.

1344: Despite their ecological and socioeconomic importance, oceanic and reef-associated elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) have experienced widespread declines. Within the Indian Ocean, Fuvahmulah Atoll, a highly exposed oceanic atoll in the southern Republic of Maldives, was recently designated as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, partly due to its extraordinary marine megafauna. However, Fuvahmulah’s elasmobranch populations have been little studied. Using remote timelapse cameras at three shallow forereef sites on the atoll, we quantified elasmobranch sightings during daylight hours between March and August 2022 (n=1,629,756 images analyzed). Elasmobranchs were sighted almost every day (95%, n=60) and most hours (72%, n=550). Of the four ray and seven shark species sighted, whitetip reef sharks were seen on the most hours (n=327) and days (n=56), but pelagic thresher sharks were sighted in the most images (n=27,447), reflecting the long periods this species spent at one site known to be a cleaning station. We document significant differences in species’ occurrences, relative abundances (MaxN), and frequency of occurrences diurnally, across sites, and seasons including the highest shark sighting rates overall, and for grey reef, whitetip reef, and tiger sharks, within the Farikede marine protected area, for which management plans are in development. Our findings, which represent the first quantitative reports of Fuvahmulah’s elasmobranchs, underscore the atoll’s importance and that of protected areas for ensuring the persistence of these megafauna.

1348: The seas around Sabah host the richest elasmobranch biodiversity in Malaysia. Currently, only shark and ray species are protected under Malaysian legislation, while others can still be legally caught and sold in markets. Many of these species are threatened by accidental capture in commercial trawl fisheries, also known as bycatch. Moreover, little is known about when and where these capture events occur. To address this gap, electronic monitoring cameras were deployed on trawlers to capture time- and GPS-stamped images of all species that were landed on a subset of fishing vessel decks. Over a 30-month period, more than 7,400 individuals were recorded, of which 36% were listed as Vulnerable, Endangered, or Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Images of species such as Scalloped Hammerhead, Grey Carpetshark, Coral Catshark, Broad Cowtail Ray, Bowmouth Guitarfish and Bottlenose Wedgefish were captured. Spatial analysis and kernel density estimation were used to identify hotspot areas of high elasmobranch bycatch rates. By overlaying these hotspots with fishing pressure, key areas for the conservation of the Critically Endangered Scalloped Hammerhead and Bottlenose Wedgefish were determined. These findings were presented to relevant authorities, including the Department of Fisheries Sabah, leading to a proposal for time-area closures to restrict fishing activities between May and October. This study informed the design of Malaysia’s first ever time-area closure for sharks and rays, which will be implemented in 2026 to reduce bycatch of endangered elasmobranchs, demonstrating a science-based pathway from data collection to policy implementation.

1351: Effective management of long-lived, slow-reproducing sharks requires a deep understanding of their reproductive biology. We revisited a historical dataset (1967–1969) from the Hawai‘i Cooperative Shark Research and Control Program to investigate reproductive patterns in three common inshore shark species: Sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus), Galapagos (Carcharhinus galapagensis), and Tiger (Galeocerdo cuvier) sharks. Our analyses explored the relationship between maternal size and litter size, litter sex ratios, and differences in embryonic size between sexes. Regression analyses and generalized linear models revealed significant positive correlations between maternal size and litter size in C. galapagensis and G. cuvier, but not in C. plumbeus, indicating species-specific reproductive strategies. Moreover, G. cuvier litters were substantially larger than those of the other species, reflecting divergent evolutionary investments in fecundity. We found no sex-based differences in embryonic size, and litter sex ratios were balanced across all species, suggesting that sex does not influence in utero embryonic development. By mining this long-unused legacy dataset, our study offers fresh insights into the reproductive ecology of these sharks and underscores the enduring value of historical data for understanding life history variation and guiding contemporary conservation and management efforts in the central Pacific.
1352: Elasmobranchs are highly susceptible to overfishing due to their low rates of intrinsic population growth and slow life histories (Gravel et al., 2024). A key challenge is understanding the role of small-scale fisheries in driving extinction risk, particularly in the tropics. Here, we report the elasmobranch landings in the Andaman and Nicobar Archipelago, which is a hotspot for elasmobranchs in India, comprising shark and ray species (Kumar et al., 2018). We sampled elasmobranch landings in the pre-monsoon and post-monsoon seasons of 2023. During which, we documented landings of individuals from fishing vessels. The landings included elasmobranch species (20 sharks, rays). Apart from species composition, we recorded fishing locations and catch per unit effort. Presently, generalised fishing locations have been obtained from fishers throughout the archipelago. We also received information that large-scale fishers are seeking new locations for elasmobranch fishing, leading many trawlers and longliners to explore untouched areas such as the Nancowry group of Islands in the Nicobar due to the sharp decline in elasmobranch populations near the Andaman Islands. Elasmobranch catch has transitioned from bycatch to a target fishery due to export demand from the Andaman Islands, where it is exported to Chennai and then to international countries (Tyabji et al., 2022). This study provides baseline data on the current scenario of elasmobranch fisheries; however, subsequent research is required to accurately map catch locations, molecularly taxonomise the landed samples for accurate identification, and understand the current trade routes of elasmobranch fisheries.
1353: An understanding of natural mortality, movement and space use, and their drivers are critical for the implementation of effective species and habitat management. Acoustic telemetry data can be used to investigate movement patterns in response to environmental conditions and can provide long-term mark-recapture data for identifying mortality. The Glyphis river sharks of northern Australia comprise two rare, threatened euryhaline species. A total of Northern River Sharks (Glyphis garricki) and Speartooth Sharks (G. glyphis) were tracked in rivers of the Northern Territory between 2013-2024. Detections were converted into capture histories and used to calculate yearly and monthly estimates of mortality. Glyphis glyphis and G. garricki neonates experienced average yearly mortality rates of 0.898 and 0.731, respectively, compared with 0.120 and 0.233 in subadults/adults. Tracked G. garricki and G. glyphis underwent seasonal up- and downstream movements, closely linked to freshwater flow. During the dry seasons, sharks occurred ~50 –120 km upstream and moved downstream to the river mouths and inshore coastal waters during the wet seasons. Results indicate that river sharks undergo high rates of mortality, limiting their capacity to withstand additional anthropogenic causes of mortality. Movements indicate that impacts of fisheries may be seasonal, and that river sharks may be sensitive to environmental change. Water resource developments may cause declines in sharks due to their small populations and low dispersal and connectivity. Insights into mortality and movements of G. glyphis and G. garricki provide recommendations for management to ensure that river sharks persist into the future.

1355: Effective conservation of wide-ranging marine predators remains challenging due to their international distributions, conservative life histories, and low overlap with marine protected areas (MPAs). However, when MPAs align with critical juvenile habitats, they may be able to improve population resilience in otherwise migratory species. Here, we integrated acoustic and satellite telemetry with correlated random walks and Brownian bridge movement models to assess dispersal, habitat use, and MPA overlap across maturity stages of tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) tagged within and the Fernando de Noronha MPA in the Brazilian Atlantic. Our results reveal pronounced ontogenetic variability: immature juvenile sharks exhibited high year-round residency at the island and high overlap of their core use areas with the MPA. Conversely, mature individuals displayed highly dispersive behavior, including transoceanic migrations and connectivity to southern MPAs. This dispersal behavior included an apparently gravid female tracked from Fernando de Noronha to the coast of Sierra Leone, highlighting potential connectivity between these understudied populations. Our findings highlight how a small (113km2), non-targeted protected area can serve as a critical habitat for a mobile apex predator, supporting juvenile growth and maturation before dispersal.

1356: The identification of critical habitats is fundamental for the effective management and conservation of threatened marine species, particularly those with vulnerable early life stages such as sharks. Along the southern Gabonese coast, the Mayumba region has long been suspected of functioning as a nursery for Sphyrna lewini (scalloped hammerhead) and Carcharhinus limbatus (blacktip shark). This study tested this hypothesis by applying the three nursery criteria defined by Heupel et al. (2007): the predominance of juveniles, their fidelity to the area, and the recurrent use of the habitat over time. Fieldwork conducted between April 2022 and March 2023 relied on artisanal fisheries by-catch data and stable isotope analyses (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N) from muscle tissues. Results revealed a high dominance of juveniles, including young of the year and newborns, combined with very limited adult presence and clear seasonal patterns in size structure. Juveniles of both species were substantially more abundant in Mayumba than in other monitored regions along the Gabonese coastline. Stable isotope signatures confirmed the prolonged residency of young sharks, suggesting sustained use of nearshore habitats during their early development. To address the third criterion, historical fisheries and monitoring records were compiled, and these data provided consistent evidence of the recurrent presence of juvenile S. lewini and C. limbatus over multiple years. Together, these findings confirm the ecological significance of Mayumba as a key multispecies nursery area for these threatened sharks. Protecting this habitat is therefore critical and should become a priority for conservation planning and fisheries management strategies in Gabon.

1358: Chondrichthyan species represent one of the most threatened vertebrate groups globally, primarily due to intensive overfishing. Moreover, negative attitudes toward these species, sharks in particular, are often prevalent in many local communities and are considered a contributing factor to population declines. Citizen science has been increasingly recognized as an effective approach for collecting information on various chondrichthyan species, especially those that are elusive and difficult to observe using conventional sampling methods. In addition, being cost-effective, this approach is often used to generate baseline data on this group of vertebrates in developing and data-poor regions worldwide. Montenegro is a small country located in the southeastern Adriatic Sea (Mediterranean region) with a population of about 620,000 people, roughly one third of whom live along the coastline. A citizen science project focused on collecting chondrichthyan observations in Montenegro was launched in 2016. It is currently carried out under the initiative #Pošaljiajkulu (“#sendtheshark”), conducted in collaboration with local fishers who provide photos and videos of encountered chondrichthyans to local scientists. The initiative has been adapted to local conditions and relies on direct phone communication with contributors, facilitated through personal relationships between scientists and fishers. This approach has proven to be the most effective in a small community setting, where fishers are often reluctant to use mobile applications or similar digital tools. To date, this initiative has proven to be a valuable tool, documenting the presence of chondrichthyan species and providing the first-ever dataset on these species in Montenegro.

1360: The shortfin mako shark (Isurus oxyrinchus) is one of four lamnid shark species inhabiting the Mediterranean Sea. All members of the family Lamnidae have experienced severe population declines in this region over recent decades, primarily as a result of intense fishing pressure. As marine apex predators, their ecological role is reflected in their top-down regulation of other organisms, thereby preventing unnatural changes within marine food webs. The mako shark has undergone a significant decline in the eastern Adriatic Sea, with no documented records for more than years in this part of the Mediterranean. However, during the past decade, sightings along the coasts of eastern Adriatic countries have increased notably. This study presents documented records of the species from Montenegro. Over individuals have been recorded in the country through citizen science. The vast majority are juveniles, including observations of young-of-the-year (YOY) specimens. Almost all records are bycatch from the local fishing fleet, with drifting longlines identified as the primary fishing gear responsible. In addition, records of free-swimming individuals have also been documented in the area. The shortfin mako shark is listed as Critically Endangered in the Mediterranean Sea according to the IUCN regional assessment and is therefore protected in many countries bordering this sea. Although a fishing ban is also in place in Montenegro and neighboring countries, it remains unclear whether the recent increase in records is a result of these conservation measures, enhanced public engagement, environmental factors, or their combination.

1361: Global shark populations continue to decline despite decades of law, policy, and management efforts, with bycatch in non-target fisheries remaining a primary driver of mortality. The most directed global effort has been through the Food and Aquaculture Organization’s International Plan of Action for Sharks (IPOA), which encourages conservation and management for the longterm sustainable use of sharks. States supporting the IPOA are encouraged to adopt and implement National Plans of Action (NPOAs). Yet recent research shows that many NPOAs are outdated, poorly implemented, and absent in key fishing nations, creating a critical implementation gap. Nevertheless, political will exists, demonstrated by the many nations that continue to update and develop NPOAs. This research responds to the challenge by providing a framework for policy- and lawmakers to fast track the development or updating of NPOAs with a focus on bycatch mitigation. We synthesise three vital viewpoints: (i)a systematic literature review of existing mitigation measures; (ii) a critical analysis of existing NPOAs to identify best practices and common shortcomings in bycatch provisions; and (iii) insights drawn from a policymaker perspective, addressing real-world barriers to implementation and compliance. The aim is to assist NPOA planners and decision makers in navigating the complexity of bycatch mitigation through actionable recommendations that governments can take, from base minimum to high ambition, to ensure optimal implementation of the IPOA.

1362: Demand for shark and ray meat is the major driver of overexploitation worldwide, yet they remain an understudied group within aquatic foods and their role in providing micronutrients beneficial to human health is poorly understood. Although we have acknowledged over the past decade the health risks of consuming shark and ray meat due to the presence of bioaccumulative contaminants, our knowledge of their nutrient composition remains obscured, especially when compared with highly consumed bony fish species like sardines or salmon. Here, we fostered new dimensions of shark and ray conservation and fisheries sustainability relating to global food security by quantifying the content of essential nutrients and identifying the global importance of sharks and rays for both food and nutritional security. This study is a first step as the lack of data on the nutrient composition and role of sharks and rays in food security and nutrition has limited our understanding of how these species contribute to healthy diets. Indeed, shark and ray fisheries are already data-limited, and stocks of many species are overfished, suggesting there are trade-offs between conservation goals and ecosystem services from fisheries. Our findings provide baseline information to help identify species that might be critical food sources and need direct management efforts to reduce overexploitation. We also highlight that fulfilling nutritional needs will depend on the implementation of responsible fishing practices and conservation measures for threatened stocks to ensure the long-term viability of shark and ray populations.

1365: The smooth hammerhead (Sphyrna zygaena) is often recorded as bycatch in offshore commercial fisheries in Taiwan; however, its stock status in the Northwest Pacific remains poorly understood due to limited data availability. To assess exploitation status, we applied two data-limited approaches: length-based spawning potential ratio (LBSPR) and catch–maximum sustainable yield (CMSY). The CMSY analysis utilised years of catch data (2001–2024), whilst the LBSPR model incorporated 3,280 length-frequency subsamples (1,282 males and 1,998 females) collected by fishery observers at the Nanfang’ao fish market between 2015 and 2024. The CMSY analysis estimated a maximum sustainable yield (MSY) of 67.9–104 t·yr⁻¹, comparable to recent catches (~103.5 t·yr⁻¹). However, the biomass ratio for 2024 (B2024/BMSY = 0.395– 0.789) and exploitation rate (F2024/FMSY = 1.26–4.88) indicate that the stock is overfished and experiencing ongoing overfishing. The LBSPR analysis revealed a current spawning potential ratio (SPR) of 18.7% (95% CI: 16.8–20.5), below the limit reference point of 30%. Additionally, the estimated size at 50% capture (145.87 cm fork length, FL) was smaller than the size at maturity (156.3–204.8 cm FL), indicating recruitment overfishing. Overall, these findings suggest that S. zygaena in the Northwest Pacific is experiencing unsustainable exploitation, emphasising the need for precautionary management to facilitate stock recovery and ensure long-term sustainability.

1367: Accurate morphometrics are fundamental to understanding the ecology, physiology, and conservation of large marine vertebrates. Most photogrammetric techniques rely on twodimensional dorsal or lateral perspectives, limiting the estimation of body volume and condition. Here, we present the first reproducible workflow for reconstructing threedimensional body models of whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) by integrating low-cost dronebased dorsal imagery with pre-calibrated, diver-operated stereo-video (DOV) lateral footage. Landmarks at the head, pectoral fins, and dorsal fin served as shared anatomical references to scale and align dorsal and lateral views. The dorsal drone image was additionally scaled using a m reference pole. Combined images were imported into Blender, where structured boxmodelling generated volumetric meshes of individual sharks. We then morphed the initial mesh to additional sharks, validated linear and sectional metrics against DOV measurements, and quantified scale bias introduced by the UAV reference pole. Finally, we derived quantified estimates of body volume. This open, low-cost workflow bridges aerial and underwater imaging to enable non-invasive volumetric morphometrics in whale sharks. Such volumetric data can inform assessments of individual and population health, growth, and energetic condition, which are critical indicators of ecosystem change. By providing accurate, reproducible measurements without physical contact, this approach supports long-term monitoring and evidence-based management of endangered marine megafauna and can be adapted to other elasmobranch species that have been difficult to assess so far.

1370: Protection of female elasmobranchs during gestation is likely to afford significant benefits to population recruitment, since survival of both adults and their offspring is enhanced. Despite this management value, understanding of gestation areas remains limited for many species due to challenges in obtaining in-situ observations. Historically, identifying pregnant female habitats has depended on lethal sampling. However, ubiquitous global shark declines incentivise the development and adoption of non-invasive techniques to minimise harm to vulnerable populations. Ultrasonography represents an emerging technique to assess internal fish anatomy, and the recent development of portable scanners has created an opportunity to non-invasively assess elasmobranch pregnancy in-situ. This method has demonstrated promise for exploring shark anatomy in lab settings on tropical species, but its application to temperate shark species remains limited. This study presents insights from the first application of ultrasonography to the starry smoothound (Mustelus asterias) as a tool for assessing maturity, pregnancy and fecundity. The method was first applied opportunistically to fishery specimens, whereby dissections were used to validate the identification of key reproductive features. Ultrasonography was then applied to M. asterias in-situ to confirm the presence of a predominantly female aggregation area in the UK, in which all examined females were pregnant. Common troubleshooting and methodological recommendations are presented, based on lessons learned, to aid future applications of this method. Overall, these findings aim to increase the accessibility of this method to elasmobranch researchers.

1374: More than one-third of the world’s sharks, rays, and chimaeras – or elasmobranchs – are threatened with extinction due to overfishing. Conservation of this taxon is particularly challenging in Southeast Asia (SEA) where species are often caught as bycatch in small-scale fisheries and retained for various uses. Moreover, conventional approaches to gather social insights, i.e. focus group discussions and interviews, often feel forced when species conservation is the primary goal. Pilaut is a board game designed to foster more inclusive and genuine interaction with fishers through behavioral research that explores fishers’ responses to different intervention scenarios. The game was developed from case studies in seven SEA countries to address common elasmobranch conservation issues across the region. It features three different gameplays that mimic real-life fishing scenarios and makes it highly adjustable, depending on the research question and target demographics. As a research tool, Pilaut enables fishers to freely make choices based on different scenarios and incentives in a fun and engaging environment. Pilaut could act as a complementary tool in conservation science by providing social insights that are useful for scientists, conservation practitioners, and management authorities.

1375: Collecting ecological data for the Raja Ampat epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium freycineti), locally known as Kalabia, is resource-intensive. To address this, Elasmobranch Project Indonesia (EPI) initially utilized Photo-ID methods and developed a citizen science platform to explore practical ways of involving the public in data collection. Due to its simplicity and accessibility, this method became the foundation for creating a responsible citizen science–based tourism scheme in Arborek Village, Raja Ampat, where tourism flourishes and Kalabia is frequently observed. The scheme allows visitors to participate in activities led by trained locals known as ‘Kalabia Rangers’, who play a key role in introducing tourists to Kalabia and its habitat while encouraging awareness and stewardship. Insights from tourists’ preferences in observing wildlife in natural settings and the locals’ strong background in locally-owned tourism further reinforced the scheme’s development. To increase Kalabia’s value as a conservation icon, additional capacity-building activities such as craft-making training were provided, and a carrying capacity study was integrated to mitigate negative environmental impact. However, locals’ participation level varied, with higher enthusiasm among women compared to men-likely due to differing perceived benefits and potential dependency on EPI could inhibit establishment of the scheme-showing limited initiative to lead and sustain the scheme independently. Moving forward, the initiative aims to strengthen local leadership, foster a sense of ownership, and enhance understanding of long-term benefits for both livelihoods and conservation. Overall, this initiative demonstrates how citizen science-integrated responsible tourism may empower local communities and support long-term conservation of Kalabia in Raja Ampat.

1377: The sicklefin devil ray (Mobula tarapacana) is a Critically Endangered, highly migratory elasmobranch species of significant conservation concern. Predictable seasonal aggregations at seamounts in the Azores (Portugal) present opportunities for unique research to support evidence-based management strategies. This study presents outcomes from Manta Catalog, which established the first regional photo-identification database for M. tarapacana worldwide. Since 2012, over individuals have been catalogued, enabling comprehensive analyses of population structure, reproductive activity, site fidelity, and temporal occurrence dynamics in the Eastern Atlantic. To enhance the scalability of individual recognition, the Manta Trust developed IDtheManta, a deep similarity model jointly trained on our dataset alongside reef and oceanic mobulid photo-ID collections. Deployed for the first time on M. tarapacana, within a human verification workflow, the system allows efficient and reliable re-identification. A strategic collaboration with Oceanário de Lisboa further expanded field capacity and enabled the incorporation of stereo-video photogrammetry—a non-invasive technique yielding precise biometric measurements for over individuals to date. These data have elucidated size distributions, reproductive parameters, and individual longevity, thereby informing conservation prioritisation. These partnerships have strengthened scientific collaboration and dissemination, as well as public engagement initiatives. Manta Catalog and the Manta Trust’s MantaBase employ a citizen science framework that broadens data acquisition while promoting stakeholder participation in M. tarapacana conservation, recently leading to the recognition of these seamounts as ISRAs, aiding management efforts. These research innovations and collaborative efforts provide essential contributions to conservation science of this species globally.

1380: Elasmobranch nursery areas (ENAs) are prime critical habitats for conservation and management and significant for the designation of ISRAs, but research on ENAs is lagging behind in many regions and particularly in Mexico. We present preliminary results of a unique research project that for the first time brings together social and natural sciences approaches to study the past and present importance of two coastal sites as possible ENAs: Laguna Yalahau and Bahía Ascensión, both in the Mexican Caribbean. We interviewed local fishers to recover LEK information on the former utilization (30-50 years-ago) of these sites as ENAs, then we surveyed both sites times across a 17-month period using BRUVs, eDNA, UAVs and longlining. All assessments considered well-established criteria for the designation of ENAs. Our findings suggest that both sites were important communal ENAs 30-50 years ago: Laguna Yalahau for Carcharhinus limbatus, Negaprion brevirostris, Hypanus americanus and Styracura schmardae, and Bahía Ascensión for Carcharhinus leucas, C. limbatus, Negaprion brevirostris, Ginglymostoma cirratum, Hypanus americanus and Styracura schmardae. However, Laguna Yalahau has suffered severe human impacts and is probably no-longer an ENA, while Bahía Ascensión remains an important ENA for at least shark species. Our study demonstrates the benefits of: a) using LEK to rescue valuable information from past ENAs, and b) applying transdisciplinary approaches for the study of ENAs. In addition, it highlights the importance of effective conservation measures to secure the ecological function of coastal ENAs in the long run.

1383: Predators can shape ecosystems not only through direct consumption, but also via nonconsumptive effects that alter prey behaviour and community dynamics. In coral reef ecosystems, these effects may extend to the acoustic domain, where sound plays a central role in ecological interactions. Using the combination of passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) and baited underwater remote videos (BRUVs), we investigated how the presence of predators influences reef soundscape dynamics. To do so, we deployed BRUVs and underwater acoustic recorders (hydromoths) at reef sites around D’Aros Island, Seychelles. Acoustic data were analysed using machine learning (ML)-assisted sonotype classification, quantifying changes in sonotype occurrence and snapping shrimp activity. We found that predator presence significantly suppressed both fish-generated acoustic metrics and snapping shrimp activity. These effects were not mediated by habitat structure, but piscivorous reef sharks were found to illicit a larger effect compared to other reef predators. Together, these results demonstrate that predator-driven acoustic suppression occurs within coral reef communities, and provide novel insights into the non-consumptive effects sharks have on functions associated with reef sounds (i.e. courtship). Importantly, we demonstrate a scalable method for quantifying behavioural responses in complex reef system by integrating long-term PAM with ML-assisted analysis. As anthropogenic pressures reshape predator-prey interactions, understanding how fear propagates through ecological soundscapes and drives functionality will be critical for conserving these complex habitats.

1387: Cabo Pulmo National Park, located on the Baja California Peninsula, Mexico, is a no-take marine protected area that has shown an exceptional recovery in fish biomass since its closure to fishing. Since 2019, unoccupied aerial vehicles (UAVs) have surveyed sand and rocky-reef habitats to estimate the relative abundance of blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus). Blacktip sharks were only observed during winter months and wind speed, sea surface temperature, and time of day were significant predictors of abundance and on some surveys, over 1,000 individuals were recorded. The close association of sharks to the shore likely reflects refuging behavior, where individuals use these areas for thermoregulation. Acoustic and satellite telemetry indicated a northward migration in late spring, with sharks returning each winter. Other shark species observed included lemon (Negaprion brevirostris), bull (Carcharhinus leucas), and nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma unami), with a notable increase in nurse sharks since surveys began. Observations of orcas (Orcinus orca) attempting to prey on blacktip sharks appeared to trigger a redistribution of aggregations across the park, emphasizing the role of apex predators in shaping spatial patterns and risk-related behavior. This orca pod specializes in hunting elasmobranchs and has also been observed preying on bull sharks within the park, as well as whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) farther north in the Gulf of California. This work is part of a long-term community monitoring program that builds local capacity by training women from the region to conduct the surveys themselves.

1388: Understanding key reproductive traits in sharks, such as age at maturity, reproductive frequency, and gestation periods, is critical for effective conservation and supporting fisheries management. However, obtaining the biological data needed to define these parameters for wild populations is challenging, as traditional approaches have relied on biochemical measurements taken at single time points. Therefore, there is a lack of repeated measurements from the same individual across its lifetime. This work explores novel approaches to overcome this limitation by analysing reproductive hormones archived within the growth increments of shark vertebrae, which could enable the reconstruction of age-specific reproductive parameters. First, we reviewed the application of hormone analysis in accretionary structures (i.e., incrementally grown tissues) in vertebrates to identify the best pathways to expand this approach to sharks. Guided by these insights, we extracted and quantified reproductive hormones from gummy shark (Mustelus antarcticus) vertebrae using an immunoassay approach (ELISA), and investigated whether hormone concentrations varied across growth increments representing different maturity stages. These results provided the first evidence that vertebral tissue can preserve measurable reproductive hormone profiles that reflect expected maturity patterns. Building on this foundation, we are developing a mass spectrometry-based approach (GC-MS, GC-MS/MS) to enhance analyte identification and detection sensitivity in vertebral increments. Ultimately, hormone analysis in vertebrae provides an opportunity to reconstruct individual reproductive histories and refine estimates of age-specific reproductive parameters. Thereby advancing our understanding of shark life histories and providing population specific information for enhanced shark conservation and fisheries management.

1390: Hemiscyllium is a genus comprising nine species of small, benthic-dwelling sharks, commonly referred to as "walking sharks" that are endemic to northern Australia, the island of New Guinea, and its satellite islands. Of these, five species are currently classified as threatened, including three species endemic to Papua New Guinea (PNG). Despite their conservation status, there are no local or national species-specific protections for walking sharks in PNG, and limited data exist to inform effective management, particularly regarding species distributions. Walking sharks are characterised by non-overlapping, small geographic distributions and siteassociated individual ranges typically spanning only a few hundred meters to a few kilometres. These traits, coupled with limited dispersal abilities, suggest that populations may be genetically distinct but also highly vulnerable to localised disturbances and even extirpation. This study presents findings from a series of in situ surveys aimed at reassessing the distributional limits of walking sharks in PNG. We employed genetic techniques including genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) analysis and sequencing of the mitochondrial ND4 gene to delineate species boundaries and gain insights into distributional patterns. Here we present a concept of a mosaic of disjunct, non-overlapping distributions previously unreported for this genus. We report updated range boundaries for two endemic species, Hemiscyllium michaeli and Hemiscyllium hallstromi.

1391: Understanding predator–prey dynamics in tropical coral reef ecosystems is crucial for effective conservation, particularly where threatened species coexist. This study investigated the trophic linkage between the near-threatened blacktip reef shark (Carcharhinus melanopterus) and hatchlings of the endangered green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) at a tropical coral reef in Peninsular Malaysia. Using stable isotope ratios of δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N, we quantified the dietary contribution of turtle hatchlings to the diet of neonate and juvenile blacktip reef sharks over three nesting seasons (2018, 2019, and 2021). Fin clip and blood samples from sharks (neonates and <100 cm TL juveniles) were analyzed alongside potential prey items, including turtle hatchlings, reef fishes, and cephalopods. Stable isotope mixing models (MixSIAR) revealed that turtle hatchlings contributed substantially to shark diets, with median proportional estimates of 49% and 81% in 2018 and 2021, respectively, while squid and reef fish dominated in 2019 (~49% and 16%). Gut content analysis further supported these findings, revealing up to eight hatchling carcasses within individual shark stomachs. These results highlight a strong seasonal trophic dependence of juvenile blacktip reef sharks on turtle hatchlings, suggesting that hatchling emergence events provide critical energetic subsidies supporting early shark survival. The study underscores the ecological interconnectedness between sharks and turtles within reef systems and emphasizes that conserving sea turtle nesting populations indirectly benefits the macropredator blacktip reef sharks in pristine tropical environments.

1392: The Critically Endangered great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran; IUCN, 2019) is a large coastal apex predator that depends heavily on nearshore habitats supporting various stages of its life cycle. Adults primarily prey on teleosts and elasmobranchs, with regional differences in trophic ecology documented across areas such as the northwestern Atlantic and eastern Australia. For the first time, we investigate the movement patterns and trophic ecology of S. mokarran within atoll ecosystems of the Central Pacific. Research was conducted in Rangiroa and Tikehau, two neighboring atolls in French Polynesia characterized by three main habitats: lagoon, passes, and pelagic zones. Thirty-four individuals (26 in Rangiroa – in Tikehau; total length 2.5–4.0 m) were acoustically tagged to assess spatial connectivity and habitat use within and between atolls. In parallel, muscle tissues from individuals (12 from Rangiroa – from Tikehau; total length 2.5–4.0 m) and from a wide range of potential prey species across habitats were analyzed using stable isotope analysis to infer dietary sources. Results revealed a predominant reliance on reef- and lagoon-associated resources (mean δ¹³C ± SD = −11.1 ± 1.2 ‰), coupled with marked intraspecific variability in trophic level (mean δ¹5N ± SD = 13.3 ± 1.3 ‰). Movement data indicated both site-specific and seasonal patterns in habitat use and inter-atoll connectivity. Individual differences in lagoon use were evident, with some sharks showing prolonged residency while others rarely entered. These findings highlight the ecological importance of atoll habitats for S. mokarran and provide valuable insights for its regional conservation.

1393: Abstract The oceanic whitetip shark (Carcharhinus longimanus) is a slow-growing, late-maturing apex predator with low fecundity and limited capacity for population recovery. Once widespread in tropical oceans, it has declined by over 90% globally due to incidental capture in pelagic fisheries and is now listed as Critically Endangered. In the central North Pacific, oceanic whitetips are incidentally caught in Hawaii’s pelagic longline fishery, which comprises deep-set (tuna-targeting) and shallow-set (swordfish-targeting) sectors. I analyzed years of observer data encompassing ~118,000 sets and million hooks, yielding 13,025 OWT captures (11,435 deep, 1,514 shallow). Catch-per-unit-effort declined significantly over time in both sectors, while spatial models revealed strong geographic and seasonal structure in bycatch risk. Most sharks were retrieved alive (deep: 76.6%, shallow: 92.8%), indicating high potential for postrelease survival under proper handling protocols. A dominant bycatch hotspot was identified in the southwestern fishing grounds (south of 20°N, west of 160°W), where 52.6% of all OWT captures occurred. A hypothetical year-round closure of this area would eliminate ~53% of OWT interactions but would also reduce deep-set tuna and swordfish catches by ~34% and ~24%, respectively. Shallow-set impacts would be negligible due to limited effort in that region. These results underscore a clear management trade-off: substantial bycatch reduction is achievable through spatial mitigation, but not without cost to deep-set target yield. Adaptive area-based strategies or seasonal and gear-based interventions may offer more balanced outcomes for shark conservation and fishery sustainability.
Beyond the Net: Addressing the Impacts and Innovations in Shark & Ray Bycatch

1396: Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) are the largest extant fish, characterised by long lifespans, slow growth rates, and late maturity. As a highly migratory species that frequently occupies surface waters, they are particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic threats. Despite advances in tracking technologies and photo-identification methods, fine-scale movement patterns of whale sharks in the Maldives remain poorly understood. Elucidating these movements is essential for developing effective management strategies to support the conservation of this globally declining species. Citizen science provides a valuable, non-invasive approach to monitoring enigmatic marine megafauna. The Big Fish Network (BFN) was established to harness the contributions of ocean stakeholders and improve understanding of whale shark ecology in the Maldives. Historically, monitoring efforts were concentrated within the South Ari Atoll Marine Protected Area, where the Maldives Whale Shark Research Programme (MWSRP) operates yearround. Initial knowledge of Maldivian whale sharks derived from this aggregation, primarily composed of juvenile males. Integration of BFN and MWSRP datasets has facilitated a broader understanding of population demographics and inter-atoll connectivity. Analysis of demographic and encounter data, supported by a Resource Selection Function Model, revealed that movement patterns were influenced by environmental variability. Notably, a region exhibiting a distinct demographic composition, including a higher proportion of females, was identified - presenting a rare opportunity to investigate a poorly studied demographic. This study demonstrates the efficacy of citizen science in advancing knowledge of whale shark movement ecology in the Maldives and underscores the need to refine spatial management strategies to enhance species conservation.
1397: As mid to upper trophic level predators, elasmobranchs (sharks, skates, and rays) are known to have elevated levels of a potent neurotoxicant, methylmercury (MeHg). The lethality of MeHg across different vertebrate taxa is well established, but its sublethal effects have only been investigated in depth at the scope of human health. The sublethal effects of exposure to MeHg, which are known to impact animal physiology and behavior, remain largely undescribed in elasmobranchs. In this study, a new approach was tested for assessing bioaccumulation and the sublethal effects of MeHg in a coastal shark species over extended time periods (five months) in a spatially constrained research setting. By the end of the experiment, shark muscle in the high-dose treatment had 24.03 μg/g MeHg, while low-dose shark muscle had 10.11 μg/g MeHg, compared to the 1.18 μg/g MeHg in the muscle of control sharks. Regardless of treatment, the highest concentrations of MeHg were found within the muscle, brain, heart, and kidneys while the lowest concentrations were found in the liver, intestine, and stomach. This work provides insight into how biological processes may respond to MeHg exposure, a widespread contaminant in aquatic environments.

1400: To investigate the feeding ecology of rhino rays, stomach content analysis (SCA) and stable isotope analysis (SIA) were conducted for three wedgefish species (Rhynchobatus spp.) and two guitarfish species (Rhinobatos spp.). A total of specimens were collected from Taiwanese waters during 2023–2024, comprising Rhynchobatus australiae, R. immaculatus, R. springeri, Rhinobatos hynnicephalus, and R. schlegelii. Stomachs from all individuals and muscle tissues from wedgefishes (2 R. australiae, R. immaculatus, and R. springeri) were analyzed. The overall vacuity index was 10.8%. SCA showed that crustaceans were the primary prey for all species, although the standardized Index of Relative Importance (%IRI) varied from 68.2% in R. springeri to 94.8% in R. hynnicephalus. In R. immaculatus, SIA revealed that δ15N and δ13C values were positively correlated with total length, and that δ15N and δ13C values were also positively correlated with each other. Trophic levels (TrLs) based on SCA were estimated as follows: R. australiae 3.60, R. immaculatus 3.73, R. springeri 3.83, R. hynnicephalus 3.61, and R. schlegelii 3.73. Based on SIA (δ15N), the TrLs for R. australiae, R. immaculatus, and R. springeri were calculated as 3.52, 3.91, and 4.12, respectively. This study demonstrates that the five rhino rays exhibit generally similar, yet slightly distinct feeding strategies, reflecting differences in their respective fishing grounds. Future conservation planning for each species should therefore be developed accordingly, in conjunction with other life history parameters.

1404: The flapper skate, Dipturus intermedius (Parnell, 1837), is a large-bodied, slow-growing and latematuring, Critically Endangered elasmobranch, with a constrained population distribution. A growing body of evidence suggests that they exhibit extended periods of coastal residency in areas that experience a multitude of pressures such as fishing and renewable energy development. Using two longitudinal catch and release angling datasets, we identified hotspots of flapper skates in Irish waters. We also carried out a 3-year acoustic telemetry study at one of these hotspots to investigate flapper skate residency, inter-annual site fidelity and demographics of the population. A total of flapper skates were acoustically tagged and tracked for extended periods within the acoustic array. A distinct seasonal absence of individuals from the embayment was identified, which may be linked with reproductive movements. Genetic analysis determined nine haplotypes were present and suggests higher genetic diversity than other known hotspots.
From Data to Policy: Managing Shared and Migratory Shark and Ray Populations

1406: Asian non-marine elasmobranchs are poorly known, though highly threatened. Fundamental questions persist on species ranges, taxonomy, and ecology, and some species such as the Ganges Shark (Glyphis gangeticus) face severe near-term extinction risks. In 2023, a team from James Cook University and Hasanuddin University collaborated with local university and government institutions to survey eastern and southern Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo) to determine the presence of non-marine elasmobranchs and to better understand their populations and pressures. Southern Kalimantan appears to provide a stronghold for three Fluvitrygon species (freshwater whiprays), while the Giant Freshwater Whipray (Urogymnus Polylepis) remains relatively abundant throughout the region. A concern encountered was that while Indonesia’s freshwater rays are nationally protected, there is little knowledge of this among fishers, highlighting a policy awareness and enforcement gap between national and provincial governments. In North Kalimantan, a previously undocumented population of the Ganges Shark was found. The capture of Ganges Sharks’ in one week by a single fisher in the Sesayap River indicates this is the most globally significant, and possibly only remaining viable population of the species. Over the 2026/27 period, our team will work with local university institutions to set in motion a range of activities aimed at raising awareness of existing policy for freshwater rays, and seek national protection of the Ganges Shark through engagement with local government actors and fishing communities. Here, I will overview our findings and future steps as we seek to secure Borneo as a non-marine elasmobranch stronghold.
Non-marine Frontiers: uncovering the secrets and charting the future of unique sharks and rays

1407: Sharks and rays, within the subclass Elasmobranchii, face significant threats, with overfishing being a primary concern. Especially in small-scale artisanal fisheries. Sri Lanka has a large and expanding artisanal fisheries fleet and an important part of the total landings from these fisheries comprises elasmobranchs. Yet, research on nearly every aspect of elasmobranch ecology such as diversity, temporal and spatial distribution, migration and fishing pressure is lacking. Here we present a four year time series analysis of elasmobranch landings combined with GPS tracking of the fishing vessels and the first mark and recapture project of elasmobranchs in the country. To the best of our knowledge, this study also represents the first spatial and seasonal analysis for Stripenose guitarfish (Acroteriobatus variegatus). For Bluespotted maskray (Neotrygon indica), it marks the first such investigation conducted in Sri Lanka. Our findings show a large diversity of elasmobranchs, with species caught, but with a marked decline in total elasmobranch landings between 2019 and 2023. It is also evident that the landings of A. variegatus and N. indica differ spatially and seasonally. The key findings include that A. variegatus and N. indica were found to increase in landing frequency in different seasons and A. variegatus mainly occupied the areas north and south of Vandalous bay, whereas N. indica used the whole area surveyed. Preliminary results indicate site affinity for A. variegatus and poor survivability of specimens with poor health assessment scores during tagging.

1409: Argos is the main satellite technology used by the wildlife research community, environmental agencies, NGOs, foundations, charities, parks, reserves, aquariums, etc. for animal tracking and animal behavioral data collection all around the globe, to observe, to analyze, and to understand large-scale migrations. Argos tracking data collected from hundreds of animal species among birds, marine species, make available a high-precision mapping of migratory corridors, stopovers, feeding and foraging areas, breeding, and birth areas, and the fine description of seasonal, interannual and other time-scale dependent behavioral factors. Fisheries scientists are an important community of Argos wildlife tracking users and have been using Argos on sharks since the availability of this technology. Interactions with fisheries, either volunteer or by-catch, seasonal migrations and behavioral patterns of sharks and other elasmobranchs species have been discovered thanks to Argos. The talk will illustrate the Argos-tracked elasmobranchs species by figures, global and regional maps at a crucial moment of Argos technology: the availability since 1st October 2025 of the “Argos Neo” constellation made of “Legacy” satellites belonging to the institutional space agencies and more new Kineis nanosatellites, fully compatible with the legacy one. Kineis is offering decisive functional and technical steps: an improved revisit time, a much-improved Doppler positioning (multisat, clustering), new modulation frequencies, allowing more miniaturization steps, a new downlink capacity, a new platform, etc.
1410: Acoustic telemetry has become a powerful tool for investigating the spatiotemporal movements of marine animals. This method has been successfully applied to species that spend extended periods underwater and exhibit site fidelity during life history stages, including elasmobranchs. The present study aims to expand acoustic receiver coverage in Taiwanese waters and to develop a shared data network among researchers across the Northwest Pacific. Since 2023, Vemco acoustic receivers (VR2W and VR2Tx) have been deployed along the eastern and southwestern waters of Taiwan. Simultaneously, animals were successfully tagged and released with Vemco transmitters (69 kHz), including Rhincodon typus, Negaprion acutidens, Rhinobatos schlegelii, Rhynchobatus immaculatus, Galeocerdo cuvier, R. australiae, Megachasma pelagios, Chiloscyllium plagiosum, Rhina ancylostoma, and Mobula alfredi. A total of 1,639 detections were recorded for tagged animals, mostly from R. immaculatus in Penghu, reflecting the generally low mobility of small benthic rays. In addition, detections were attributed to nine unidentified individuals detected by the receivers of this study. Future work will focus on expanding the receiver network and increasing tagging efforts, in collaboration with regional partners. The overarching goal of this project is to advance understanding of elasmobranch movement ecology throughout the Northwest Pacific.
From Data to Policy: Managing Shared and Migratory Shark and Ray Populations

1412: Las Canteras Beach (L. P. Gran Canaria, Canary Islands, Spain) was recently designated as an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). This recognition emerged from a multidisciplinary initiative that integrates coastal ecotourism, environmental education, and citizen science to advance the conservation of elasmobranchs in an urbanized marine environment. This contribution outlines the participatory approach used to document species presence, abundance, and behavior, leveraging guided snorkeling programs, collaborative monitoring activities, and open-access educational tools to strengthen public engagement and data collection capacity. Citizengenerated observations, validated by marine scientists, provided robust evidence of the ecological relevance of the area, revealing consistent use of the bay by multiple species of rays and sharks for feeding, resting, and developmental purposes. Beyond the scientific results (‘‘Urbanite’’ rays and sharks: Presence, habitat use and population structure in an urban semienclosed lagoon), the project fostered a community committed to conservation, raising environmental awareness among residents, tourists, and local stakeholders. The integration of responsible ecotourism practices ensured minimal disturbance while generating a scalable model for community-based marine conservation in heavily frequented coastal environments. The ISRA designation of Las Canteras highlights the effectiveness of combining citizen science with public outreach to inform conservation planning. It also positions this coastal urban ecosystem as a strategic site for ongoing research, protection measures, and citizen participation. The Las Canteras case demonstrates that human-impacted coastal areas can become key players in elasmobranch conservation when supported by inclusive, science-based initiatives with a strong social component.
Leveraging Important Shark and Ray Areas
1413: The Halavi guitarfish (Glaucostegus halavi) is a Critically Endangered and poorly studied Rhinopristiform found in the northern Indian Ocean. This study investigates the movement patterns of this species within the Al Wajh lagoon in the Saudi Arabian Red Sea. Both fine- and broad-scale tracking techniques were used to quantify residency, monitor habitat use, and describe ontogenetic shifts in behaviour. Individuals were captured via bottom longlines or seine net, with animals spanning three life stages (young-of-the-year, juvenile, and adult) acoustically tagged (V9s, V13s, and V16s; InnovaSea) across eight islands. Thirteen adults were also tagged with microPATs (Wildlife Computers). An array of acoustic receivers was deployed in the lagoon, and detection data were analysed using residency indices, kernel utilisation distributions, and Markov state-switching frameworks to infer habitat and temporal site use. Preliminary findings reveal strong residency across all life stages, with mature individuals exhibiting broader movement patterns and increased use of deeper habitats. Satellite data indicated energy-efficient U-, V-, or W-shaped dives, as well as potential thermoregulatory behaviour. Further analyses will assess the influence of seasonal, lunar, and tidal cycles. Collectively, these findings advance our understanding of guitarfish movement ecology, providing valuable insights that can guide conservation strategies, particularly in lagoonal systems where environmental extremes are expected to intensify under changing climate conditions.
International Rhino Ray Research and Conservation

1414: Overfishing and incidental capture remain major threats to the sustainability of many elasmobranch species. Several mitigation measures have been developed to reduce catches and associated mortalities in different fisheries, but each entails trade-offs between conservation benefits and operational feasibility. Therefore, efforts to implement mitigation measures should focus on fisheries with the greatest impact. Quantifying fleet–species interactions helps identify where elasmobranch catches and mortalities are highest, guiding the prioritization of mitigation efforts. In the Atlantic Ocean, under the management framework of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), this study updates and expands previous assessments of elasmobranch bycatch. It incorporates recent data (2010–2023) and provides species-level estimates of catches and fishery-related mortalities by fleet and region. We compiled public fisheries data from logbooks, observer records, and published sources documenting fleet-level shark and ray catches across ICCAT fisheries. Species-level target catch/bycatch ratios were estimated for each fleet, region, and year, and total catches were then derived by extrapolating from fleet-level effort or targetspecies catches. Fishery-related mortality estimates combined retained catches, dead discards, and post-release mortality rates. This study provides the first comprehensive and updated quantification of elasmobranch catches and mortalities across ICCAT fleets and fisheries in the Atlantic Ocean. By identifying high-risk species–fleet interactions and the fisheries contributing most to overall impacts, it delivers essential knowledge for evidencebased bycatch management. These results form a foundation for prioritizing and implementing the most appropriate mitigation measures within ICCAT to reduce elasmobranch bycatch and mortality, where required.
Beyond the Net: Addressing the Impacts and Innovations in Shark & Ray Bycatch

1418: Environmental DNA (eDNA) methods are rapidly transforming biodiversity monitoring by enabling scalable, non-invasive detection of species across broad spatial and temporal scales. Here, we analyse more than 6,000 marine eDNA samples collected from over sites between 2019 and 2024 across Australia’s Exclusive Economic Zone. Sampling encompassed diverse oceanographic and depth gradients—from tropical Christmas Island to temperate Tasmania— including continental shelves, offshore pelagic waters, and deep-sea habitats. Using a multimarker metabarcoding approach (16SFishD, MiFish-U&E2, and MarVer1 assays), we characterised chondrichthyan, and broader marine vertebrate biodiversity. Our results reveal how eDNA captures spatial and temporal patterns of chondrichthyan assemblages, detects elusive and cryptic taxa rarely recorded by conventional survey methods, and establishes valuable biodiversity baselines in data-poor regions. These findings demonstrate the potential of eDNA technologies to complement traditional biodiversity observations to inform ecosystem models and strengthen conservation planning across Australia’s marine estate.

1420: Reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) face ongoing conservation challenges due to global population declines and anthropogenic pressures, especially in tourism-driven environments. Fine-scale, site-specific studies are critical for understanding aggregation dynamics and informing management strategies. Here, we analyze years (2010-2022) of citizen science data to investigate patterns of site use, sex-specific movements, and prey influence at two nighttime feeding sites, Garden Eel Cove (GEC) and Keauhou (KH), along the Kona coast of Hawai‘i Island. Over 23,000 recorded sightings identified M. alfredi individuals, revealing both shared and distinct site-specific patterns. GEC supported larger, more variable aggregations with nearparity sex ratios, while KH was strongly female-skewed (91% of sightings) and more consistently hosted smaller groups. Lagged Identification Rate analyses indicated strong site fidelity by females at KH and greater interchange among males, suggesting sex-based differences in spatial behavior. Aggregation sizes fluctuated seasonally and were correlated with zooplankton density, highlighting prey availability as a primary driver of M. alfredi site use. Despite sustained tourism pressure, both sites exhibited stable or increasing mean annual sighting rates and consistent demographic composition. These findings provide new insight into the fine-scale spatial ecology of M. alfredi and emphasize the value of long-term, community-sourced datasets in supporting the management of vulnerable elasmobranchs.

1422: Scyliorhinus canicula (Linnaeus, 1758), commonly known as the small-spotted catshark, is one of the most abundant demersal elasmobranchs in the Mediterranean Sea. Although this species is frequently captured by commercial trawlers as both bycatch and for consumption in the French Mediterranean, its exploitation status remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we analysed MEDITS survey data collected between 1994 and 2025 to describe, for the first time, the spatio-temporal abundance, distribution, and population structure of S. canicula in the Gulf of Lion. Both density and biomass peaked on the continental shelf at depths of 100–150 m, progressively decreasing toward deeper grounds. Following the establishment of a temporary spatial closure in 2020, a marked increase in adult density was observed beyond m. Overall, shallow areas were dominated by larger individuals of both sexes, whereas juveniles were concentrated on the slope, co-occurring with adults in two distinct density hotspots—potential nursery grounds for the species. Adult males reached larger sizes and matured earlier than females, with no evidence of sexual segregation. These findings provide new insights into the population dynamics of S. canicula in the Gulf of Lion and contribute valuable information for the development of future management and conservation strategies.

1423: Stable isotope analysis is a central tool for studying ecological niches, based on the premise that the isotopic composition of primary producers is transferred through the food web in a relatively predictable manner, allowing the retrospective tracing of trophic interactions. This method enables a quantitative assessment of a consumer’s diet and presents practical advantages, such as low cost and the possibility of sampling dead, archived, or living specimens through non-lethal and minimally invasive techniques. While isotopic analyses have mainly focused on carbon and nitrogen, and to a lesser extent on sulfur, oxygen, and hydrogen, nontraditional mercury (Hg) isotopes remains little explored. Hg, now ubiquitous in marine ecosystems from anthropogenic sources, bioaccumulates with increasing size and age and is efficiently transferred from prey to predators in marine food webs. This presentation provides an overview of the different Hg isotopic fractionations in the water column, how these baseline isotopic variations are transferred through the food web, and how they can be leveraged to offer novel insights into the trophic ecology of mobile predators, such as elasmobranchs. Drawing on different case studies, the addition of Hg isotope analysis in the study of elasmobranchs reveals: (i) depth-related resource partitioning in offshore species, (ii) ontogenetic diet shifts, (iii) the diversity of food resources in coastal settings, and (iv) new perspectives on the trophic structure at large spatial scale. For each study case, an emphasis is placed on the complementarity between Hg and traditional carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur stable isotope analyses to explore elasmobranch trophic dynamics.
Quantifying the Chase: New Frontiers in Predator-Prey Dynamics

1424: Species conservation programs are inherently technical, involving aspects such as animal husbandry, genetic management, assisted reproduction techniques like artificial insemination, and post-release monitoring. ReShark, an international coalition dedicated to scalable shark and ray rewilding, and its first and flagship initiative, the Stegostoma tigrinum Augmentation and Recovery (StAR) Project, which began in Indonesia in 2020 and expanded to Thailand in 2024, exemplifies these integrated efforts. ReShark unites over partners across more than countries, linking ex situ and in situ conservation through breeding programs and translocations. The task at hand extends beyond executing these interventions to making the science accessible for diverse audiences. The scope of science communication has grown in parallel with ReShark, evolving to meet the needs of a global coalition while ensuring all stakeholder voices are represented. This presentation highlights strategies developed to engage partners worldwide, balancing data-driven scientific education with visual storytelling, pop culture framing, and milestone narratives. Case studies illustrate how complex science can be communicated responsibly, without oversimplification, and how culturally grounded storytelling builds trust. Science communication is framed as a core operational tool that will continue driving the growth of a new and exciting frontier in elasmobranch conservation.
1425: As research shifts towards non-invasive methods, photo-identification (photo-ID) of individuals has the potential to be a powerful research and monitoring tool for rays yet, it remains underutilised. A review of studies revealed strong taxonomic and geographic biases in the use of photo-ID, with efforts concentrated on ray species with bold spot patterns. Consequently, the use of photo-ID on the vast pattern diversity present in rays remains unvalidated. Therefore, we provide the first systematic test of the use of photo-ID on a marbled type patterning in rays (using the southern African endemic Dasyatis chrysonota). Individual identification was undertaken with different approaches identified in literature (manual matching and the semi-automated identification software I#S Spot and I3S Pattern) and a custom-developed deep-learning system (“Raydar”). The marbled pattern displayed significant inter-individual variability and stability through time (for days). The accuracy and processing time to ID individuals varied between methods - manual matching was the slowest (mean = 74s) yet most accurate; I3S Spot and Raydar delivered high accuracy (both achieved 78%) with faster processing time (64s and 22s, respectively); I3S Pattern was the fastest (18s) but least accurate. This study expands the use of photo-ID beyond spots to include marbled patterning for the first time and highlights tools that can aid in the time-consuming task of identifying individuals. Use of photo-ID on other ray species and pattern types is encouraged, as it provides critical insights for threatened species, informing conservation in a costeffective, non-invasive manner.
