1428: For shark conservation to be effective and sustainable, local communities must play an active role. When science is communicated through an accessible, relatable, and inclusive lens, awareness is more likely to lead to action. However, there is often a disconnect between scientists and the communities most affected by conservation issues, particularly due to the use of complex, jargon-filled language. In South Africa, where official languages coexist, English remains dominant in scientific discourse. This poses a significant barrier for Afrikaans, Kaaps (a blend of Afrikaans and English widely spoken in Cape Town), and isiXhosa-speaking learners from under-resourced communities. At the Save Our Seas Foundation Shark Education Centre (SOSFSEC), this language gap has resulted in reduced engagement during education programmes conducted solely in English. Students frequently struggled to respond to interactive questions or grasp complex terminology, especially when their home language was not English. To address this, the SOSFSEC team adopted multilingual and culturally responsive approaches. Lessons were adapted to include translations into Afrikaans, Kaaps, and isiXhosa, using not only direct translations but also familiar idioms and culturally familiar references. This approach also addresses the psychological and spatial challenges learners experience when visiting historically white-dominated coastal institutions. By creating a more inclusive and emotionally safe learning environment, the SOSFSEC demonstrates that language can serve as a bridge for empowerment and understanding. This model offers a framework for conservationists and educators seeking to build stronger connections with diverse linguistic communities in marine education.
Save Our Seas Foundation Shark Education Centre (SOSFSEC)
1429: Conservation science often grapples with the challenge of transforming complex, data-heavy topics into stories that resonate with the public. When budgets are tight and media experience is limited, communicating these critical issues can feel overwhelming - but it doesn’t have to be. This talk will guide attendees through the process of designing and executing powerful media campaigns that inspire engagement and drive impact, even with minimal resources. Using the #SaveTheMantas campaign as a case study, we’ll explore how the Manta Trust translated a highly technical policy issue (the CITES CoP20 proposal to uplist mobulid rays to Appendix I) into an accessible, emotionally compelling public movement. The campaign combined consistent branding, strategic social media storytelling, targeted press outreach, and creative partnerships with influencers, journalists, and brands, all achieved on a limited budget. Participants will gain practical insights into how to identify key messages, leverage free or low-cost communication tools, and build collaborations that amplify reach. Beyond conservation, the lessons shared apply broadly to any researcher or organisation seeking to communicate science in ways that connect, empower, and mobilise audiences. This session is ideal for anyone looking to elevate their science communication strategy - whether you’re launching your first outreach campaign or seeking to refresh an existing approach. Attendees will leave with an actionable roadmap for creating meaningful, resource-efficient media campaigns that make complex science matter.
1430: Elasmobranchs are encountered by mixed and directed fisheries on a global scale. The Shark Trust has produced commercial Fisheries Advisories for the fishing industry and enforcement agencies since 2010. The Trust engaging with fisheries enforcement agencies and the fishing industry to provide materials and advice supports and promotes sustainable fisheries. Until now, while available in several languages, these advisories were exclusively designed to give rapid access to the current legislative status of sharks, skates, and rays for UK and EU vessels in the Northeast Atlantic. This year, we have developed Fisheries Advisories for the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT). This Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (RFMO) is responsible for the management and conservation of tuna and tuna-like species (including sharks) in the Atlantic Ocean. Oceanic sharks are encountered by fishing vessels in the high seas of the Atlantic, and many of these species are exceptionally threatened by overfishing. Within the management framework of ICCAT, some shark species are prohibited to target and retain, whereas other species can be caught and sold, with a range of different management measures in place. A need for Fisheries Advisories has been identified in this context; to enable fishers and managers to quickly and easily determine which management measures apply to which species, and in which hemisphere. This poster will showcase the ICCAT Fisheries Advisories, their development, and how they can help to achieve sustainable fisheries. Working in partnership with RFMOs, we will continue to create more Fisheries Advisories for additional areas.
1431: Environmental variability plays a crucial role in shaping the site use of apex predators, yet its influence under human-modified conditions remains unclear. From August 2021 to March 2024, we conducted visual surveys of tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) at Fuvahmulah, Maldives. We used photo-ID to identify individual tiger sharks, and agglomerative hierarchical clustering to classify sharks into clusters. We fitted generalized additive mixed models to the different shark lusters to test whether sea surface temperature, monsoon phase, lunar–tide interactions, dive depth and duration, and wind and wave metrics, influenced shark abundance at the Tiger Harbour dive site. Models explained 24–38% of deviance and revealed that resident females preferred warm temperatures and monsoonal cycles, whereas transient sharks responded more to weather patterns, wind direction, and lunar–tidal effects. Our results underscore that natural environmental rhythms continue to influence tiger shark occurrence even under regular provisioning, informing ecological insights.
Leibniz Centre for Tropical Marine Research
1433: Purse seine fishing technology has become increasingly efficient since the 1950s and now catches roughly 66% of global tuna. Tuna purse seines also capture large quantities of bycatch species, particularly elasmobranchs (sharks and rays). Approximately 13,000 manta and devil rays (mobulids) are caught each year by tuna purse seine vessels. Mobulid rays have low reproductive rates (as few as one pup every two years) and low population growth rates, making them particularly vulnerable to overexploitation and less able to recover when depleted. Conservation efforts in purse seine fisheries have focused on reducing post-release mortality. However, growing evidence suggests that variability in fisher decision-making and operational choices can influence bycatch risk. This project draws on years of observer data for tuna purse seine vessels in the Eastern Pacific Ocean to evaluate the role that individual vessel captains have on mobulid bycatch. We apply, generalized additive models (GAMs), generalized linear models (GLMs), and hierarchical models to identify potential drivers of bycatch variation across vessels. Predictor variables include: 1) vessel captain and behavior 2) flag affiliation 3) technological and operational characteristics, and 4) spatiotemporal fishing patterns. Preliminary results indicate notable variability in mobulid bycatch among vessels that cannot be explained solely by fishing area or effort, suggesting that captain-level or operational factors may play an important role. Ongoing work aims to disentangle these effects to better understand how behavioral and institutional contexts influence bycatch outcomes. Our results suggest that individual decision-making can be an important management-relevant factor in bycatch mitigation.
1435: Global conservation agreements often rely on protected area coverage targets, such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework’s “30x30” goal. While these area-based targets are widely adopted, their effectiveness at safeguarding biodiversity, particularly at the species level, remains uncertain. This study evaluates the relationship between marine protected area (MPA) coverage and the spatial protection of individual shark and ray species. Using global species range data and MPA boundaries within national Exclusive Economic Zones, we calculated the proportion of each species’ range that falls within MPAs, with a focus on NoTake areas. Our findings reveal a significant shortfall in meaningful species-level protection. No Critically Endangered shark or ray species has more than 5% of its range within No-Take MPAs, and 79% of all threatened species have less than 1% of their range protected. When considering all MPA types (not just No-Take), average coverage across threatened species is around 11%, below the average MPA coverage in national waters of 18.5%. These results highlight a major gap between international coverage targets and actual biodiversity outcomes. While areabased targets lay a critical foundation, their effectiveness depends on integrating clear goals for species-level protection. To effectively conserve sharks and rays, global conservation strategies must prioritize biologically meaningful protection that targets species distributions. As part of this analysis, we also present insights into species-level protection within the Indian Ocean.
Advancing Area-Based Management for Chondrichthyans: Challenges and Opportunities

1437: Mobulids (family Mobulidae) are one of the most vulnerable groups of elasmobranchs to overfishing due to their slow growth, long gestation periods and low reproductive output, which severely limit their capacity for population recovery. In the Atlantic Ocean, bycatch of mobulids in fisheries is poorly documented, their spatial ecology remains largely unresolved, and the effectiveness of existing mitigation measures is still unknown. To address this knowledge gap, we developed hierarchical spatiotemporal Species Distribution Models (SDMs) examining the spatiotemporal patterns of mobulid occurrences, assessing how environmental variability influences their habitat use, and identifying areas with elevated bycatch risk. The models were fitted using fishery observer data from the French and Spanish tropical-tuna purse-seine fleets (2009 - 2023), explicitly accounting for spatiotemporal autocorrelation through structured random effects, efficiently capturing nonlinear relationships with environmental variables. Predicted distributions revealed two consistent hotspots along the Mauritanian and Angolan inshore areas, closely associated with the Guinea Dome and coastal upwelling dynamics, respectively. Comparisons between family-level and species-specific models (e.g. Mobula mobular, M. birostris) showed similar spatial patterns, suggesting that family-level modelling can enhance statistical power and reduce uncertainty caused by species misidentification onboard. The unified “one family level approach” provides a practical tool for fisheries management and conservation, simplifying decision-making processes and reducing bias caused by the potential misidentification of mobulids at sea. Our ultimate goal is to provide a unified SDM that offers essential insights into the effectiveness and limitations of existing mitigation strategies, guiding efforts to minimize mobula bycatch in the Atlantic Ocean.

1439: Carrion windfalls influence population dynamics and ecosystem processes. These events are well studied in terrestrial systems but poorly understood in marine environments. In Hawai‘i, tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) make predictable seasonal movements into Maui Nui waters coinciding with peak humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) abundance, suggesting shark reproductive energetics may be influenced by whale‐scavenging opportunities. To explore this possibility, we adapted a marine mammal bioenergetic model within a Population Consequences of Resource Enhancement (PCoRE) framework - an inversion of the traditional “disturbance” paradigm (PCoD) - to examine how seasonal pulses of high-energy prey affect female tiger shark energy budgets, fecundity, and population growth. The model incorporates species-specific physiology, including the dominance of diacylglyceryl ether in tiger shark livers, and simulates “baseline” vs. “enhanced” resource conditions that reflect the energetic impact of whale carcass availability. Our simulations show that access to energy-dense whale resources can substantially boost reproductive output, increasing litter size particularly when lipid bioavailability is high. These results suggest that periodic whale-fall events may play a key role in sustaining tiger shark populations in Hawai‘i. More broadly, the PCoRE framework offers a powerful new tool for linking individual energy use to population dynamics, revealing how short-term resource pulses can ripple through marine ecosystems in surprising and beneficial ways.
1442: The spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) is an ecologically and commercially important small shark with a global distribution across boreal and temperate waters. Its life history is characterized by slow growth, late maturity, and low fecundity, making it exceptionally vulnerable to exploitation and slow to recover from historical overfishing. Despite some stock recoveries, major uncertainties persist regarding its global population structure, connectivity, and adaptive potential, which are crucial for defining appropriate management units and developing effective conservation strategies. This study addresses these gaps using low-coverage whole-genome resequencing (LC-WGS), building on a high-quality, chromosome-level reference genome for S. acanthias, involving over individuals from key populations across the North and South Atlantic, Mediterranean, and Pacific. This genome-wide SNP dataset enables detailed analysis of genetic diversity, population structure, and connectivity across the species’ broad geographic range. The resulting genomic data will clarify global and regional connectivity, resolve genetically distinct population units, and quantify patterns of genetic diversity. Crucially, identifying genomic regions under selection will reveal the adaptive potential underpinning the species’ resilience to environmental pressures. By providing a comprehensive perspective on S. acanthias population dynamics and adaptive capacity, this work provides an essential genomic foundation to inform evidence-based conservation policy and support the sustainable responsible management of this vulnerable shark.

1443: Shark deterrent technologies that use electric fields offer promising tools to reduce depredation and negative shark–human interactions, yet comparisons among devices have been hindered by inconsistent measurement standards. Previous studies relied primarily on one-dimensional field measurements and did not account for nearby insulating materials, limiting the accuracy of models for human-worn deterrents. To address these limitations, we developed a two-dimensional submerged “clothesline” rig with evenly spaced sensors to map the electric potential around two dipole-based deterrent systems: one with symmetric cylindrical electrodes and another combining a flat and cylindrical electrode. Field mapping revealed consistent radial voltage-decay patterns in both designs, but the flat-electrode configuration produced a % stronger peak field opposite the insulator. Introducing a humanshaped insulator above the flat electrode further amplified peak voltage without altering overall field geometry. Modeling of voltage attenuation using isotonic regression predicts that sharkdetectable voltages (~5 nV) can extend up to m from the source. This work provides a reproducible field-mapping benchmark, quantifies insulator effects, and enables predictive modeling of deterrent voltage decay for future field and animal-behavior trials.

1447: Although shark fin trafficking is receiving increasing media attention, no scientific article has been dedicated to it in the field of criminology. Since the 2010s, green criminologists have nevertheless produced numerous papers on illegal wildlife trade. Conceptualized by Michael J. Lynch, green criminology indeed leads scientists to focus on “a wider variety of class-related injustices that [poison] the environment of all classes, peoples and animals”. Adopting the methodology of green criminologists in my PhD, I therefore decided to investigate shark fin smuggling in the Gulf of Guinea and the eastern tropical Pacific, two hotspots for smuggled fin shipments. During eight months of research in Gabon, Sao Tome and Principe, Costa Rica, Colombia and Ecuador, I could observe that shark trafficking goes far beyond their fins. Different patterns emerge depending on states and the types of regulations in force. In Costa Rica and Sao Tome and Principe, some companies use their legal facade to facilitate the shipment of shark fins or drugs hidden in shark bodies. In Colombia and Gabon, the decline in shark fin trafficking is offset for by the rise in swim bladder smuggling. Ecuador stands out for a particular type of criminal symbiosis between fishermen and drug traffickers. While sharks are massively fished by Manabi coastal communities, many of them are in fact a cover for the fishermen involved in drug trafficking. By highlighting the criminal convergence between shark fin trafficking and other illegal transnational activities, this study underscores the pressure that drug trafficking places on shark populations.

1448: Shark populations in Nigerian waters face increasing threats from overfishing, pollution, habitat degradation, and limited management interventions, yet scientific data on their status remain scarce. This study employs a Local Ecological Knowledge (LEK) approach to assess the conservation status of sharks in selected coastal communities of Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Data were collected through structured interviews aided by Kobo-Collect on artisanal fishers, with the aim to document species occurrence, population trends, fishing practices, and community perceptions of shark conservation. Findings from the study reveal a percent perceived decline in shark population over the previous year, driven primarily by targeted fishing and bycatch, with limited awareness of conservation laws and minimal institutional support for sustainable management. The results further revealed an overwhelmingly male-dominated gender composition, with 87.9 percent of respondents being men and only 12.1percent women. Similarly, there was a statistically significant correlation between local knowledge of shark species and training on conservation. In particular, the Chi-square test recorded 10.356, at pvalue of 0.006, while Fisher's Exact p-value was found to be 0.014; suggesting that formal conservation awareness activities might directly improve local knowledge of shark species. Also, only percent of the respondents reported awareness of cultural taboos on sharks fishing, indicating that remnants of cultural norms still persist in some segments of the fishing communities. The study underscores the urgent need for integrated conservation strategies that combine community knowledge, legal frameworks, and alternative livelihood programs to ensure the long-term sustainability of shark populations in Nigeria.

1449: Elasmobranchs play critical roles in maintaining marine ecosystem balance, yet information on their natural distribution remains scarce across much of the Indo-Pacific, including Taiwan. In Taiwan, most of what we know about sharks and rays still comes from fishery data including landings, bycatch, or market surveys. These fishery-dependent data, which reflect catch and exploitation instead of natural distribution or habitat use. To address this gap, we applied baited remote underwater video (BRUV) surveys to obtain standardized, non-invasive observations of elasmobranch species across three regions – Dongsha Atoll, Penghu South Islands, and Green Island between 2024 and 2025. A total of deployments were conducted, with elasmobranchs detected in 38.8% of the videos. Across all regions, seven species were recorded, all listed as Endangered (EN) or Vulnerable (VU) under the IUCN Red List. Detection rates varied markedly among sites: Dongsha showed the highest occurrence (52% of deployments) and relative abundance (mean MaxN = 1.03; 1.0 MaxN/h), followed by occasional detections at Green Island (40%), while Penghu had only 5% occurrence rate. Seasonal differences were most evident at Dongsha, where relative abundance peaked in summer (mean MaxN = 1.4; 1.72 ManN/h) and declined during winter (MaxN =0.47; 0.27 MaxN/h). In contrast elasmobranchs were rarely recorded in Penghu across all seasons. These results establish the first standardized, non-invasive baseline for elasmobranch monitoring in Taiwan water and demonstrate the potential of BRUV surveys to support long-term ecological assessments and regional conservation planning.

1450: Chondrichthyes are distributed circumglobally, inhabiting environments ranging from shallow coastal waters (<200 m) to the deep sea (>3000 m), often migrating between shallow and deep habitats. Various hypotheses have been suggested to explain these vertical migrations behaviourally. Yet, the mechanisms by which skeletal tissues facilitate movement across varying hydrostatic pressures, without experiencing significant damage, remain poorly understood. Mobulid rays provide unique models for investigating depth-specific adaptations, as they span depth ranges between 0–2000 m through diel vertical migrations. In this study, the neurocranial cartilage of two surface-oriented species (Mobula eregoodoo, M. thurstoni) and two depth-oriented species (M. mobular, M. tarapacana) was examined to identify interspecific differences in mechanical, biochemical, and structural properties in relation to depth range. Mechanical properties including stiffness, toughness, ultimate strength, energy dissipation, and stress-relaxation behaviour were quantified through a multiscale approach combining uniaxial compression, micro- and nanoindentation. Complementary biochemical analyses assessed mineralisation (TMD), glycosaminoglycan (GAG) content, and water distribution, using micro-CT, biochemical assays, histology, and differential scanning calorimetry. Structural differences were identified through microscopic and immunohistochemical assessments. Our results showed an inverse relationship between the depth range and most mechanical parameters. Biochemical composition was broadly conserved among species and showed significant correlation between mechanical properties and the water content but not GAG content or TMD. This highlights the importance of structural differences underlying functional adaptations to hydrostatic pressure. These findings offer key first insights in the skeletal integrity maintained by these protected species, which evolved to withstand extreme environmental pressures.

1452: Manta rays are globally threatened due to their conservative life histories and targeted exploitation. In Australia, where direct fisheries are absent, relatively stable populations provide an opportunity to examine key ecological questions regarding movement, habitat use, and population connectivity. While several manta ray aggregation sites have been identified along Australia’s east coast, questions about fine-scale movements and the degree of connectivity between sites remain. Between 2021 and 2024, GPS Fastloc-enabled SPLASH10F-321E satellite tags were deployed on reef manta rays at Lady Elliot Island, in the southern Great Barrier Reef. Tagged individuals included both sexes and four visibly pregnant females. Nine of the tags were retrieved post-deployment, providing high resolution archival datasets for analysis. Horizontal and vertical movements were analysed using state-space models and integrating environmental variables to assess potential drivers of movement and habitat use. Manta rays exhibited extended surface occupancy at previously undocumented locations, indicating potential foraging or pupping areas. Behavioural models identified alternating transiting and resident phases across both managed and unmanaged marine zones. Vertical analyses revealed diel diving behaviour, with dives exceeding m off the continental shelf, consistent with deep foraging activity. This study provides the first high-resolution movement data for manta rays in eastern Australia, highlighting areas of ecological importance. These findings enhance understanding of manta ray movement ecology and support spatial conservation initiatives such as the IUCN Important Shark and Ray Areas project. Continued integration of telemetry and environmental data will refine identification of critical habitats for effective management of these vulnerable species.

1453: Manta rays are globally threatened species, primarily due to their conservative life histories, slow reproductive rates, and vulnerability to targeted fisheries and bycatch. Habitat degradation and shifting ocean conditions further exacerbate pressures on their populations. In Australian waters, manta rays are relatively protected from targeted fisheries; however, global pressures persist and knowledge gaps on key biological and ecological parameters remain. For two decades Project Manta has harnessed the power of citizen science to monitor manta ray populations along Australia’s east coast. Citizen scientists—divers, snorkellers, and photographers—submit photographs through dedicated online platforms and social media. Each image is manually verified and catalogued based on the individual’s unique ventral spot pattern, allowing for long-term tracking of individuals across both space and time. Partnerships with tourism operators have been instrumental in sustaining engagement and expanding survey coverage, providing consistent data from key aggregation sites and beyond. Photographic identification has resulted in a catalogue of 1,800 individual reef manta rays, with over 10,000 verified sightings of these individuals. These data have revealed distinct seasonal migration patterns and record-breaking point-to-point movements for reef manta rays. Remarkably, citizen scientists also contributed to the discovery of the world’s only known pink manta ray and documented the world’s oldest known manta ray. These findings demonstrate the critical contribution of citizen science to marine megafauna research, and highlight its transformative role in generating robust datasets, advance ecological understanding, and inspire marine stewardship among the wider community.

1454: Malaysia is home to eleven rhino ray species, including the giant guitarfish Glaucostegus typus, which are often caught as bycatch in commercial fisheries or targeted by recreational anglers. However, very little is known about the spatial distribution of these species, and detection efforts remain challenging due to their rarity. Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a powerful non-invasive method for detecting rare and endangered species like rhino rays. This study therefore aims to advance eDNA applications for rhino ray detection by developing eDNA metabarcoding assays targeting mitochondrial ND2 and COI gene regions. Water samples were collected from multiple nearshore sites on the east coast of Johor, where frequent sightings of Glaucostegus typus had been reported, and processed using optimized water filtration and DNA extraction protocols. Preliminary 12S metabarcoding analyses using MiFish primers provided baseline data on local fish communities but also highlighted challenges in detecting elasmobranchs, likely due to low eDNA concentrations, limited sequencing reads, and the incompleteness of available 12S reference sequences. Ongoing work will focus on expanding regional ND2 and COI reference libraries and validating newly designed assays to improve detection accuracy and monitoring capabilities for rhino rays. Ultimately, this study will help identify critical habitats, support conservation planning, and promote public awareness and local engagement initiatives along the east coast of Johor and the wider Malaysian coastal waters.

1455: Recent new species records of rhino rays (order Rhinopristiformes) from within the Malacca Strait indicates greater species richness of this highly endangered group than previously thought in an area of major human activities. One of these records – the eyebrow wedgefish (Rhynchobatus palpebratus) – remains one of the few rhino rays not listed as Critically Endangered. The discovery of an actively exploited population in the Strait necessitates the collection of biological, ecological, and fisheries data in order to better inform risk assessments and future management. This study was undertaken to examine the demographic profile of eyebrow wedgefish caught in the Strait’s fisheries via market and landing site surveys, alongside their feeding ecology via stomach content analysis. Fifty individuals sampled from August 2024 to date from a landing site in west Johor comprised all size classes from newborn to mature adults of both sexes including gravid females (50% male, 50% female; 86% immature, 14% mature) which appeared to mature at larger sizes compared to males (minimum total length for mature males = 116cm; females = 180cm). Their diet was mostly represented by inshore prey such as prawns (families Penaeidae and Sergestidae), swimming crabs (Portunidae), mantis shrimps (Squillidae), and demersal fish (Sciaenidae, Leiognathidae, and Bregmaceros sp.), with little ontogenetic variation in dietary composition. These findings suggest a population present in the southern part of the strait with affinity towards inshore waters throughout their life history, facing exploitation pressure and should be considered for inclusion for reassessment of the species’ global risk status.

1456: Whale sharks exhibit complex movement behaviors influenced by seafloor geomorphology and oceanographic variability, yet the mechanisms driving their seasonal habitat segregation remain unclear. This study examines how seafloor features and dynamic ocean conditions influence whale shark movement behavior (migration and feeding) across spatial and temporal scales. Using one of the most comprehensive datasets in the Indo-Pacific region, consisting of fin-mounted satellite tracks (64 juvenile males, adult male, and juvenile females) collected between 2015 and 2025, we applied a correlated random walk state-space model to classify foraging and migrating behaviors. Behavioral states were then used to construct ecological niche models across nine regions, sexes, life stages, behaviors, and seasons, resulting in optimized models. Niche segregation was assessed using IsoMDS, while spatial overlap analyses quantified shared spatial niches. Results identified region and bathymetry as the strongest predictors of niche segregation, with behavior, sex, and season also contributing significantly. Juvenile males primarily occupied shallow, productive waters, though some moved offshore seasonally following regional oceanographic changes. Adult males migrated along seamounts and escarpments, while juvenile females favored deeper, vertically productive habitats. Niche overlap was low between large juvenile males and females (mean 21%, p < 0.001), between behavioral states (28%, p < 0.001), and across seasons for both sexes (around 25%, p < 0.001). This study provides the first quantitative evidence of seasonal niche partitioning in whale sharks and emphasizes the need for dynamic, sex, behavioral, and season specific management approaches to protect critical habitats across the Indo-Pacific.

1457: The Mobulidae family comprises nine extant manta and devil ray (mobulid) species in the monogeneric genus Mobula, of which five occur in Peruvian waters. This study assessed mobulid ray landings and trade along Peru’s coast by analysing historical captures, monitoring landing sites, and interviewing fishers (n = 37) and traders (n = 21). From 2000 to 2023, artisanal fisheries reported 7444.9 tons of mobulids, according to the Marine Institute of Peru. Between 2013 and 2023, annual landings in northern Peru averaged about 11,520 individuals (7414 M. munkiana, 3126 M. mobular, and M. thurstoni), ranking Peru among the world’s largest mobulid fisheries. However, landings declined by 75.05% between 2013–2023 compared to 2000–2012. Six key landing sites in Tumbes and Piura were monitored between April 2017 and February 2019, with specimens examined for morphometric data. The most common species was M. mobular (60.7%), followed by M. thurstoni (18.3%), M. munkiana (9.3%), and M. birostris (1.6%). Interviews indicated higher landings during the warm season (December–May). Although M. birostris has been protected in Peruvian waters since 2016, and recent legislation now protects all mobulid species, these rays remain globally threatened. The large number of mobulids landed annually in Peru underscores the urgent need for effective fisheries management and conservation measures to protect these highly vulnerable species.

1459: The Indo Pacific region is the centre of diversity for highly threatened wedgefish and guitarfish, collectively known as rhino rays. However, the lack of basic research on taxonomic status, distribution, biology, and fisheries profile prevents science-based advocacy for better conservation and management of these animals. Using integrated approaches of fisheriesdependent surveys, fisher interviews, social media data mining, morphological and molecular approaches, we present contemporary information on species richness, finer scale spatial distribution, and fisheries threats for eight species in Malaysia. Low genetic diversity and some fine scale genetic structuring is seen for the most commonly encountered species, bottlenose wedgefish Rhynchobatus australiae, that is broadly distributed across coastal Malaysia. Novel information on two new species records of rhino rays and their restricted distribution within Malaysian waters is discussed. Both commercial trawl and artisanal fishing gears appear to be major fishing gear threats to rhino rays, specifically in terms of higher volume caught and greater mortality rates. Fisher respondents across Malaysia showed cohesive agreement regarding the declining catch status of rhino rays and generally supported catch and release as the more feasible mitigation approach for managing the fisheries. This study provides conservation context for the importance of certain spatial locations, especially southwestern Malaysian Borneo, as potential sanctuaries for various species of highly threatened rhino rays.

1460: Captive reproduction in Sand Tiger Sharks (Carcharias taurus) remains a rare event, with only a few successful live births reported worldwide. Following the 2022 birth of two pups at The Scientific Center Kuwait (TSCK), this study examined behavioural patterns and environmental conditions associated with reproductive activity among captive individuals. From March to June 2025, continuous behavioural monitoring of adult sharks (Bandar♂ and Bibi♀) was conducted using an integrated underwater camera system (Fathom Octopus) coupled with an AI-assisted motion tracking platform (SharkTrack) and complemented by citizen-science observations. Monthly water samples were collected and analysed for physicochemical and trace element parameters. Results showed that while most water quality metrics remained within acceptable limits, mean Total Petroleum Hydrocarbon (TPH) concentrations were elevated (155.14 ± 24.96 µg/L), surpassing regulatory thresholds. A significant decline in TPH coincided with the onset of mating behaviours, which exhibited clear temporal patterns where most breeding activity occurred between and p.m. and was less concentrated on specific weekdays (Saturday, Sunday, and Wednesday). These findings suggest that both environmental qualities, particularly TPH, and diel cycles may influence reproductive behaviour in captive C. taurus. This study provides one of the first non-invasive quantitative assessments linking environmental and behavioural parameters in captive C. taurus. It underscores the need for long-term monitoring and refined water management to optimize welfare and reproductive success in aquaria. Such evidence-based approaches are crucial for enhancing global ex situ conservation and husbandry practices for this critically endangered shark species.

1463: In Malaysia, trawl fisheries contribute nearly half of national fish landings and are among the primary contributors to the bycatch and mortality of sharks and rays. Despite their ecological and economic significance, fine-scale data on when and where elasmobranch bycatch occurs are largely lacking, constraining the development of effective management interventions. To address this data gap, electronic monitoring systems known as SharkCam were deployed on trawl vessels in Kuching, Miri and Sibu in Sarawak to document bycatch events with time- and GPS-stamped imagery. Over a one-year period, SharkCams installed on vessels recorded 1,578 bycatch events: 55.3% rays, 43.7% sharks, 0.6% wedgefish and guitarfish, and 0.5% other marine megafauna such as sea turtles and dolphins. Notably, the records included Critically Endangered Scalloped Hammerheads (Sphyrna lewini), four Bottlenose Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus australiae), three Broadnose Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus springeri), and three Bowmouth Guitarfish (Rhina ancylostoma); Endangered Whitespotted Whiprays (Maculabatis gerrardi); and Vulnerable Dwarf Whiprays (Brevitrygon heterura) and Indonesian Sharpnose Whiprays (Telatrygon biasa). Bycatch of Olive Ridley sea turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea) and Spinner dolphins (Stenella longirostris) was also documented. Preliminary analyses identified shark bycatch hotspots near Bruit Island in the Daro District and ray bycatch concentrated in coastal waters off Kuching. When extrapolated to Sarawak’s licensed trawl vessels, these observations suggest around 17,000 shark and ray bycatch events could occur annually. These findings provide the first fine-scale spatial insights into trawl-caught elasmobranchs in Sarawak and form the foundation for evidence-based mitigation measures and, ultimately, more sustainable fisheries in Malaysia.

1464: The bluntnose sixgill shark (Hexanchus griseus) is one of the largest extant chondrichthyans and among the most globally distributed deepwater predators, yet its life history across ontogeny remains poorly understood. Here, we integrate global occurrence records to examine ontogenetic distribution patterns, together with biologger data from adult sixgill sharks around Hawaiʻi to assess potential physiological constraints that may preclude neonates from occupying oceanic islands. The global distribution of H. griseus includes numerous seamounts and oceanic islands spanning the Indian, Atlantic, and Pacific Oceans. However, neonate and young-of-the-year records occur exclusively along continental shelves, slopes, and inland seas, with no verified neonates reported from oceanic islands or seamounts. These findings suggest a life history spanning entire ocean basins, with pupping and early development restricted to productive continental margins. Biologger data show that large sixgills around Hawaiʻi undertake diel vertical migrations between ~200–700 m, traversing thermal gradients from 5–16 °C, likely in pursuit of vertically migrating prey. Continuous body-temperature recordings reveal substantial thermal inertia, allowing adults to maintain gradual internal temperature changes throughout these migrations. Thermal modeling indicates that smaller neonates would experience far greater body-temperature fluctuations beyond their thermal optima under similar movements, exposing them to physiologically unfavorable conditions compared with nearshore neonates that experience narrow (<2 °C) temperature ranges in thermally stable nursery habitats. Collectively, these findings indicate an ontogenetic expansion from thermally stable continental-margin nurseries to deep habitats of oceanic islands and seamounts, linking continental and island deepwater ecosystems across ocean basins.

1469: Deepwater sharks are highly vulnerable to the effects of exploitation due to their relatively low productivity, with populations becoming rapidly depleted following intensive fishing. In this context, ongoing stock assessments are important to avoid over-exploitation. Within Australia’s Southern and Eastern Scalefish and Shark Fishery (SESSF), deepwater shark species are managed collectively as a basket under a single quota. Management is difficult due to challenging species-level identification and high unreported discards, meaning speciesspecific analytical assessments are not currently possible for most species. Additionally, substantial data quality improvement is unlikely given the low gross value of production. This study applied the FishPath Tool to explore potential assessments for these data-poor basket species, considering four alternate data approaches from the current aggregated “basket” approach to an indicator-species-only approach focusing on the Centrophoridae family. While species-level identification remains challenging, Centrophoridae are retained by fishers and can therefore be more reliably identified, are comparatively data-rich, and account for 80% of landings. Under the current “basket” approach (aggregated assessment treating all species as a single unit), only qualitative risk assessments or empirical indicator frameworks are possible. Two hypothetical approaches involving family disaggregation and inclusion of observer data expanded options to include life-history-based and integrated model-based assessments. The Centrophoridae family indicator-species-only approach demonstrated that age-structured integrated models could be applied using existing data. This study demonstrates the range of assessment options for data-poor “basket” species given alternate data approaches and incremental investments in improving data quality.

1470: Karimunjawa National Park (KJNP) in the northern Java Sea, Indonesia, is potentially a critical habitat for the critically endangered rhinorays (Glaucostegidae and Rhinidae), yet lacks targeted management for their protection. To address this, Elasmobranch Project Indonesia (EPI) has developed participatory approaches since 2022 to balance livelihood needs and species conservation. To understand local fisheries dynamics and fishers’ interaction with rhinorays, a baseline study involving fishers was conducted. Although adult rhinorays are highly valuable, most fishers expressed willingness to release juveniles (<5 kg) due to their low market value. Then these fishers show preference for size, quota, and/or seasonal schemes for future management. Building on this insight, EPI designed and piloted a locally tailored common-pool resource game to explore fishers’ behavioral responses toward rhinorays. The results indicated that community-based management — where fishers collaboratively discuss rules — produced higher compliance than top-down approaches. These findings informed an initiative involving fishers in population monitoring through a capture–mark–recapture program, where participants were compensated through a “Fisher Scientist” service-payment scheme. This initiative continues to supplement the future focus towards size and critical habitat management in order to align ecological findings with stakeholders’ view. Key lessons highlight the importance of aligning conservation activities with what fishers value — as voluntary reporting alone proved ineffective without clear local benefits. Building trust is vital, however it requires significant time. Collectively, these experiences guide EPI in developing a locally managed marine area (LMMA) framework for rhinorays, offering a scalable model for community-driven elasmobranch conservation in Indonesia and beyond.

1472: Launched in early 2020, the Stegostoma tigrinum Augmentation and Recovery (StAR) project has progressed from ideation to permitting to implementation and expansion from Indonesia to Thailand in a short years. The first project under the ReShark Initiative, StAR Indonesia aims to re-establish a genetically diverse breeding population of endangered Indo-Pacific leopard sharks in the protected waters of Raja Ampat by rewilding pups hatched from eggs that are imported from approved breeder facilities around the world. Importantly, this bold initiative is driven by a unique coalition of over partners in countries, benefitting from the diverse skills and knowledge base of large public aquariums, national and local government fisheries and coastal management agencies, shark scientists and conservationists. To date, the StAR project Indonesia has successfully imported over genetically-appropriate Stegostoma eggs into Indonesia and has released pups into the wild, with post-release monitoring (using acoustic and satellite telemetry and citizen science photo ID monitoring) confirming the rewilded pups are able to forage naturally and survive for at least months beyond release. The project has now trained young Indonesian shark aquarists and has a local outreach program that involves schoolchildren from Raja Ampat in sourcing prey items for the pups and visits to the two nurseries to learn about shark conservation. Guided by the IUCN “One Plan” approach, the StAR project has developed a methodology for combining ex situ and in situ conservation approaches that can inform similar initiatives currently being developed for other threatened elasmobranch species.

1473: Effective fisheries management is essential to ensure the sustainability of tuna and billfish fisheries by reducing the bycatch of non-target species. Silky sharks (Carcharhinus falciformis) are the most frequently caught shark species as bycatch in tuna fisheries. Due to limited data, conventional stock assessments are unfeasible, hindering the evaluation of their exploitation status and conservation and management measures (CMMs). We applied the Ecological Assessment of Sustainable Impacts of Fisheries (EASI-Fish) approach to quantify cumulative impacts from multiple fisheries on the vulnerability status of Atlantic silky shark in 2023 and tested the efficacy of alternative CMMs across major fisheries managed by the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas. Our results indicate high uncertainty in the vulnerability status, ranging from “increasingly vulnerable” when uncertainty in key fishery parameters is considered, to “most vulnerable” under the most precautionary settings. Industrial longline fisheries contribute most to fishing mortality due to high spatial overlap with the species’ distribution, while other fisheries (purse seine, gillnet, handline) play smaller but non-negligible roles. We estimated that avoidance measures would produce the greatest reductions in vulnerability among evaluated CMMs. Minimization and remediation measures— such as prohibiting wire-leaders in longliners and implementing best handling and release practices in purse seiners—would further contribute to silky shark conservation, particularly when combined. Our findings highlight critical data gaps—particularly in effort, catchability, and gear selectivity—where targeted research would most improve future assessments and provide a basis for developing evidence-based conservation advice for silky sharks in the Atlantic Ocean.

1475: The Great Eggcase Hunt is the Shark Trust’s flagship citizen science initiative, encouraging members of the public to report eggcases seen developing underwater, or those seen washed ashore, from all around the world. Running since 2003, this project has now received over 60,000 entries totalling over 580,000 eggcases, of which over 87% of eggcases are verified. This dataset covers over countries, with eggcases reported from over verified species, including records of over 3,500 ground-truthed, in-situ eggcases. This project provides a valuable insight into eggcase morphology, and the diversity and range of oviparous species, both improving scientific understanding, and engaging and educating the wider public. This project engages people from all walks of life, with participation ranging from ad-hoc finds, organised group events and dedicated, long term reporters. This presentation will highlight the wealth of data that can be harnessed from a long-term, global dataset, showing the strength of citizen science and the potential applications to both research and management, such as: the growth and development of the project over the last years; our understanding of eggcase morphology; application of this data to Environmental Impact Assessments, MPA processes and the Important Shark and Ray Area process; the influence of seasonality and weather events on both reporting and the number and species of eggcases washing ashore; and trends over time from key subsets.
Sharks and Community Scientists: The Power of Collective Action
1477: Estuarine ecosystems support diverse elasmobranch assemblages, yet their spatial organisation and movement connectivity remain poorly understood in temperate Europe. A key ecological question is how species differing in size and mobility partition heterogeneous estuarine areas and whether movement corridors maintain functional connectivity across the system. To address this, we combined stereo baited remote underwater videos (BRUVs) and acoustic telemetry in the Ría de Vigo, a productive embayment in northwest Spain shaped by riverine discharge and coastal upwelling. A network of receivers tracked tagged individuals: small-spotted catsharks (Scyliorhinus canicula, n = 71), undulate skates (Raja undulata, n = 70), and eagle rays (Myliobatis aquila, n = 92) while BRUV deployments across sites and two seasons (Summer vs Winter) quantified distribution and abundance. Elasmobranchs occurred in 43% of summer and 16% of winter BRUV deployments, with peaks in the inner Ría during summer (75% of sites) shifting to mid-estuary zones in winter. Elasmobranch sightings were higher in northern and shallower sectors. M. aquila dominated summer assemblages (28%), whereas S. canicula (37%) and R. undulata (20%) increased in winter. Hotspots were centred in the northern mid–inner area of the Ría. Telemetry results confirmed these spatial trends but revealed contrasting movement strategies: eagle rays showed size-dependent area use, small-spotted catsharks and undulate skates exhibited strong site fidelity. Together, both methods depict a spatially structured yet connected community, with inner and mid-Ría zones functioning as core habitats linked by species-specific movement corridors.

1481: Known as ‘the Galápagos of the Maldives,’ Fuvahmulah Atoll, a recently designated UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, has experienced a steep rise in dive tourism within the last decade due to improved acces s and awareness of its abundant shark and ray megafauna . Although t ourism increasingly finance s conservation , unregulated tourism contributes to the decline of sensitive species and ecosystems. S trategic management plans are being developed across the Maldives to safeguard marine ecosystems and support economic growth , but it is unclear if dive tourists are willing to contribute financially to conserve the biodiversity their tourism depends on . W e sought to inform policy design by examining tourists’ willingness to pay for increased conservation action on the atoll. In collaboration with Pelagic Divers Fuvahmulah , we conducted a stated preference survey to assess tourists’ environmental attitudes, willingness to pay for an entrance fee, and preferences for conservation measures proposed by the community. Virtually all (97%) tourists supported paying a one-time “Reserve” entrance fee at an average of US$58 per person. E ncounters with tiger sharks or pelagic threshers positively i nfluenced the amount tourists were willing to pay. V isitors to Fuvahmulah Atoll represent committed members of the dive community and highly value marine conservation . T heir financial support creates opportunities to safeguard biodiversity and ensure the sustainability of the nation’s largest industry.

1483: Marine ecosystems are under increasing pressure globally, underscoring the urgent need for effective, community-driven conservation strategies. Environmental education offers a powerful way to address this challenge by fostering awareness, responsibility, and long-term commitment to environmental protection among young people. Over the past decade, the Maldives Manta Conservation Programme (MMCP) has delivered the Moodhu Madharusaa Programme—an immersive marine education initiative implemented nationally wherever MMCP teams are based. MMCP’s outreach has reached over 4,500 individuals nationwide, with more than 1,000 Maldivians—many for the first time—gaining in-water experience through swimming, snorkelling, and diving. Since its inception, students across multiple atolls have completed the six-month Moodhu Madharusaa course, gaining hands-on experience and a deeper connection to the marine ecosystems that sustain their communities. To evaluate effectiveness, this study focused on Moodhu Madharusaa delivery in Baa Atoll (2018–2024), where MMCP maintains a permanent base enabling consistent implementation. Across five schools, students aged 12–15 participated in pre- and post-programme surveys assessing changes in environmental attitudes, behaviours, knowledge, and engagement. Statistical analyses using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and ordinal logistic regression revealed significant improvements in knowledge (W₁,₁₁₄ = 5089, p < 0.000001), attitudes (W₁,₁₂₁ = 5416, p < 0.0001), and behaviours (W₁,₁₂₁ = 4976.5, p = 0.002). Female students showed more positive attitudes (β = –0.28, p < 0.001), and older students demonstrated stronger environmental concern (β = 0.18, p < 0.001). These findings show that Moodhu Madharusaa effectively enhances ocean literacy and pro-environmental values among Maldivian youth, empowering a generation of ocean stewards.

1484: While BRUVs have long been used to study sharks, their application in the deep sea remains scarce and limited, and not always the same procedures apply. In the Azores, Portugal, research efforts have been developed in the recent years to deploy deep-sea BRUVs, with the objectives to test the effectiveness of this non-invasive tool to monitor deep-water sharks elasmobranch and to study their behavior in different contexts. While working in the deep sea creates additional challenges, they provide valuable insights into these little-known data-poor species. Over BRUVs videos, totaling hours of bottom recording time, have now been collected enabling us to observe species of deep-sea sharks, rays, and chimeras in their natural habitat. For some species that are not, or rarely, caught by local fishing gears and scientific surveys, BRUVs provide invaluable information on their distribution and relative abundance. Deployments also allowed us to document elasmobranchs behavior when exposed to different lights colors for bycatch mitigation purposes and to find the nursery area of one rare deepwater shark species. The current ongoing work aims at testing AI tools to fasten and ease the processing of BRUV videos. This presentation will explain these progress, main achievements and best guidelines identified to use BRUVs in the deep sea.

1485: The flapper skate, Dipturus intermedius, is a critically endangered species that has long been misidentified and reported as a single species together with D. batis, leading to inappropriate management measures and rapid declines of the populations in Northern Europe. Under a catch prohibition in European fisheries, no landings of flapper skate are allowed anymore, but interactions with fishers still occur when they unintentionally catch the skate while fishing for other (commercial) species. In the Portuguese Azores archipelago, D. intermedius is known to occur but very little data exist to assess its population status and vulnerability to local fisheries. To overcome this limitation, we applied a multi-disciplinary approach, combining fishers interviews, BRUVs and analyses of fishing observers and scientific survey data. Most of the fishers declared to have caught flapper skates, but rarely with hand lines, and more commonly with bottom longlines. While not all fishers were aware of the fishing prohibition applied to this species, most of them declared to release the skate anyway upon capture. In most cases, they said the skates were still clearly alive and vigorous when released, suggesting potential for high post-release survival. Fishers’ answers about the areas and depths where the skates were most commonly captured were consistent with results found using BRUVs, observer and survey data, highlighting the adequacy between local ecological knowledge and scientific knowledge. Fisher involvement in studies of vulnerable, data-poor species is highly valuable, providing complementary information to inform management, raise awareness, and aid in species conservation efforts.

1487: This study examines the ingestion of microplastics by the bentho-pelagic elasmobranch Squalus megalops along the southeastern coast of Gran Canaria (Canary Islands), with the aim of assessing its level of exposure to marine plastic pollution. A total of specimens were analyzed, of which 92% contained microplastic particles in their stomachs. Visual analyses revealed that most particles consisted of lines and fragments, with black, transparent, and blue being the most frequently observed colors. Micro-FTIR analysis confirmed the presence of both synthetic polymers (such as polyester and nylon) and semi-synthetic materials (including cellulose, rayon and azlon), indicating multiple potential sources of contamination, such as fishing gear and wastewater discharges. The oceanographic dynamics of the North Atlantic may contribute to the presence of microplastics in S. megalops. We find that the regional-scale oceanographic dynamics around the Canary Islands may help explain the high levels of microplastic exposure observed in the area where S. megalops specimens were captured. A particularly intense current branch recurrently flows between the southern coasts of Lanzarote, Fuerteventura, and Gran Canaria, forming a corridor that may collect microplastics from various sources, including wastewater discharge points along the coast. These findings represent the first known record of microplastic ingestion by S. megalops globally, as well as the first report of microplastic presence in elasmobranchs from this region of the Atlantic. Furthermore, the study underscores the importance of reinforcing conservation efforts, particularly for understudied elasmobranch species within the Canary Islands archipelago.

1491: Mozambique is a global hotspot for shark and ray biodiversity, with over species recorded to date. However, small-scale fisheries exert significant pressure on coastal populations, with 49% of Mozambique’s sharks and rays now globally threatened with extinction (IUCN Red List). Sharks and rays play a crucial role in Mozambican coastal communities, particularly in Zalala, which was identified as a key landing site for juveniles and threatened species in surveys conducted between 2018 and 2022, including the Critically Endangered scalloped hammerhead. Overexploitation of these species threatens marine ecosystems and local livelihoods. To address these challenges, we implemented the project “Assisting Community Fishers to Safeguard their Livelihoods and Conserve Shark and Ray Populations at Zalala Beach, Mozambique”. This initiative explored the intrinsic value of fishing for community well-being and generated potential solutions—80% of which were community-driven. Participatory processes fostered strong local interest in collaborative governance, ensuring that management measures are equitable and effective in maintaining healthy shark and ray populations. As a result, fishers have increased awareness of regulations and the ecological roles of sharks and rays and understand how overfishing affects their livelihoods. The project reinforced that sustainable fishing does not prohibit fishing but promotes long-term resource availability. This approach aligns with REPMAR (2020), which empowers artisanal fishers to comanage fishing areas. By enhancing collaboration among stakeholders and engaging Zalala Beach communities in decision-making, we continue to foster sustainable resource use and strengthen fishers’ sense of responsibility, ultimately empowering them as active stewards of their marine environment.

1492: As countries strive to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030, assessing how well Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) encompass critical habitats for sharks, rays, and chimaeras is essential. This synthesis compares Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) delineated in the Central and South American Pacific and Asia, emphasizing species coverage and ISRA-MPA overlap. Within the Central and South American Pacific, ISRAs were identified covering 3% (~5.7 million km²) of the region and 50% (121 species) of known regional diversity. In Asia, ISRAs were identified covering 15.6% (~1 million km²) of the region and 30% (97 species) of diversity. In both regions, most delineations were based on Vulnerability (Criterion A) and Reproductive Areas (Subcriterion C1), especially for large charismatic species such as Scalloped Hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), Whale Shark (Rhincodon typus), and manta rays (Mobula spp). ISRAs in both regions are concentrated in coastal habitats, while deepwater habitats and species were underrepresented due to limited data availability. ISRAs in the Central and South American Pacific had higher overlap with MPAs (15.6% compared to 5.4% in Asia) and no-take zones (7.3% compared to 2.8%). However, MPA effectiveness is a concern with 42% of Central and South American Pacific MPAs lacking management plans and only 11% including chondrichthyans as conservation targets. Integrating ISRAs into 30×30 strategies, expanding no-take areas, and improving data for poorly represented taxa are urgent priorities for regional chondrichthyan conservation.

1495: Pelagic sharks are apex predators that structure oceanic ecosystems through their vertical and horizontal movements across vast spatial scales. This study synthesizes multi-species tagging data using pop-up satellite archival tags (PSATs) to investigate diel vertical migration (DVM) patterns and their environmental drivers across major pelagic shark taxa in the northwestern Pacific Ocean. Satellite telemetry data from shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus), longfin mako (Isurus paucus), bigeye thresher (Alopias superciliosus), megamouth shark (Megachasma pelagios), scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini) and whale shark (Rhincodon typus) reveal pronounced species-specific depth preferences strongly linked to body size, thermal tolerance, and prey field distribution.All species exhibited distinct diel depth oscillations, occupying epipelagic waters (<200 m) during nighttime and descending to mesopelagic zones (300–800 m) during daytime, presumably to exploit the deep scattering layer (DSL). Notably, individual megamouth sharks displayed extended deep dives exceeding 1,500–1,900 m, encountering temperatures below 3°C—behavior that suggests active thermoregulation and utilization of deep mesopelagic resources. In contrast, bigeye threshers and longfin mako demonstrated intermediate DVM amplitudes, likely reflecting a balance between energetic optimization and predator avoidance strategies. These findings underscore that pelagic sharks exhibit multidimensional habitat connectivity that transcends national jurisdictions, with their vertical movement behaviors influencing both vulnerability to fishing gear and their functional roles in pelagic food webs. Incorporating vertical habitat data into spatial management frameworks— including dynamic ocean management strategies and depth-restricted bycatch mitigation measures—will be essential for sustaining these populations under accelerating ocean warming and progressive deoxygenation.

1496: The evolution of marine fisheries has broadly influenced the ecology, distribution and abundance of coastal elasmobranchs. However, quantifying these interactions remains a challenge due to the scarcity of historical records. Fishers' local ecological knowledge (LEK) is an essential tool in fisheries research, providing an avenue to regain scarce information on rare or cryptic species and contextualise modern observations and trends. LEK was collected from semi-structured interviews with commercial, recreational and charter fishers to better understand the ecology and temporal population trends for the Critically Endangered angelshark (Squatina squatina) within Wales, United Kingdom. Questions were designed to identify fisher perceptions of socio-economic, ecological and legislative factors that drove changes in fishing effort for vessels operating within the ‘Welsh Zone’ between 1968 and 2019. Understanding how fleet-wide spatiotemporal changes to fishing effort and capacity within commercial, recreational and charter fisheries have influenced historical records and sightings of S. squatina is an important consideration for assessing its status in Wales and designing appropriate actions to safeguard the species. Our findings identify structural changes to fisheries in Wales and key driving factors that likely decreased fishers' likelihood of encountering S. squatina over a year period. Therefore, we suggest recent published estimates of population declines may be overstated. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of quantifying and incorporating changes in fishing effort at a regional scale into future modelling approaches for elasmobranchs and advocate for the increased consideration of LEK in the development of management strategies.

1497: The Lombok Strait, connecting the Bali Sea to the Indian Ocean, represents one of Indonesia’s major throughflow corridors, facilitating the exchange of water masses between the Pacific and Indian Oceans. This strait partially overlaps with the Nusa Penida Marine Protected Area (MPA) and has been identified as a key fishing ground for the Pelagic Thresher Shark (Alopias pelagicus) during the period from July to October. A total of 1,823 individuals were recorded from longline fisheries operating in the area and landed at Pengalon Beach, comprising 1,500 females, males, and unidentified specimens. Among the females, (approximately 10%) were pregnant, containing embryos, while were identified as neonates based on abdominal dissections conducted by fisheries observers. Species distribution modeling using MaxEnt, incorporating bathymetry, chlorophyll-a concentration, and sea surface temperature (SST), indicated that A. pelagicus exhibits a higher probability of occurrence in areas shallower than m, with chlorophyll-a concentrations between 0.2 and 0.4 mg m⁻³ and SST ranging from 29.8°C to 30°C. Additionally, the presence of seamounts at depths of 300–500 m may contribute to suitable habitat conditions. These findings suggest that the Lombok Strait functions as a potential gestation habitat for the Pelagic Thresher Shark. Strengthened species-specific management measures, regulatory enforcement, and possible expansion of the existing MPA are recommended to ensure the protection of this critical habitat in Indonesian waters.

1498: Improving our understanding of elasmobranch biodiversity and ecosystems along Central Africa’s poorly described coast is essential for identifying and protecting key habitats. In Gabon and Congo, long term catch monitoring of commercial fisheries and description of the fishing techniques including selectivity of the fishing gears, fishing efforts and fishing zones bring valuable information. Moreover, recent research combining participatory catch monitoring, stomach content and stable isotope analyses has revealed the nursery role of southern coastal waters for juvenile Sphyrna lewini (scalloped hammerhead) and Carcharhinus limbatus (blacktip shark), two globally threatened species frequently caught in fisheries in Mayumba region in Gabon. At the same time, documenting the main threats to these species including habitat loss, target and non-target capture in fisheries, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, coastal and offshore petrochemical exploitation, and wildlife trafficking has been critical for guiding management actions. The results of this work have informed national regulations, marine spatial planning and fisheries management plans aimed at mitigating pressures on shark and ray populations. Recognising the cultural and economic importance of sharks to coastal communities is critical for designing realistic and equitable conservation measures. In Gabon, livelihoods often depend on shark catches, creating challenges for compliance with new regulations. Research integrating ecological findings with local perspectives has guided the formulation of national policies, including bans on targeted elasmobranch fisheries and fin exports, alongside efforts to strengthen community participation and enforcement capacity.

1499: Small-scale fisheries are essential for food security and livelihoods, yet many face increasing pressure from overfishing and limited community involvement in management. In Sri Lanka, fishers often lack access to clear, culturally relevant information about how management practices support long-term sustainability. Addressing this communication gap is crucial for raising awareness and encouraging participation in sustainable fisheries management. An animated educational video was created to communicate key concepts including the current state of fisheries, the impacts of overfishing, and the role of management in securing future livelihoods. Through visual storytelling and locally relevant examples, the video translates complex scientific ideas into understandable and engaging content for fishing communities. This study explores how exposure to information about fisheries management through an animated video influences (i) fishers’ baseline knowledge and perceptions of overfishing and management, and (ii) willingness to participate in sustainable fishing practices. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach as an educational tool, pre- and post-exposure surveys are used to assess community knowledge, perceptions, and interest in learning more about sustainable fishing practices. Visual storytelling has the potential to be an effective medium for closing knowledge gaps and shifting perspectives around fisheries management. It provides an engaging, low-cost, and scalable tool for community education and outreach, with the capacity to foster stronger participation in sustainable fishing practices.
